item.title: San Francisco Viewpoints and Overlooks
item.description: Everyone drives up Twin Peaks, but the locals climb the little rock knob just below it called Tank Hill for the same view with none of the tour buses. Six
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Viewpoints and Overlooks

Everyone drives up Twin Peaks, but the locals climb the little rock knob just below it called Tank Hill for the same view with none of the tour buses. Six San Francisco overlooks with the whole city at your feet.

Tank Hill — Clarendon Heights. A rocky knob just below Twin Peaks with a sweeping view from the bridges to downtown, a locals' sunset spot with room to sit. Walk up from Belgrave Avenue.

Twin Peaks — The two hills at the geographic center of the city, the postcard panorama straight down Market Street to the bay. Windy and busy, but the view earns it. Go at dawn to beat the buses.

Bernal Heights Hill — Bernal Heights. A grassy off leash summit with a full turn of the southeast city, dogs everywhere and the fog spilling over Twin Peaks across the way. The neighborhood living room.

Corona Heights Park — Castro. A bare red chert outcrop jutting above the Castro for a clean downtown and bay view with no trees in the way. Short steep climb, big payoff.

Grandview Park — Golden Gate Heights. A sand and cypress summit reached by the 16th Avenue tiled steps, a hidden view over the Sunset to the ocean. Two staircases and you are on top.

Billy Goat Hill — Glen Park. A grassy hill with a rope swing and a wide eastern view, the swing arcing out over the city a local rite of passage. Bring your nerve.

Six at the top: Tank Hill, Twin Peaks, Bernal, Corona Heights, Grandview, and Billy Goat Hill. Which view is your favorite?

item.title: San Francisco Hidden Staircase Walks
item.description: A San Francisco staircase in the Sunset is a 163 step mosaic mural of the sea and the stars, built by hand by the whole neighborhood. Five hidden stairways
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Hidden Staircase Walks

A San Francisco staircase in the Sunset is a 163 step mosaic mural of the sea and the stars, built by hand by the whole neighborhood. Five hidden stairways that turn a walk into a climb.

16th Avenue Tiled Steps — Golden Gate Heights. A 163 step mosaic of the sea, moon, and sun flowing up the hillside, made by neighbors and artists, with Grandview Park at the top. The most photographed stairs in the city.

Filbert Steps — Telegraph Hill. Wooden stairs winding down through gardens under Coit Tower, wild parrots overhead and the bay straight ahead. The Grace Marchant garden lines the whole descent.

Lyon Street Steps — Pacific Heights. A grand staircase past the mansions with the Palace of Fine Arts and the bay laid out below, a favorite of runners doing repeats. Views the whole way up.

Hidden Garden Steps — Inner Sunset. A second tiled mosaic staircase over on 16th Avenue, a ceramic ribbon of flowers and creatures, quieter than its famous neighbor. The locals' one.

Vulcan Stairway — Corona Heights. A leafy stairway lined with cottages and gardens tucked between Ord and Levant, a hidden green world a block from the Castro. Feels like a secret.

Five to climb: 16th Avenue Tiled Steps, Filbert, Lyon, Hidden Garden, and Vulcan. Which staircase first?

item.title: City Hikes Hidden Inside San Francisco
item.description: In the dead center of San Francisco there is a dripping eucalyptus cloud forest most residents have never walked into, silent and green a block off the fre
item.content:encoded:
City Hikes Hidden Inside San Francisco

In the dead center of San Francisco there is a dripping eucalyptus cloud forest most residents have never walked into, silent and green a block off the freeway. Five hikes hidden inside the city.

Mount Sutro — Inner Sunset. A misty eucalyptus forest laced with soft trails in the middle of the city, fog dripping off the branches and the traffic gone silent. Enter from the Stanyan or Medical Center gates.

Lands End — Outer Richmond. The Coastal Trail around the city's wild northwest corner, cypress tunnels, shipwrecks at low tide, and the Sutro Baths ruins. The best walk in San Francisco, hands down.

Glen Canyon — Glen Park. A rugged creek canyon with rock outcrops and red tailed hawks, wild and steep right off the BART line. The city's hidden backcountry.

Batteries to Bluffs — Presidio. A short steep coastal trail past old gun batteries to a pocket beach under the Golden Gate, wildflowers in spring and the bridge overhead. Stairs and big views.

Mount Davidson — Miraloma. The highest point in the city topped by a hundred foot cross and a eucalyptus forest, a foggy summit loop with a downtown view when it clears. The quiet giant.

Five hidden in the city: Mount Sutro, Lands End, Glen Canyon, Batteries to Bluffs, and Mount Davidson. Which trail surprised you?

item.title: San Francisco Museums
item.description: Under a single living roof in Golden Gate Park sits an aquarium, a planetarium, and a rainforest you climb through inside a glass dome. Six San Francisco m
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Museums

Under a single living roof in Golden Gate Park sits an aquarium, a planetarium, and a rainforest you climb through inside a glass dome. Six San Francisco museums worth the day.

California Academy of Sciences — Golden Gate Park. An aquarium, a planetarium, and a four story rainforest dome under a living roof, penguins and a coral reef and an albino alligator. A full day for all ages.

de Young Museum — Golden Gate Park. American art and global textiles in a copper clad building, with a free observation tower for a full turn over the park and the city. Go up the tower even if you skip the galleries.

Legion of Honor — Lincoln Park. A neoclassical palace of European art above the ocean, Rodin's Thinker in the courtyard and the Golden Gate through the colonnade. The most beautiful setting of any museum in the city.

Exploratorium — Pier 15. Hundreds of hands on science exhibits on the Embarcadero, a playground for curious brains of every age, plus a glass Bay Observatory. Touch everything.

SFMOMA — SoMa. Seven floors of modern and contemporary art with a free ground floor and a living wall on the terrace. The Richard Serra you walk through is worth the trip alone.

Walt Disney Family Museum — Presidio. The story of Walt himself in a Presidio barracks, early animation, the original Disneyland model, and the Golden Gate out the window. A charmer even for skeptics.

Six for the day: Cal Academy, de Young, Legion of Honor, Exploratorium, SFMOMA, and the Disney Museum. Which one first?

item.title: San Francisco Half Moon Bay and the Coastside (Peninsula)
item.description: Just off Pillar Point sits Mavericks, a big wave surf break where winter swells can top 50 feet and the world's best surfers come to test their nerve. Six
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Half Moon Bay and the Coastside (Peninsula)

Just off Pillar Point sits Mavericks, a big wave surf break where winter swells can top 50 feet and the world's best surfers come to test their nerve. Six stops for a Half Moon Bay coastside day.

Pillar Point Harbor — Princeton by the Sea. The working fishing harbor and gateway to the Mavericks break, crab boats, a bluff trail out to the point, and calm water for a paddle. Watch the surfers from the cliff in winter.

Sam's Chowder House — 4210 N Cabrillo Hwy. The coastside seafood institution with a deck over the water, a Maine style lobster roll that draws lines and a proper clam chowder. Reserve for sunset.

Barbara's Fishtrap — 281 Capistrano Rd. A ramshackle Princeton seafood shack right over the harbor, fried everything and a bowl of chowder, cash and a wait. The unfussy classic.

Half Moon Bay Brewing Company — 390 Capistrano Rd. A waterfront brewpub with fire pits and its own beer, fish tacos and a heat lamp patio facing the harbor. The easy hangout after the beach.

Half Moon Bay State Beach — Half Moon Bay. Four miles of sand with a paved Coastside Trail on the bluff, tide pools, and pumpkin fields behind for the October rush. The long walk with the ocean beside you.

Pigeon Point Light Station — Pescadero. One of the tallest lighthouses on the West Coast at 115 feet, a hostel at its base and tide pools below, twenty minutes down the coast. The postcard finish to the day.

Six for the coastside: Pillar Point, Sam's, Barbara's, HMB Brewing, the State Beach, and Pigeon Point. Which stop first?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Parks and Hikes (Peninsula)
item.description: At the end of a long reflecting pool on the Peninsula stands a Roman style temple most people never find, built to mark where Yosemite's water finally reac
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Parks and Hikes (Peninsula)

At the end of a long reflecting pool on the Peninsula stands a Roman style temple most people never find, built to mark where Yosemite's water finally reaches the Bay Area. Five Peninsula parks and trails worth the drive.

Pulgas Water Temple — Redwood City. A hidden neoclassical temple at the end of a reflecting pool, marking where the Hetch Hetchy aqueduct delivers Sierra water after a 160 mile journey. Quiet, free, and surreal.

Sawyer Camp Trail — San Mateo. A paved six mile shoreline trail along Crystal Springs Reservoir past the 600 year old Jepson Laurel, flat and open to bikes and strollers. The Peninsula's main artery.

Windy Hill — Portola Valley. A grassy double summit with hang gliders launching off the top and a full turn of a view from the bay to the ocean, oak canyons on the climb. Earn the ridge.

Purisima Creek Redwoods — Half Moon Bay. A shaded redwood canyon dropping toward the coast, fern lined switchbacks and creek crossings, cool on the hottest day. The hidden redwood hike.

Edgewood Park — Redwood City. A serpentine grassland that erupts in wildflowers every spring, rare native blooms and butterflies on an easy loop. Go in April for the color.

Five on the Peninsula: Pulgas Water Temple, Sawyer Camp, Windy Hill, Purisima Creek, and Edgewood. Which trail first?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Landmarks and Things to Do (San Jose)
item.description: Sarah Winchester kept builders working on her San Jose mansion around the clock for 36 years, leaving 160 rooms, doors that open onto walls, and staircases
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Landmarks and Things to Do (San Jose)

Sarah Winchester kept builders working on her San Jose mansion around the clock for 36 years, leaving 160 rooms, doors that open onto walls, and staircases that climb to the ceiling. Five San Jose stops beyond the tech.

Winchester Mystery House — 525 S Winchester Blvd. The rifle heiress's 160 room Victorian maze, built nonstop for 36 years, with stairs to nowhere and doors that open onto thin air. Take the flashlight tour.

San Jose Municipal Rose Garden — Naglee Ave. Five and a half acres of more than 3500 rose bushes in a beloved neighborhood park, peak bloom in May, free and fragrant. Bring a picnic.

The Tech Interactive — 201 S Market St. A downtown hands on science and tech museum, a maker lab, an IMAX dome, and exhibits kids can break and rebuild. A full rainy day.

San Pedro Square Market — 87 N San Pedro St. A downtown food hall built around the 1797 Peralta Adobe, the oldest building in San Jose, tacos to oysters under one roof with live music. Graze and stay.

Japantown — Jackson Street. One of only three Japantowns left in the country, family run since before the war, tofu makers and taco shops and Obon in summer. Walk it hungry.

Five beyond the tech: Winchester Mystery House, the Rose Garden, the Tech, San Pedro Square, and Japantown. Which one first?

item.title: San Francisco Grand Gardens and Estates (Peninsula and South Bay)
item.description: Filoli is a 654 acre Gilded Age estate south of the city whose formal gardens and mansion you may recognize as the opening shot of Dynasty. Five grand Bay
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Grand Gardens and Estates (Peninsula and South Bay)

Filoli is a 654 acre Gilded Age estate south of the city whose formal gardens and mansion you may recognize as the opening shot of Dynasty. Five grand Bay Area gardens and estates to wander.

Filoli — 86 Canada Rd, Woodside. A 1917 country estate with sixteen acres of formal gardens, a grand house, and orchards, the camellias and roses in spring drawing crowds. Give it a half day. @filoliestate

Hakone Estate and Gardens — 21000 Big Basin Way, Saratoga. One of the oldest Japanese gardens in the hemisphere, koi ponds, a moon bridge, and a tea house on a wooded hillside. Serene and over a century old. @hakonegardens

Elizabeth Gamble Garden — 1431 Waverley St, Palo Alto. A historic house and two and a half acres of gardens run by volunteers, roses and a wisteria arbor, free to stroll. The hidden Palo Alto retreat.

Montalvo Arts Center — 15400 Montalvo Rd, Saratoga. A 1912 Mediterranean villa and arboretum in the Saratoga hills, gardens, trails, and an artist residency, plus summer concerts. Culture and nature in one.

Allied Arts Guild — 75 Arbor Rd, Menlo Park. A 1929 Spanish colonial complex of artist studios, courtyards, and gardens tucked off the road, a tea room and shops among the fountains. A quiet time capsule.

Five to wander: Filoli, Hakone, Gamble Garden, Montalvo, and Allied Arts Guild. Which garden first?

item.title: San Francisco Walkable South Bay Downtowns
item.description: You can spend a whole afternoon on foot in downtown Los Gatos, browsing shops and cafes with the creek trail a block over, and never move your car. Five wa
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Walkable South Bay Downtowns

You can spend a whole afternoon on foot in downtown Los Gatos, browsing shops and cafes with the creek trail a block over, and never move your car. Five walkable South Bay downtowns worth a stroll.

Downtown Los Gatos — Santa Cruz Ave. A leafy main street of boutiques, cafes, and wine bars with the Los Gatos Creek Trail a block away and the foothills rising behind. Park once and wander.

Saratoga Village — Big Basin Way. A tiny historic strip of tasting rooms, patios, and a bakery at the mouth of the mountains, quaint and slow. Pair it with Hakone up the hill.

Willow Glen — Lincoln Ave, San Jose. A neighborhood main street of independent shops and restaurants with a small town feel inside the city, holiday lights and a walkable mile. The local favorite.

Downtown Campbell — Campbell Ave. A revived brick main street with a big farmers market, breweries, and the Ainsley House, plus the Los Gatos Creek Trail through town. Easygoing and fun.

Downtown Mountain View — Castro St. A buzzing restaurant row of every cuisine steps from the Caltrain, patios and a plaza and the best variety in the South Bay. Come hungry.

Five to stroll: Los Gatos, Saratoga, Willow Glen, Campbell, and Mountain View. Which downtown is your favorite?

item.title: San Francisco Sausalito and the Marin Waterfront
item.description: In a cavernous Sausalito warehouse left from the wartime shipyards sits a working hydraulic model of the entire San Francisco Bay, the size of a couple of
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Sausalito and the Marin Waterfront

In a cavernous Sausalito warehouse left from the wartime shipyards sits a working hydraulic model of the entire San Francisco Bay, the size of a couple of football fields, free to walk. Five stops for a Sausalito waterfront day.

Bay Model Visitor Center — 2100 Bridgeway. A free, room sized working model of the whole bay and delta built by the Army Corps in a WWII shipyard building, water actually flowing through it. Surreal and educational.

Bar Bocce — 1250 Bridgeway. A waterfront pizza and cocktail hangout with a bocce court and a little beach, wood fired pies and a fire pit over the water. The sunset spot. @barbocce

Scoma's Sausalito — 588 Bridgeway. A pier to plate seafood institution right on the water, cracked crab and cioppino with ferries drifting past. The dressed up waterfront meal.

Fish — 350 Harbor Dr. A dockside seafood shack where you order at the window and eat at picnic tables over the harbor, wild salmon and crab rolls, cash only. The unpretentious classic.

Sausalito houseboats — Gate 6 1/2 Road. The famous floating home community of hundreds of quirky houseboats, walk the docks and gawk at the architecture. A whole neighborhood on the water.

Five on the Sausalito waterfront: the Bay Model, Bar Bocce, Scoma's, Fish, and the houseboats. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Japantown
item.description: San Francisco's Japantown is among the last handful left in the country, a few square blocks of ramen counters, mochi shops, and a towering peace pagoda. E
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Japantown

San Francisco's Japantown is among the last handful left in the country, a few square blocks of ramen counters, mochi shops, and a towering peace pagoda. Eight stops to eat and browse your way through Japantown.

Marufuku Ramen — Kinokuniya Building, 1581 Webster St. The Japan Center ramen counter with the hour long line, a silky Hakata tonkotsu with hair thin noodles. Put your name on the list and browse the mall. @marufukuramenofficial

Hinodeya Ramen — 1737 Buchanan St. A modern shop known for a lighter dashi based broth, a delicate alternative to the heavy tonkotsu, walk in only. The refined bowl. @hinodeya_sf

Isobune Sushi — 1737 Post St. Conveyor belt sushi where little wooden boats float your nigiri around the bar, a kitschy Japan Center classic for decades. Grab plates as they drift by.

On the Bridge — 1581 Webster St. A tiny counter on the covered bridge between the malls doing Japanese style pasta and omurice, anime posters on the walls. Order the omurice and watch the crowd.

Belly Good Cafe and Crepes — 1737 Post St. A crepe window in the Kintetsu mall folding sweet and savory Japanese style crepes to order, matcha and red bean the move. Dessert on the go. @happy_face_crepe

Nijiya Market — 1737 Post St. A Japanese grocery for fresh sushi, mochi, and snacks, grab a bento and eat it out in the plaza. The pantry of Japantown.

Kinokuniya Books — 1581 Webster St. A two floor Japanese bookstore of manga, magazines, art books, and stationery, easy to lose an hour in. Anime heaven.

Japan Center and Peace Plaza — Post St at Buchanan. The malls and the five tiered peace pagoda gifted by Osaka in 1968, cherry blossoms in April and festivals all year. The heart of it all.

Eight in Japantown: Marufuku, Hinodeya, Isobune, On the Bridge, Belly Good, Nijiya, Kinokuniya, and the Peace Plaza. Which first?

item.title: San Francisco Independent Bookstores
item.description: City Lights published Allen Ginsberg's Howl in 1956 and then won the obscenity trial that made it legal, and the Beat landmark still sells books on Columbu
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Independent Bookstores

City Lights published Allen Ginsberg's Howl in 1956 and then won the obscenity trial that made it legal, and the Beat landmark still sells books on Columbus today. Eight San Francisco bookstores worth a browse.

City Lights Booksellers — 261 Columbus Ave. The Beat Generation landmark and publisher since 1953, three floors of books and a poetry room upstairs, a literary shrine you can shop. Buy something upstairs.

Green Apple Books — 506 Clement St. A creaky Inner Richmond warren of new and used since 1967, floors that tilt and shelves to the ceiling. The lose yourself for hours store.

Dog Eared Books — 900 Valencia St. A beloved Mission shop of new, used, and remaindered books with a sharp local and queer section. The neighborhood favorite.

The Booksmith — 1644 Haight St. The Haight Street independent since 1976, a strong events calendar and a curated front table, counterculture in the stacks. Catch an author night.

Omnivore Books — 3885 Cesar Chavez St. A jewel box shop devoted entirely to food and cookbooks, new, used, and rare, with author dinners and a cult following. Chef heaven. @omnivorebooks

Bird and Beckett — 653 Chenery St. A Glen Park indie of books and records that has hosted live jazz every week since 2002, a bookstore that swings. Catch a Friday set. @bird.beckett

Fabulosa Books — 489 Castro St. The Castro's LGBTQ and general interest bookstore, warm and community minded, the shop that mails banned books to red states. Buy local, do good.

Borderlands Books — 1740 Haight St. A science fiction, fantasy, and horror specialist in the Haight, fiercely curated with a cafe next door, a genre reader's clubhouse. The genre one.

Eight to browse: City Lights, Green Apple, Dog Eared, the Booksmith, Omnivore, Bird and Beckett, Fabulosa, and Borderlands. Where do you buy your next read?

item.title: San Francisco Pacifica Beach Day (Peninsula)
item.description: Pacifica is home to the only Taco Bell in the world with a beachfront patio, a fire pit, and a walk up window for surfers, unironically the prettiest fast
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Pacifica Beach Day (Peninsula)

Pacifica is home to the only Taco Bell in the world with a beachfront patio, a fire pit, and a walk up window for surfers, unironically the prettiest fast food on earth. Eight stops for a Pacifica beach day.

Taco Bell Cantina — 5200 Coast Hwy. The famous beachfront Taco Bell right on Linda Mar Beach, a fire pit, beer and freezes, and a walk up window for surfers straight off the sand. Order a Baja Blast and sit on the wall.

Linda Mar Beach — Pacifica. A long gentle surf beach that is the Bay Area's favorite spot to learn, board rentals and lessons right there, the fog burning off by midday. Beginner waves and bonfires.

Nick's Rockaway — 100 Rockaway Beach Ave. An oceanfront institution on Rockaway Beach since the fifties, breakfast to dinner with the surf out the window and a lounge that time forgot. Right on the water.

Puerto 27 — 525 Crespi Dr. A bright Peruvian kitchen near Linda Mar, ceviche and pisco sours and lomo saltado, a step up dinner after the beach. Book a window table.

Gorilla BBQ — 2145 Coast Hwy. A roadside barbecue joint smoking brisket and ribs out of a bright orange train car parked on the highway, weekends only until it sells out. Line up for the tri tip.

A Grape in the Fog — Rockaway Beach Plaza. A cozy wine bar in the Rockaway pocket with flights, light bites, and live music, the grown up stop after the beach. Watch the fog roll in with a glass.

Rockaway Beach — Pacifica. A dramatic pocket cove of dark sand and jagged bluffs with a paved promenade and tide pools, quieter than Linda Mar. The scenic walk.

Mori Point — Pacifica. A GGNRA headland of bluff trails and spring wildflowers above the sea, the dramatic walk out to the point over Rockaway. Hike to the overlook.

Eight for the Pacifica day: Taco Bell Cantina, Linda Mar, Nick's, Puerto 27, Gorilla BBQ, A Grape in the Fog, Rockaway Beach, and Mori Point. Where do you post up?

item.title: San Francisco Daly City and Peninsula Filipino Food
item.description: Daly City has the largest Filipino population of any city in the country, and the tapsilog and lechon here rival anything in Manila. Eight Peninsula stops
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Daly City and Peninsula Filipino Food

Daly City has the largest Filipino population of any city in the country, and the tapsilog and lechon here rival anything in Manila. Eight Peninsula stops for Filipino food.

Tselogs — 6860 Mission St, Daly City. The silog specialist, tapsilog and longsilog with garlic rice and a fried egg, breakfast all day and a cult following. The morning after cure.

Lucky Chances — 1700 Hillside Blvd, Daly City. A 24 hour Filipino diner inside the casino, kare kare and crispy pata at 3am, the round the clock institution. Go late, go hungry.

Isla Restaurant — 448 San Mateo Ave, San Bruno. A modern Filipino kitchen for sizzling sisig and kamayan feasts eaten by hand off banana leaves, celebratory and generous. Book the boodle fight.

Kuya's Asian Cuisine — 460 San Mateo Ave, San Bruno. A San Bruno favorite for lumpia, pancit, and lechon kawali, warm service and big plates. The reliable family feast.

Russ Fam Kitchen — 1216 Hillside Blvd, Daly City. A family run Filipino fusion spot on Hillside, silogs and rice bowls with a modern twist, small and warm. The neighborhood newcomer worth knowing.

Chibog — Daly City. A local favorite for Filipino comfort plates and lumpia, generous and cheap, the kind of spot with a line of regulars. Order family style.

Fil-Am Cuisine — Daly City. A turo turo steam table of Filipino classics, adobo, kaldereta, and pancit by the scoop, point and eat. The everyday feast.

The Original Kadok's — Daly City. The fried chicken and Filipino comfort spot locals swear by, crackly chicken and sweet spaghetti the kids love. The takeout staple.

Eight for Filipino: Tselogs, Lucky Chances, Isla, Kuya's, Russ Fam, Chibog, Fil-Am, and Kadok's. Whose lumpia wins?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Golden Gate Park (SF)
item.description: There has been a herd of American bison living in the middle of San Francisco, in Golden Gate Park, since 1891, and most visitors walk right past them. Eig
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Golden Gate Park (SF)

There has been a herd of American bison living in the middle of San Francisco, in Golden Gate Park, since 1891, and most visitors walk right past them. Eight Golden Gate Park stops beyond the museums.

The Bison Paddock — Golden Gate Park. A small herd of American bison grazing a paddock near the park's west end, here since 1891, an only in San Francisco sight. Bring binoculars and go early.

Japanese Tea Garden — 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Dr. The oldest public Japanese garden in the country, from the 1894 World's Fair, koi ponds, a drum bridge, and the birthplace of the fortune cookie. Tea and quiet.

Conservatory of Flowers — 100 John F Kennedy Dr. A gleaming white Victorian glass palace from 1879, the oldest in the Americas, dripping with orchids and tropical plants inside. The photo everyone takes.

San Francisco Botanical Garden — 1199 Ninth Ave. Fifty five acres of gardens from cloud forest to redwoods in Strybing Arboretum, magnolias blooming in winter. Wander for hours.

Stow Lake — Golden Gate Park. The park's boating lake wrapping Strawberry Hill, rent a pedal boat, walk to Huntington Falls, and climb to the summit view. The classic park afternoon.

Dutch Windmills and Tulip Garden — Golden Gate Park. Two restored Dutch windmills at the park's ocean end with the Queen Wilhelmina tulip garden blazing in spring. The surprise at the far west edge.

Music Concourse — Golden Gate Park. The sunken plaza of fountains and pollarded trees between the de Young and Cal Academy, free summer band concerts at the old bandshell. The park's living room.

National AIDS Memorial Grove — Golden Gate Park. A hushed dell of redwoods and stone set aside as a living memorial, benches and inscriptions among the ferns. The park's quiet heart.

Eight in the park: the Bison Paddock, Tea Garden, Conservatory, Botanical Garden, Stow Lake, the Windmills, Music Concourse, and the AIDS Memorial Grove. Which corner first?

item.title: San Francisco Point Reyes Station and West Marin Food (North Bay)
item.description: In the Bay Area's own oyster country, Point Reyes Station is a walkable ranch town where a beloved bakery has fired sourdough in a wood oven since 2000 and
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Point Reyes Station and West Marin Food (North Bay)

In the Bay Area's own oyster country, Point Reyes Station is a walkable ranch town where a beloved bakery has fired sourdough in a wood oven since 2000 and the whole main drag fits in a few blocks. Eight stops in the town of Point Reyes Station.

Brickmaiden Breads — 40 Fourth St. The tiny bakery that supplies the whole town, wood fired sourdough and pastries from a Fourth Street kitchen, sold out most afternoons. Come early for a loaf.

Bovine Bakery — 11315 Highway 1. The morning line for organic scones, morning buns, and strong coffee, the first stop for every West Marin day. Get there before the buns go.

Toby's Feed Barn — 11250 Highway 1. A working feed barn and general store since 1942, coffee, art, produce, and a Saturday farmers market, the town's living room. Browse and linger.

Station House Cafe — Main St at Third. The Point Reyes Station institution since 1964, back in its original corner home for hearty American plates and local oysters. The sit down meal.

Point Reyes Books — 11315 Highway 1. A tiny, fiercely curated independent bookstore that punches far above the town's size, staff picks worth trusting. Leave with something unexpected.

Side Street Kitchen — 60 Fourth St. A rotisserie and sandwich kitchen with a shaded patio, porchetta and roast chicken and a beer garden feel, the town's easy lunch. Grab a bird for the road.

Palace Market — Highway 1. The town grocery with a back deli counter and, the local secret, soft serve made from buffalo milk. Fuel up and get the cone.

Cafe Reyes — Highway 1. A wood fired pizza spot with a leafy patio, local ingredients, and a laid back West Marin pace. The unhurried dinner.

Eight in Point Reyes Station: Brickmaiden Breads, Bovine Bakery, Toby's, Station House Cafe, Point Reyes Books, Side Street Kitchen, Palace Market, and Cafe Reyes. Which stop first?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Downtown Petaluma (North Bay)
item.description: Lagunitas grew from a tiny Petaluma operation into a craft beer giant, and its flagship beer sanctuary still pours in the town where it all started. Eight
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Downtown Petaluma (North Bay)

Lagunitas grew from a tiny Petaluma operation into a craft beer giant, and its flagship beer sanctuary still pours in the town where it all started. Eight stops for a day in downtown Petaluma.

Lagunitas Brewing Company — 1280 N McDowell Blvd. The flagship beer sanctuary where the giant started, a huge taproom and beer garden with live music and an amphitheater out back. Tour, taste, and stay for a set. @lagunitasbeer

Della Fattoria — 141 Petaluma Blvd N. A rustic downtown bakery and cafe famous for its wood fired breads, a hearty breakfast and a courtyard. The morning anchor.

Petaluma Pie Company — 125 Petaluma Blvd N. A downtown pie shop turning out sweet and savory pies fresh every morning, some ingredients grown by them. Get a hand pie for the road.

Lala's Creamery — 134 Petaluma Blvd N. A downtown ice cream parlor with rotating flavors and dairy free options, the sweet finish to the stroll. Cone in hand, walk the river.

Central Market — 42 Petaluma Blvd N. A farm to table New American kitchen in a historic downtown storefront, a wood oven and a nightly changing menu off local farms. The special dinner.

Seared — 170 Petaluma Blvd N. A downtown steak and seafood house with a serious cocktail bar and a happy hour worth timing, the dressed up night out. Sit at the bar.

Copperfield's Books — 140 Kentucky St. The beloved local independent bookstore's Petaluma shop, deep shelves and a busy author calendar. Browse before dinner.

Downtown Petaluma — Petaluma Blvd. The intact iron front Victorian downtown that stands in for old timey America in the movies, antique shops and a river walk. Wander the blocks.

Eight in Petaluma: Lagunitas, Della Fattoria, Petaluma Pie, Lala's, Central Market, Seared, Copperfield's, and the historic downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Chinatown Classics
item.description: Golden Gate Bakery's egg tarts are so legendary and its hours so unpredictable that fans built a website just to answer, is Golden Gate Bakery open today.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Chinatown Classics

Golden Gate Bakery's egg tarts are so legendary and its hours so unpredictable that fans built a website just to answer, is Golden Gate Bakery open today. Eight San Francisco Chinatown classics worth the line.

Golden Gate Bakery — 1029 Grant Ave. The cult egg custard tarts with the flaky crust, cash only, open when they feel like it, the line forming when the sign flips. Get a box while you can.

Mister Jiu's — 8 Waverly Pl. The Michelin starred Cantonese room in a historic banquet hall, modern California technique on classic roots. The special occasion in Chinatown.

R&G Lounge — 631 Kearny St. The Cantonese institution since 1985 famous for the salt and pepper Dungeness crab, deep fried and dusted with a secret seasoning. Order the crab, always. @randglounge

Z&Y Restaurant — 655 Jackson St. The Sichuan Michelin Bib Gourmand spot, numbing chili wontons and fish with pickled greens that wake you up. Bring the heat lovers.

House of Nanking — 919 Kearny St. The chaotic Shanghai favorite since 1988 where the owner tells you what to order, sesame chicken and a line down Kearny. Trust the process.

Great Eastern — 649 Jackson St. A big Cantonese banquet hall doing daily dim sum and live seafood, the one a president famously took out. Closed Tuesdays, go for the carts.

Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory — 56 Ross Alley. A tiny alley factory folding fortune cookies by hand since 1962, watch them fold and buy a warm bag. A one of a kind stop.

Li Po Lounge — 916 Grant Ave. A dim, cavernous Beat era dive under a big red lantern, home of the legendary Chinese Mai Tai. A drink where the poets drank.

Eight in Chinatown: Golden Gate Bakery, Mister Jiu's, R&G, Z&Y, House of Nanking, Great Eastern, the Fortune Cookie Factory, and Li Po. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Inside the SF Ferry Building
item.description: The 1898 Ferry Building survived the big earthquakes and decades as a freeway ramped parking lot before it was reborn as the Bay Area's grandest food hall
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Inside the SF Ferry Building

The 1898 Ferry Building survived the big earthquakes and decades as a freeway ramped parking lot before it was reborn as the Bay Area's grandest food hall under its clock tower. Eight stops inside the Ferry Building.

Hog Island Oyster Co — 1 Ferry Building. A raw bar of oysters pulled from Tomales Bay, shucked to order with a bay view and a glass of muscadet. The splurge with a view. @hogislandoysterco

Gott's Roadside — 1 Ferry Building. The valley born burger stand's waterfront outpost, ahi tuna burgers and shakes with the bay out front. The easy lunch.

Blue Bottle Coffee — 1 Ferry Building. The Oakland born roaster that helped start third wave coffee, a New Orleans iced or a perfect cappuccino to walk with. Caffeinate here.

Acme Bread Company — 1 Ferry Building. The Berkeley baker supplying half the city's best restaurants, sourdough and baguettes sold straight from the counter. Get a loaf before they go.

Cowgirl Creamery — 1 Ferry Building. The Point Reyes cheesemaker's city shop, the Mt Tam triple cream and a grilled cheese to go. Build a picnic.

Humphry Slocombe — 1 Ferry Building. The cult ice cream shop with the Secret Breakfast, bourbon and cornflakes, and flavors that sound wrong and taste right. Try the weird one.

Dandelion Chocolate — 1 Ferry Building. The bean to bar chocolate maker's kiosk, single origin bars and a thick drinking chocolate. The sweet finish.

Ferry Plaza Farmers Market — 1 Ferry Building. The Saturday market wrapping the building with the region's best farms, chefs shopping beside you. Come Saturday morning.

Eight at the Ferry Building: Hog Island, Gott's, Blue Bottle, Acme, Cowgirl, Humphry Slocombe, Dandelion, and the Saturday market. Which first?

item.title: San Francisco Around the Sonoma Plaza (North Bay)
item.description: Sonoma Plaza is where California declared independence in 1846, and today the grassy square is ringed by tasting rooms, a historic mission, and some of win
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Around the Sonoma Plaza (North Bay)

Sonoma Plaza is where California declared independence in 1846, and today the grassy square is ringed by tasting rooms, a historic mission, and some of wine country's best food. Eight stops around the Sonoma Plaza.

The Girl and the Fig — 110 W Spain St. A Sonoma Plaza favorite since 1997, country French cooking and a Rhone focused wine list in a warm room. The reliable special dinner.

El Dorado Kitchen — 405 First St W. A stylish plaza restaurant and hotel with a Mediterranean menu and a courtyard, hundreds of wines by the list. Sit in the courtyard.

Sunflower Caffe — 421 First St W. A sunny plaza cafe for breakfast and lunch with a garden patio, egg dishes and sandwiches under the trees. The easy morning.

Vella Cheese Company — 315 Second St E. A cheesemaker on the plaza since 1931, the Dry Jack aged for years the signature. Buy a wedge for the road.

Sonoma Mission — 114 Spain St E. The last and northernmost California mission, from 1823, a quick history stop on the plaza's edge. Walk the old adobe.

Sonoma Plaza — First St E. The eight acre National Historic Landmark square with a duck pond, City Hall, and the Bear Flag monument, the town's beating heart. Picnic on the grass.

Sonoma Valley Museum of Art — 551 Broadway. A small contemporary art museum a block off the plaza, changing shows worth a look. The cultural stop.

Sonoma Farmers Market — Depot Park. The weekly market with the valley's produce and prepared food, live music and neighbors. Time your visit for it.

Eight around the Plaza: the Girl and the Fig, El Dorado Kitchen, Sunflower Caffe, Vella Cheese, the Mission, the Plaza, the art museum, and the farmers market. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Mill Valley (Marin)
item.description: The oldest trail race in America, the Dipsea, starts in downtown Mill Valley with a staircase of nearly 700 steps climbing straight up toward Mount Tam. Ei
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Mill Valley (Marin)

The oldest trail race in America, the Dipsea, starts in downtown Mill Valley with a staircase of nearly 700 steps climbing straight up toward Mount Tam. Eight stops in Mill Valley at the foot of the mountain.

Depot Cafe and Bookstore — 87 Throckmorton Ave. The town's living room on the plaza, coffee and a bookstore in the old rail depot, reopened in 2026 after a refresh. Start on the plaza.

Sweetwater Music Hall — 19 Corte Madera Ave. A legendary small music venue and club, national acts a few feet away in a low ceilinged room. Check who is playing.

Bungalow 44 — 44 E Blithedale Ave. A lively California bistro and bar, good for oysters at happy hour and a full dinner after. The neighborhood dinner.

Corner Bar — 106 Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. A lively neighborhood bar and kitchen in the old Vasco space off the plaza, seasonal plates and cocktails. The easy dinner.

Equator Coffees — 129 Miller Ave. The Marin roaster's cafe in the Lumber Yard, a certified B corp pour among the shops. Caffeinate and browse.

Mill Valley Lumber Yard — 129 Miller Ave. A restored 1890s lumberyard turned open air village of makers, cafes, and shops along the creek. Wander the boardwalk.

Old Mill Park — 375 Throckmorton Ave. A redwood shaded park around the town's namesake old sawmill, a creek and a playground under big trees. The quiet green stop.

Dipsea Steps — Cascade Way. The nearly 700 step staircase that launches the historic Dipsea race, a calf burning climb with a Mount Tam payoff. Take the stairs.

Eight in Mill Valley: the Depot, Sweetwater, Bungalow 44, Corner Bar, Equator, the Lumber Yard, Old Mill Park, and the Dipsea Steps. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco's Hayes Valley
item.description: When the 1989 earthquake brought down the freeway that ran over Hayes Valley, the neighborhood traded an overpass for boutiques, wine bars, and a park. Eig
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco's Hayes Valley

When the 1989 earthquake brought down the freeway that ran over Hayes Valley, the neighborhood traded an overpass for boutiques, wine bars, and a park. Eight stops in San Francisco's Hayes Valley.

Rich Table — 199 Gough St. A Michelin starred, unfussy California room, the sardine chips and porcini doughnuts the signatures. The special dinner.

Absinthe Brasserie — 398 Hayes St. A Parisian style brasserie for oysters, steak frites, and a proper cocktail before the symphony. The grown up night out.

Souvla — 517 Hayes St. The Greek fast fine spot that rescued the gyro, lamb or chicken wraps and a frozen Greek yogurt. The reliable quick lunch.

Chez Maman — 401 Gough St. A cozy French bistro for burgers and pots of mussels, tight tables and a warm room. The neighborhood standby.

Smitten Ice Cream — 432 Octavia St. Ice cream frozen to order with liquid nitrogen right in front of you, a cloud of fog and a fresh scoop. Watch it freeze.

Blue Bottle Coffee Kiosk — 315 Linden St. The original Blue Bottle, a garage window on a back alley where the roaster began. A pilgrimage cup.

Patricia's Green — Hayes St at Octavia Blvd. The neighborhood's central park with rotating public art where the freeway once stood, benches and a playground. Sit with a coffee.

Hayes Street shops — Hayes St. A walkable strip of independent boutiques, a distillery tasting room, and design shops. Browse the block.

Eight in Hayes Valley: Rich Table, Absinthe, Souvla, Chez Maman, Smitten, the Blue Bottle kiosk, Patricia's Green, and the Hayes Street shops. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Guerneville On the Russian River (North Bay)
item.description: Guerneville is where San Francisco has escaped to float the Russian River and walk among old growth redwoods for a century, a woodsy resort town ninety min
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Guerneville On the Russian River (North Bay)

Guerneville is where San Francisco has escaped to float the Russian River and walk among old growth redwoods for a century, a woodsy resort town ninety minutes north. Eight stops in Guerneville on the Russian River.

Johnson's Beach — 16215 First St. The classic river beach where you rent a tube or a kayak and float the green Russian River all afternoon. Put in here in summer.

Boon Eat and Drink — 16248 Main St. The town's farm to table anchor, a small seasonal California menu that put Guerneville dining on the map. Book ahead on weekends.

Pat's International — 16236 Main St. A classic diner since 1940 for cinnamon sugar donuts and thick coffee, plus a few wild modern plates. The breakfast institution.

Piknik Town Market — 16205 First St. The market that took over Big Bottom, still baking the world famous biscuits daily, plus sandwiches for the beach. Grab a biscuit.

Armstrong Redwoods — 17000 Armstrong Woods Rd. An old growth grove of coast redwoods minutes from downtown, the Parson Jones tree over 300 feet tall. Walk the flat loop.

Korbel Delicatessen and Market — 13250 River Rd. The deli at the historic champagne cellars, gourmet sandwiches and a garden to eat them in. Pair with a cellar tour.

Korbel Champagne Cellars — 13250 River Rd. The 1882 sparkling wine estate with free tours through ivy covered brick and a rose garden. See how the bubbles are made.

Downtown Guerneville — Main St. A few walkable blocks of cafes, bars, and shops in a woodsy river town long a welcoming getaway. Stroll and people watch.

Eight on the river: Johnson's Beach, Boon, Pat's, Piknik, Armstrong Redwoods, the Korbel deli, the champagne cellars, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Coastside Pescadero (Peninsula)
item.description: Pescadero is a tiny farm town off Highway 1 where people drive over the hills just for the artichoke garlic bread and a slice of olallieberry pie. Eight st
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Coastside Pescadero (Peninsula)

Pescadero is a tiny farm town off Highway 1 where people drive over the hills just for the artichoke garlic bread and a slice of olallieberry pie. Eight stops in coastside Pescadero.

Duarte's Tavern — 202 Stage Rd. A James Beard American Classic since the late 1800s, famous for cream of artichoke soup and olallieberry pie. Order both.

Arcangeli Grocery, Norm's Market — 287 Stage Rd. The old country store baking hot artichoke garlic bread all day, the smell pulling you in. Buy a warm loaf.

Harley Farms Goat Dairy — 205 North St. A photogenic goat dairy with farm tours and a shop of fresh chevre and ricotta. Meet the goats.

Pie Ranch — 2080 Cabrillo Hwy. A coastal educational farm with a heart shaped field and a farm stand of produce, grain, and pie. Stop at the stand.

Pescadero State Beach — Cabrillo Hwy. A wide beach of tide pools and driftwood with a marsh behind it thick with herons. Tide pool at low tide.

Bean Hollow State Beach — Cabrillo Hwy. A rocky cove of pebbles and honeycombed tafoni sandstone just south of town, a quick dramatic stop. Walk the pebble beach.

Pigeon Point Lighthouse — 210 Pigeon Point Rd. One of the tallest lighthouses in America, a 115 foot tower on the bluffs just down the coast. Time it for sunset.

Downtown Pescadero — Stage Rd. Two short blocks of a country town, a bakery, a pub, and a white chapel, unchanged for decades. Stroll Stage Road.

Eight in Pescadero: Duarte's, Arcangeli, Harley Farms, Pie Ranch, the state beach, Bean Hollow, Pigeon Point, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco's North Beach (Little Italy)
item.description: North Beach is where the Beat Generation was born, where City Lights published Howl and won the obscenity trial that changed American writing, all in San F
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco's North Beach (Little Italy)

North Beach is where the Beat Generation was born, where City Lights published Howl and won the obscenity trial that changed American writing, all in San Francisco's Little Italy. Eight North Beach stops from espresso to poetry.

City Lights Booksellers — 261 Columbus Ave. The landmark Beat era bookstore and publisher of Ginsberg's Howl, three floors of books and history. Browse the poetry room upstairs.

Caffe Trieste — 601 Vallejo St. The West Coast's first espresso house, from 1956, where Coppola wrote part of the Godfather script. Order a cappuccino and stay.

Vesuvio Cafe — 255 Columbus Ave. The Beat bar beside Kerouac Alley, little changed since Kerouac and Ginsberg drank here. A drink under the stained glass.

Molinari Delicatessen — 373 Columbus Ave. Slicing salumi since 1896, the definitive North Beach sandwich built at the counter. Get the Renzo and eat in the park.

Liguria Bakery — 1700 Stockton St. A cash only focaccia bakery, family run since 1911, that sells out by late morning. Go before 11am.

Tony's Pizza Napoletana — 1570 Stockton St. World Pizza Champion Tony Gemignani's shrine to a dozen pizza styles, the Margherita limited to a set number a day. Line up early.

Washington Square — Filbert St at Stockton. The neighborhood's green heart under Saints Peter and Paul Church, tai chi at dawn and picnics all day. Sit with a coffee.

Coit Tower — 1 Telegraph Hill Blvd. The Art Deco tower atop Telegraph Hill wrapped in 1930s murals, an elevator to a full bay view. Ride up for the panorama.

Eight in North Beach: City Lights, Caffe Trieste, Vesuvio, Molinari, Liguria, Tony's, Washington Square, and Coit Tower. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Los Gatos (South Bay)
item.description: Los Gatos is the foothill town where Netflix was founded in 1997, a walkable downtown of old brick and patios at the base of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Eigh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Los Gatos (South Bay)

Los Gatos is the foothill town where Netflix was founded in 1997, a walkable downtown of old brick and patios at the base of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Eight stops in downtown Los Gatos.

Dio Deka — 210 E Main St. A Michelin starred Hellenic dining room in the Hotel Los Gatos, lamb chops and a deep Greek wine list. The special dinner.

Forbes Mill Steakhouse — 206 N Santa Cruz Ave. A clubby steakhouse named for the town's old flour mill, dry aged cuts and a big wine list. The celebration steak.

The Bywater — 532 N Santa Cruz Ave. Chef David Kinch's lively New Orleans kitchen from the Manresa team, gumbo, po'boys, and a raw bar with strong cocktails. The neighborhood standby.

Willow Street Pizza — 20 S Santa Cruz Ave. A downtown pizzeria for wood fired pies and salads, easy and family friendly. The casual lunch.

Fleur de Cocoa — 39 N Santa Cruz Ave. A French patisserie for croissants, macarons, and chocolates made in house. The morning pastry.

Icing on the Cake — 50 W Main St. A beloved bakery since 1985 for towering layer cakes and cupcakes. Grab a slice.

Los Gatos Coffee Roasting — 101 W Main St. The town roaster since 1982, a corner cafe for a pour and people watching. Caffeinate here.

Oak Meadow Park and Billy Jones Railroad — 233 Blossom Hill Rd. A leafy park with a vintage steam train and a carousel kids love. Ride the little train.

Eight in Los Gatos: Dio Deka, Forbes Mill, the Bywater, Willow Street, Fleur de Cocoa, Icing on the Cake, the coffee roaster, and Oak Meadow Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Calistoga (North Bay)
item.description: Calistoga sits on a bed of volcanic ash and hot springs at the top of Napa Valley, where you can soak in a mud bath and watch a geyser erupt on the same af
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Calistoga (North Bay)

Calistoga sits on a bed of volcanic ash and hot springs at the top of Napa Valley, where you can soak in a mud bath and watch a geyser erupt on the same afternoon. Eight stops in Calistoga.

Old Faithful Geyser — 1299 Tubbs Ln. One of only a few faithful geysers on earth, shooting hot water 60 feet up every 30 minutes or so. Wait for the blast.

Indian Springs — 1712 Lincoln Ave. California's oldest continuously operating spa, from 1861, with a giant mineral pool and volcanic ash mud baths. Book the mud.

Dr Wilkinson's — 1507 Lincoln Ave. The classic Calistoga mud bath resort, freshly renovated, the original mid century soak. The old school treatment.

Sam's Social Club — 1712 Lincoln Ave. The rustic American restaurant at Indian Springs with a big patio, named for the town's founder. Lunch by the pool.

Calistoga Roastery — 1426 Lincoln Ave. One of Napa's original coffee roasters since 1992, a friendly downtown cafe. Start the morning here.

Château Montelena — 1429 Tubbs Ln. The winery whose Chardonnay won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, a stone castle and a Chinese garden. Taste history.

Petrified Forest — 4100 Petrified Forest Rd. A grove of redwoods turned to stone by an ancient Mount St Helena eruption, an easy interpretive walk. See the stone logs.

Downtown Lincoln Avenue — Lincoln Ave. A few walkable blocks of tasting rooms, shops, and cafes in a low key spa town. Stroll and taste.

Eight in Calistoga: Old Faithful, Indian Springs, Dr Wilkinson's, Sam's Social Club, the Roastery, Château Montelena, the Petrified Forest, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Clement Street (Inner Richmond)
item.description: Locals call Clement Street the second Chinatown, a foggy Richmond District stretch where Burmese tea leaf salad, dim sum, and a legendary bookstore share a
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Clement Street (Inner Richmond)

Locals call Clement Street the second Chinatown, a foggy Richmond District stretch where Burmese tea leaf salad, dim sum, and a legendary bookstore share a few blocks. Eight stops on Clement Street.

Burma Superstar — 309 Clement St. The Richmond institution since 1992, the tea leaf salad tossed at your table and coconut noodles worth the wait. No reservations, put your name in.

B Star — 127 Clement St. Burma Superstar's smaller sister a few blocks down, the same Burmese flavors with a brighter room and a patio. The easier table.

Good Luck Dim Sum — 736 Clement St. A cash friendly counter of dumplings and buns, three for a couple of dollars, a line of regulars out front. Load up a box.

Wing Lee Bakery — 503 Clement St. A dim sum to go shop with a case of char siu bao and rice rolls for pocket change. Point and pile a tray.

Green Apple Books — 506 Clement St. A rambling independent bookstore since 1967, creaky floors and stacks to get lost in. Lose an hour here.

Toy Boat Dessert Cafe — 401 Clement St. A quirky old school ice cream and dessert spot packed with toys, a neighborhood sugar fix. Get a sundae.

Pizzetta 211 — 211 23rd Ave. A tiny corner pizzeria off Clement doing thin crust with a changing menu, a beloved weekend line. Worth the short wait.

Clement Street Farmers Market — Clement St at 3rd Ave. The Sunday market bringing produce and prepared food to the heart of the strip. Come Sunday morning.

Eight on Clement: Burma Superstar, B Star, Good Luck Dim Sum, Wing Lee, Green Apple Books, Toy Boat, Pizzetta 211, and the Sunday market. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Outer Sunset By the Beach
item.description: The Outer Sunset is San Francisco's foggy far edge, a surf and sand neighborhood by Ocean Beach where a cult coffee and brunch scene grew up between the du
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Outer Sunset By the Beach

The Outer Sunset is San Francisco's foggy far edge, a surf and sand neighborhood by Ocean Beach where a cult coffee and brunch scene grew up between the dunes. Eight Outer Sunset stops by the beach.

Outerlands — 4001 Judah St. The neighborhood's cult brunch, a driftwood walled room famous for the Dutch baby pancake and grilled cheese on levain. Wait for a table.

Andytown Coffee Roasters — 3655 Lawton St. The Irish inspired roaster behind the Snowy Plover, an espresso soda over ice with cream. Order the Snowy Plover.

Devil's Teeth Baking Company — 3876 Noriega St. A beloved bakery for the breakfast sandwich on a buttery biscuit and beignets on weekends. Get the breakfast sandwich.

Hook Fish Co — 4542 Irving St. A sustainable seafood counter for poke burritos and fish and chips a few blocks from the sand. The post beach lunch.

Java Beach Cafe — 1396 La Playa St. The old school surfer cafe at the end of the N line, coffee and burritos steps from Ocean Beach. The local hang.

Sunset Reservoir Brewing — 1735 Noriega St. A neighborhood brewpub on Noriega for house beers and pizza, families and dogs welcome. The easy pint.

Ocean Beach — Great Hwy. Miles of wild Pacific sand with bonfire pits and surfers, the fog rolling in at sunset. Build a fire at dusk.

Beach Chalet and the windmills — 1000 Great Hwy. The 1930s WPA murals inside and the restored Dutch windmills of Golden Gate Park just behind. See the murals and the mill.

Eight in the Outer Sunset: Outerlands, Andytown, Devil's Teeth, Hook Fish, Java Beach, Sunset Reservoir, Ocean Beach, and the Beach Chalet. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Yountville, Napa's Michelin Town
item.description: Yountville packs among the highest concentrations of Michelin stars per capita in America, a tiny Napa town where Thomas Keller built a culinary empire. Ei
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Yountville, Napa's Michelin Town

Yountville packs among the highest concentrations of Michelin stars per capita in America, a tiny Napa town where Thomas Keller built a culinary empire. Eight stops in Yountville.

The French Laundry — 6640 Washington St. Thomas Keller's three Michelin star flagship in an old stone house, a tasting menu people plan trips around. Book two months out.

Bouchon Bistro — 6534 Washington St. Keller's Parisian bistro for steak frites and roast chicken, the accessible star on the block. The easier Keller table.

Bouchon Bakery — 6528 Washington St. The bakery beside the bistro for macarons, the famous TKO cookie, and a morning croissant. Grab pastries to go.

Ad Hoc — 6476 Washington St. Keller's family style spot with one set menu each night, the buttermilk fried chicken legendary. Go on fried chicken night.

Bottega — 6525 Washington St. A warm Italian dining room in the historic Groezinger winery, bold Napa Italian cooking. The lively dinner.

Ciccio — 6770 Washington St. A wood fired Italian spot with pizzas and pastas from a family that farms the ingredients. The neighborhood Italian.

V Marketplace — 6525 Washington St. A brick winery from 1870 turned marketplace of shops, tasting rooms, and cafes. Browse and taste.

Napa Valley Wine Train — Yountville stop. The vintage rail dining excursion rolling through the vineyards, lunch or dinner aboard. Ride the rails.

Eight in Yountville: the French Laundry, Bouchon Bistro, the bakery, Ad Hoc, Bottega, Ciccio, V Marketplace, and the Wine Train. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Mountain View (South Bay)
item.description: Mountain View is Google's hometown, but its real draw is Castro Street, a few blocks packed with some of the most globally diverse dining in the Bay Area.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Mountain View (South Bay)

Mountain View is Google's hometown, but its real draw is Castro Street, a few blocks packed with some of the most globally diverse dining in the Bay Area. Eight stops in downtown Mountain View.

Scratch — 401 Castro St. A polished New American restaurant and patio, a downtown anchor for a full dinner or weekend brunch. The reliable sit down.

Cascal — 400 Castro St. A pan Latin tapas spot with sangria and a lively patio, plates made for sharing. The group dinner.

Doppio Zero — 160 Castro St. A Neapolitan pizzeria with a certified Vera Pizza oven, blistered pies and burrata. The pizza night.

Ludwig's Biergarten — 383 Castro St. A German beer hall with communal tables, soft pretzels, and schnitzel, the block's social anchor. Grab a stein.

Steins Beer Garden — 895 Villa St. A big beer garden and grill with a rotating tap list and a shaded patio. The afternoon pint.

Dana Street Roasting — 744 W Dana St. The town's independent roaster and cafe, live music some nights and strong coffee always. Caffeinate here.

Books Inc — 317 Castro St. The Bay Area independent bookstore chain's cozy Castro Street shop. Browse a while.

Mountain View Farmers Market — Caltrain Station. A large Sunday market by the tracks with the valley's produce and prepared food. Come Sunday morning.

Eight in Mountain View: Scratch, Cascal, Doppio Zero, Ludwig's, Steins, Dana Street, Books Inc, and the Sunday market. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Tiburon On the Bay (Marin)
item.description: Tiburon sits on a narrow peninsula with a head on view of the San Francisco skyline across the bay, a waterfront village and the closest launch to Angel Is
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Tiburon On the Bay (Marin)

Tiburon sits on a narrow peninsula with a head on view of the San Francisco skyline across the bay, a waterfront village and the closest launch to Angel Island. Eight stops in Tiburon.

Sam's Anchor Cafe — 27 Main St. The classic on the water since 1920, a sun soaked deck for crab cakes and a Ramos fizz over the bay. Get a deck table.

Guaymas — 5 Main St. A waterfront Mexican spot at the ferry landing with a patio facing the city skyline. Margaritas at sunset.

Luna Blu — 35 Main St. A small sustainable seafood restaurant on Main, house pastas and the day's catch. The intimate dinner.

Servino Ristorante — Ark Row. A family Italian institution back at its original Ark Row home, pastas and thin crust pizza. The old reliable.

Caffe Acri — Main St. An all day bakery and bistro by the ferry landing with gelato and live music on weekends. The morning coffee.

Ark Row — Main St. The historic stretch of Main Street lined with old arks turned into boutiques and tasting rooms. Stroll the shops.

Angel Island Ferry — 21 Main St. The little ferry that crosses to Angel Island in about ten minutes, the fastest way to the island. Hop the boat.

Old St Hilary's — Esperanza St. A preserved 1888 carpenter Gothic church on a wildflower hillside with a sweeping bay view. Walk up for the view.

Eight in Tiburon: Sam's Anchor, Guaymas, Luna Blu, Servino, Caffe Acri, Ark Row, the Angel Island ferry, and Old St Hilary's. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Marina and Cow Hollow
item.description: The Marina was built on rubble and landfill for the 1915 world's fair, and the domed Palace of Fine Arts is the grand building they never tore down. Eight
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Marina and Cow Hollow

The Marina was built on rubble and landfill for the 1915 world's fair, and the domed Palace of Fine Arts is the grand building they never tore down. Eight stops in the Marina and Cow Hollow.

A16 — 2355 Chestnut St. A Campania inspired room named for an Italian highway, blistered Neapolitan pizza and a deep southern Italian wine list. Order the pizza and a Falanghina.

Causwells — 2346 Chestnut St. A snug bistro with one of the city's best burgers, the Americana double the reason to come. Get the Americana burger.

Delarosa — 2175 Chestnut St. A lively pizza and small plates spot for a late lunch or a glass at the bar. The easy Chestnut stop.

The Tipsy Pig — 2231 Chestnut St. A gastropub with a big back patio, comfort plates and a Marina crowd. The weekend day drink.

Rose's Cafe — 2298 Union St. A sunny Italian corner cafe on Union for breakfast pizza and a cappuccino on the sidewalk. The morning table.

Greens Restaurant — Fort Mason. The pioneering vegetarian restaurant in a Fort Mason pier building with a Golden Gate Bridge view. The special vegetarian dinner.

Palace of Fine Arts — 3601 Lyon St. The lone domed survivor of the 1915 fair, a lagoon and colonnade made for a sunset walk. Stroll the rotunda.

Marina Green — Marina Blvd. A waterfront lawn of joggers and kite flyers with the bridge and Alcatraz across the water. Walk out to the wave organ.

Eight in the Marina: A16, Causwells, Delarosa, the Tipsy Pig, Rose's Cafe, Greens, the Palace of Fine Arts, and Marina Green. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco St Helena, Napa's Main Street
item.description: St Helena is Napa Valley's Main Street, where the Model Bakery has pulled English muffins from ovens dating to the 1920s and Beringer has poured since 1876
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco St Helena, Napa's Main Street

St Helena is Napa Valley's Main Street, where the Model Bakery has pulled English muffins from ovens dating to the 1920s and Beringer has poured since 1876. Eight stops in St Helena.

Model Bakery — 1357 Main St. A Main Street bakery since 1908, the English muffin Oprah made famous still baked in ovens from the 1920s. Get the English muffin.

Gott's Roadside — 933 Main St. The original 1999 roadside burger stand with picnic tables on the lawn, ahi tuna burgers and shakes. Eat outside.

The Charter Oak — 1050 Charter Oak Ave. A Michelin recommended restaurant from the French Laundry team, live fire cooking and a courtyard. The special dinner.

Farmstead at Long Meadow Ranch — 738 Main St. A big barn restaurant sourcing from its own ranch, wood grilled meats and garden vegetables. The farm to table night.

Goose and Gander — 1245 Spring St. A wine country public house for craft cocktails and elevated bar food, a basement bar and a garden. The cocktail stop.

Cook St Helena — 1310 Main St. A small, warm Italian trattoria beloved by locals, house pastas and a short menu. The reservation to snag.

Napa Valley Olive Oil Co — 835 Charter Oak Ave. A family Italian grocery and olive oil maker since 1931, hidden on a back street. Stock up on oil and salami.

Beringer Vineyards — 2000 Main St. The oldest continuously operating winery in Napa, from 1876, with the historic Rhine House. Tour the old cellars.

Eight in St Helena: the Model Bakery, Gott's, the Charter Oak, Farmstead, Goose and Gander, Cook, the olive oil company, and Beringer. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Campbell (South Bay)
item.description: Campbell was once the Orchard City, its downtown built on drying apricots and prunes, and the old water tower still stands over a strip that fills up every
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Campbell (South Bay)

Campbell was once the Orchard City, its downtown built on drying apricots and prunes, and the old water tower still stands over a strip that fills up every weekend. Eight stops in downtown Campbell.

Aqui Cal-Mex — 201 E Campbell Ave. A local favorite since 1994 for wild caught fish tacos and organic Cal Mex, a patio on the corner. Get a fish taco and a sangria.

Orchard Valley Coffee — 349 E Campbell Ave. The town's independent roaster and cafe, house roasted beans and a spot for live music. Start the morning here.

Katie Bloom's — 369 E Campbell Ave. A proper Irish pub for a pint and shepherd's pie, the block's social living room. Grab a booth.

Distrito Federal — 379 E Campbell Ave. A lively downtown Mexican kitchen and bar in the old Liquid Bread space, tacos and margaritas. The dinner stop.

Campbell Farmers Market — E Campbell Ave. A large Sunday market down the main drag with the valley's produce and food stalls. Come Sunday morning.

Ainsley House — 300 Grant St. A 1925 English Tudor cottage and museum with period gardens, a step back a century. Tour the house.

Campbell Historical Museum — 51 N Central Ave. A small museum in the old firehouse telling the Orchard City story. The quick history stop.

Los Gatos Creek Trail — Campbell. A shaded creekside path and percolation ponds running right through town for a walk or ride. Walk off lunch.

Eight in Campbell: Aqui, Orchard Valley Coffee, Katie Bloom's, Distrito Federal, the Sunday market, the Ainsley House, the history museum, and the creek trail. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco San Rafael (Marin)
item.description: San Rafael is where Frank Lloyd Wright built his final masterpiece, the blue roofed Marin Civic Center, a spaceship of a building you have seen in the movi
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Rafael (Marin)

San Rafael is where Frank Lloyd Wright built his final masterpiece, the blue roofed Marin Civic Center, a spaceship of a building you have seen in the movies. Eight stops in San Rafael.

Marin Civic Center — 3501 Civic Center Dr. Frank Lloyd Wright's last major work, a long arched building with a gold spire and blue roof, a National Historic Landmark. Walk the soaring atrium.

Sol Food — 901 Lincoln Ave. The wildly popular Puerto Rican kitchen since 2004, the pork sandwich and plantains worth the line. Get the pernil sandwich.

Il Davide — 901 A St. A downtown Italian mainstay for house pasta and a warm room off Fourth Street. The reliable dinner.

Whipper Snapper — 1613 4th St. A colorful Latin and Caribbean spot with strong cocktails and a party feel. The night out.

Mission San Rafael Arcángel — 1104 5th Ave. A reconstructed 1817 mission, the second to last of the California chain, a quick history stop. See the white chapel.

Falkirk Cultural Center — 1408 Mission Ave. A grand 1888 Victorian mansion and gardens turned arts center. Wander the grounds.

Fourth Street — 4th St. The walkable downtown spine of shops, cafes, and the historic Rafael film center. Stroll and catch a movie.

China Camp State Park — N San Pedro Rd. A bayfront park preserving a historic Chinese shrimp fishing village, trails and a quiet beach. Walk the shoreline.

Eight in San Rafael: the Marin Civic Center, Sol Food, Il Davide, Whipper Snapper, the mission, Falkirk, Fourth Street, and China Camp. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Haight-Ashbury
item.description: The corner of Haight and Ashbury was the epicenter of the 1967 Summer of Love, and the psychedelic street around it still runs on record stores, vintage sh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Haight-Ashbury

The corner of Haight and Ashbury was the epicenter of the 1967 Summer of Love, and the psychedelic street around it still runs on record stores, vintage shops, and tie dye. Eight Haight-Ashbury stops.

Amoeba Music — 1855 Haight St. A world famous record store in an old bowling alley, aisles of vinyl and free in store concerts. Lose an hour in the stacks.

The Booksmith — 1644 Haight St. A beloved independent bookstore hosting author events since 1976, the neighborhood's literary heart. Browse the front tables.

Cha Cha Cha — 1801 Haight St. A loud, festive Caribbean tapas spot across from Amoeba, sangria by the pitcher and fried plantains. Share plates with a group.

Magnolia Brewing — 1398 Haight St. A Haight Street brewpub at the historic corner, house beers and now cocktails in a cozy room. The neighborhood pint.

The Alembic — 1725 Haight St. A candlelit craft cocktail bar with a wall of whiskey and elevated bar food. The grown up nightcap.

Wasteland — 1660 Haight St. A cavernous vintage and secondhand shop behind an ornate facade, racks of denim and leather. Dig for a find.

Buena Vista Park — Haight St. The city's oldest park, steep wooded trails climbing to a Golden Gate view above the Haight. Hike up for the vista.

Hippie Hill — Golden Gate Park. The grassy amphitheater at the park's east end where drum circles still gather, the Summer of Love's living room. Catch the drums on a Sunday.

Eight in the Haight: Amoeba, the Booksmith, Cha Cha Cha, Magnolia, the Alembic, Wasteland, Buena Vista Park, and Hippie Hill. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Burlingame (Peninsula)
item.description: Burlingame's downtown is built around the Peninsula's prettiest, most walkable shopping avenue, a mile of independent shops, bakeries, and cafes a quick tr
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Burlingame (Peninsula)

Burlingame's downtown is built around the Peninsula's prettiest, most walkable shopping avenue, a mile of independent shops, bakeries, and cafes a quick train ride south from San Francisco. Eight stops in downtown Burlingame.

Copenhagen Bakery and Cafe — 1216 Burlingame Ave. A Scandinavian bakery and cafe since the 1970s, Danish pastries and a marzipan cake case. Get a Danish.

Mingalaba — 1213 Burlingame Ave. A beloved Burmese and Chinese spot, the tea leaf salad and samusa soup the draws. Order the tea leaf salad.

Il Fornaio — 327 Lorton Ave. A handsome Italian trattoria and bakery, house pasta and wood fired bread. The reliable dinner.

Burlingame Avenue — Burlingame Ave. The tree lined main shopping street of boutiques, cafes, and ice cream, made for a stroll. Walk the whole strip.

Broadway Burlingame — Broadway. A second, older dining street with family run restaurants and bakeries a bit north. The local's block.

Therapy Stores — 1348 Burlingame Ave. A playful indie boutique for gifts, jewelry, and home goods, a fun browse right on the avenue. Find a gift.

Washington Park — Burlingame Ave. A big green park with old oaks, a playground, and picnic tables just off the avenue. Picnic under the trees.

Kabuki Sushi — Burlingame Ave. A dependable neighborhood sushi bar for a fresh lunch off the strip. The easy sushi stop.

Eight in Burlingame: Copenhagen Bakery, Mingalaba, Il Fornaio, the Avenue, Broadway, Therapy Stores, Washington Park, and Kabuki. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Willow Glen (San Jose)
item.description: Willow Glen feels like a small town dropped inside San Jose, its Lincoln Avenue lined with indie shops like Hicklebee's, a children's bookstore famous enou
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Willow Glen (San Jose)

Willow Glen feels like a small town dropped inside San Jose, its Lincoln Avenue lined with indie shops like Hicklebee's, a children's bookstore famous enough to draw authors from around the world. Eight stops in Willow Glen.

The Table — 1110 Willow St. A bustling farm to table restaurant and a Willow Glen favorite for brunch and dinner. Book ahead.

Bill's Cafe — 1115 Willow St. A breakfast tradition since 1977, big plates and a weekend line out the door. Come hungry for brunch.

Willow Street Pizza — 1072 Willow St. A neighborhood wood fired pizza and pasta spot, easy and family friendly. The casual dinner.

Hicklebee's — 1378 Lincoln Ave. A legendary children's bookstore that draws famous authors, doors and walls covered in art. Bring the kids.

Powell's Sweet Shoppe — Lincoln Ave. An old fashioned candy store packed with nostalgia and a wall of gelato. The sweet stop.

Garden Theater — 1165 Lincoln Ave. A restored 1949 movie house and event space on the avenue, a neighborhood landmark. Catch a show.

Lincoln Avenue — Lincoln Ave. The walkable main strip of boutiques, cafes, and restaurants, the heart of Willow Glen. Stroll the avenue.

Cafe Rosalena — Lincoln Ave. A cozy corner cafe for coffee and a pastry to fuel the stroll. Caffeinate here.

Eight in Willow Glen: the Table, Bill's Cafe, Willow Street Pizza, Hicklebee's, Powell's, the Garden Theater, Lincoln Avenue, and Cafe Rosalena. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Fairfax (Marin)
item.description: Fairfax is where mountain biking was born in the 1970s, a funky, tree shaded Marin town still running on bikes, live music, and a beloved natural foods mar
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Fairfax (Marin)

Fairfax is where mountain biking was born in the 1970s, a funky, tree shaded Marin town still running on bikes, live music, and a beloved natural foods market. Eight stops in Fairfax.

Good Earth Natural Foods — 720 Center Blvd. A Marin institution and organic grocery since 1969, a deli and hot bar for a healthy lunch. Build a lunch from the bar.

Fairfax Brewing Company — 765 Center Blvd. A community gastropub in the old Iron Springs space, house beers like Repack Red and pub food. The town pint.

19 Broadway — 17 Broadway Blvd. A legendary little live music club and bar, local bands most nights in a low ceilinged room. Catch a show.

Gestalt Haus — 28 Bolinas Rd. A sausage and beer hall built for cyclists, bikes parked inside and a big tap list. The post ride pint.

Sunshine Coffee — Bolinas Rd. A friendly local coffee stop to fuel a bike ride or a stroll downtown. The morning cup.

Peri Park — 200 Park Rd. A shady town park with a playground and the summer Fairfax concert series. Catch a free concert.

Fairfax trailheads — Bolinas Rd. The roads and fire trails where mountain biking began, climbing straight into the Marin hills. Ride where the sport started.

Downtown Fairfax — Broadway Blvd. A few funky blocks of vintage shops, cafes, and murals, tie dye and Birkenstocks. Wander the strip.

Eight in Fairfax: Good Earth, Fairfax Brewing, 19 Broadway, Gestalt Haus, Sunshine Coffee, Peri Park, the trailheads, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Russian Hill and Polk Street
item.description: Swan Oyster Depot has served oysters over the same marble counter on Polk Street since 1903, just down the hill from the crookedest street in the world. Ei
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Russian Hill and Polk Street

Swan Oyster Depot has served oysters over the same marble counter on Polk Street since 1903, just down the hill from the crookedest street in the world. Eight Russian Hill and Polk Street stops.

Swan Oyster Depot — 1517 Polk St. A narrow marble counter slinging the freshest oysters and crab since 1903, cash and a line out front. Slurp a dozen at the counter.

Bob's Donuts — 1720 Polk St. A 24 hour donut institution since 1953, home of the giant apple fritter and a late night line. Get a warm fritter at midnight.

Swensen's Ice Cream — 1999 Hyde St. The original Swensen's from 1948 on a Russian Hill corner, scooped from the shop that started a chain. Ride the cable car up to it.

Cheese Plus — 2001 Polk St. A gourmet cheese shop and deli famous for its grilled cheese, a wall of wedges and a good sandwich. Order the grilled cheese.

Nick's Crispy Tacos — 1500 Broadway. A fun Russian Hill spot for the crispy fried tacos, cheap and always packed. Get them Nick's Way.

Lombard Street — Lombard St at Hyde. The famous crooked block switchbacking down through the hydrangeas, cars creeping and cameras clicking. Walk down the brick curves.

Hyde Street Cable Car — Hyde St. The Powell Hyde line climbing over Russian Hill with the bay bursting into view at the crest. Ride it to the top.

Ina Coolbrith Park — Vallejo St. A steep terraced hillside park with one of the best quiet bay views in the city. Climb the steps for the view.

Eight on Russian Hill: Swan Oyster Depot, Bob's Donuts, Swensen's, Cheese Plus, Nick's, Lombard Street, the cable car, and Ina Coolbrith Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown San Mateo (Peninsula)
item.description: Downtown San Mateo turned part of B Street car free and wrapped it around Central Park, where a serene Japanese tea garden has sat since 1966. Eight stops
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown San Mateo (Peninsula)

Downtown San Mateo turned part of B Street car free and wrapped it around Central Park, where a serene Japanese tea garden has sat since 1966. Eight stops in downtown San Mateo.

Central Park Japanese Tea Garden — 50 E 5th Ave. A tranquil garden of koi ponds, a teahouse, and bonsai in the city's oldest park, free to wander. Cross the arched bridge.

Pacific Catch — 243 S B St. A West Coast fish house for poke bowls, fish tacos, and sustainable seafood on the strip. The easy seafood lunch.

Inchin's Bamboo Garden — 139 S B St. An Indian Chinese spot for chili chicken and Hakka noodles, bold and spicy. Order the Manchurian.

Takahashi Market — 221 S Claremont St. A Japanese and Hawaiian grocery since 1906 with a poke and bento counter, a neighborhood treasure. Grab a bento and mochi.

La Piñata — 201 S B St. A longtime family Mexican restaurant anchoring the block, generous plates and margaritas. The reliable standby.

3 Bees Coffee — B Street. A local coffee shop for a pour and a pastry on the car free stretch. Caffeinate on the plaza.

Gyukaku — B Street. A Japanese barbecue spot to grill wagyu and short rib at your table. The interactive dinner.

B Street — B St. The walkable, partly car free main drag of restaurants, bars, and shops. Stroll the whole strip.

Eight in San Mateo: the Japanese Tea Garden, Pacific Catch, Inchin's, Takahashi Market, La Piñata, 3 Bees, Gyukaku, and B Street. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Los Altos (South Bay)
item.description: Los Altos keeps a small town downtown in the heart of Silicon Valley, where the team behind the celebrated Manresa restaurant bakes bread and tech founders
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Los Altos (South Bay)

Los Altos keeps a small town downtown in the heart of Silicon Valley, where the team behind the celebrated Manresa restaurant bakes bread and tech founders browse the shops. Eight stops in downtown Los Altos.

Manresa Bread — 271 State St. The village bakery from the three Michelin star Manresa team, fresh milled breads and famous kouign amann. Get there before the pastries go.

Los Altos Grill — 233 3rd St. A polished American grill and neighborhood clubhouse, a wood grill and a great burger. The reliable dinner.

Sumika — 236 Central Plz. A tiny, authentic izakaya for charcoal grilled skewers and a classic Japan feel. Sit at the counter.

State Street Market — 170 State St. A modern food hall with a wine bar, taqueria, and bakery under one roof. Graze a few stalls.

Chef Chu's — 1067 N San Antonio Rd. A Los Altos Chinese institution since 1970, the whole family behind a huge menu. Order the lettuce cups.

Los Altos History Museum — 51 S San Antonio Rd. A free museum on the apricot orchard past of the valley beside a historic adobe. The quick history stop.

State and Main Streets — State St. The walkable downtown grid of boutiques, cafes, and galleries under leafy trees. Stroll the blocks.

Los Altos Farmers Market — State St. The Thursday market bringing produce and food trucks to downtown in season. Time your visit for it.

Eight in Los Altos: Manresa Bread, Los Altos Grill, Sumika, State Street Market, Chef Chu's, the History Museum, the downtown streets, and the farmers market. Where do you start?
