item.title: San Francisco San Anselmo (Marin)
item.description: San Anselmo is Marin's antiques capital, a leafy town where George Lucas gave the community a park with bronze statues of Indiana Jones and Yoda. Eight sto
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Anselmo (Marin)

San Anselmo is Marin's antiques capital, a leafy town where George Lucas gave the community a park with bronze statues of Indiana Jones and Yoda. Eight stops in San Anselmo.

Insalata's — 120 Sir Francis Drake Blvd. A Mediterranean institution with a warm dining room, rotisserie and mezze, the town's special occasion spot. The celebration dinner.

Comforts — 906 Sir Francis Drake Blvd. A San Anselmo staple since 1986 for the Chinese chicken salad and a bustling cafe counter. Order the famous salad.

M.H — Bread and Butter. 702 San Anselmo Ave. A beloved bakery and cafe for sourdough, seasonal pastries, and a morning coffee. The heartbeat of the avenue.

Cucina — 510 San Anselmo Ave. A California Italian spot with handmade pasta, wood fired pizza, and a heated back patio. The neighborhood Italian.

San Anselmo Avenue — San Anselmo Ave. One of Marin's best independent shopping streets, lined with antiques dealers and boutiques. Browse the antiques.

Imagination Park — San Anselmo Ave. George Lucas's gift to the town, a small park with bronze statues of Indiana Jones and Yoda. Snap a photo with Indy.

Robson-Harrington Park — Crescent Rd. A hillside park with terraced gardens around a historic estate, a quiet town retreat. Wander the gardens.

Marin Art and Garden Center — 30 Sir Francis Drake Blvd. Acres of gardens, a historic barn theater, and grand old trees just next door in Ross. Stroll the grounds.

Eight in San Anselmo: Insalata's, Comforts, M.H. Bread and Butter, Cucina, the Avenue, Imagination Park, Robson-Harrington, and the Marin Art and Garden Center. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Noe Valley
item.description: Noe Valley sits in a sunny pocket that dodges the city's fog, a village of a neighborhood where 24th Street feels like a small town Main Street. Eight Noe
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Noe Valley

Noe Valley sits in a sunny pocket that dodges the city's fog, a village of a neighborhood where 24th Street feels like a small town Main Street. Eight Noe Valley stops.

Noe Valley Bakery — 4073 24th St. The neighborhood bakery since 1995 for the double baked almond croissant and a great loaf. Get the almond croissant.

La Ciccia — 3856 24th St. A tiny, beloved Sardinian restaurant with bottarga pasta and octopus stew, dinner only and always booked. Reserve for the octopus.

Firefly — 4288 24th St. A cozy, long running New American restaurant, comfort food with a twist in a warm room. The date night dinner.

Chloe's Cafe — 1399 Church St. A sunny corner breakfast spot for banana pancakes and scrambles, a weekend line. The brunch stop.

Toast Eatery — 1748 Church St. A bright all day breakfast and lunch spot for big plates and mimosas. The easy morning.

Noe Valley Town Square — 3861 24th St. The community plaza hosting the Saturday farmers market and neighborhood events. Come Saturday morning.

24th Street shops — 24th St. A walkable strip of independent boutiques, bookshops, and toy stores. Browse the block.

Church Street — Church St. The second commercial spine with cafes and the J line rolling through. Ride the streetcar in.

Eight in Noe Valley: Noe Valley Bakery, La Ciccia, Firefly, Chloe's, Toast, the Town Square, the 24th Street shops, and Church Street. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Palo Alto (Peninsula)
item.description: Silicon Valley was born in a Palo Alto garage on Addison Avenue where Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard started HP in 1938, a few blocks from University Avenue
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Palo Alto (Peninsula)

Silicon Valley was born in a Palo Alto garage on Addison Avenue where Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard started HP in 1938, a few blocks from University Avenue's cafes. Eight downtown Palo Alto stops.

Evvia Estiatorio — 420 Emerson St. A warm, upscale Greek taverna, the whole fish and lamb chops a Valley power lunch favorite. The special dinner.

Tamarine — 546 University Ave. A sleek Vietnamese restaurant of shareable plates, once named a top power dining spot. The business dinner.

Nola — 535 Ramona St. A New Orleans themed restaurant with a maze of patios and strong cocktails, always buzzing. The party dinner.

Coupa Cafe — 538 Ramona St. A Venezuelan cafe born in Palo Alto in 2004, arepas and a good cortado for a work session. Caffeinate here.

Palo Alto Creamery Fountain — 566 Emerson St. A 1920s soda fountain and diner for burgers, milkshakes, and a slice of pie. The retro treat.

Bell's Books — 536 Emerson St. A family run bookshop since 1935 with new, used, and rare volumes floor to ceiling. Lose an hour here.

HanaHaus — 456 University Ave. A cafe and coworking space in a restored 1927 movie theater with a courtyard. Work with a coffee.

The HP Garage — 367 Addison Ave. The birthplace of Silicon Valley, the garage where HP began in 1938, a plaque and a quick photo stop. See where it started.

Eight in Palo Alto: Evvia, Tamarine, Nola, Coupa Cafe, the Creamery, Bell's Books, HanaHaus, and the HP Garage. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Redwood City (Peninsula)
item.description: Redwood City stamped its old slogan, Climate Best by Government Test, right on the downtown arch, and turned its 1910 courthouse plaza into the Peninsula's
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Redwood City (Peninsula)

Redwood City stamped its old slogan, Climate Best by Government Test, right on the downtown arch, and turned its 1910 courthouse plaza into the Peninsula's outdoor living room. Eight downtown Redwood City stops.

Courthouse Square — 2200 Broadway. The downtown plaza in front of the historic county courthouse, movie nights, concerts, and a summer splash fountain. The town's living room.

Fox Theatre — 2215 Broadway St. A beautifully restored 1929 movie palace now a concert hall on the square. Catch a show.

Vesta — 2022 Broadway. A wood fired pizza spot with blistered pies and cocktails, a downtown anchor. The pizza dinner.

Milagros — 1099 Middlefield Rd. A lively Latin kitchen and cantina with margaritas and a big patio. The group night out.

Timber and Salt — 881 Middlefield Rd. A craft cocktail bar and restaurant with make your own drink kits at the table. The cocktail stop.

Zareen's — 1477 Chapin Ave. A beloved Pakistani and Indian kitchen for chai, samosas, and chicken tikka. Order the nihari.

Limon — 2 W 4th Ave. A Peruvian restaurant for lomo saltado and ceviche, bright and bold. The Peruvian plate.

Downtown Redwood City — Broadway. A walkable core of restaurants, a movie theater, and the square, the Peninsula's night out. Stroll and pick a patio.

Eight in Redwood City: Courthouse Square, the Fox Theatre, Vesta, Milagros, Timber and Salt, Zareen's, Limon, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Sebastopol (Sonoma County)
item.description: In Sebastopol a whole street is lined with giant whimsical sculptures made of scrap metal, in an arty apple town where the old Gravenstein cannery district
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Sebastopol (Sonoma County)

In Sebastopol a whole street is lined with giant whimsical sculptures made of scrap metal, in an arty apple town where the old Gravenstein cannery district became The Barlow. Eight Sebastopol stops.

The Barlow — 6770 McKinley St. A 12 acre open air market district of makers, restaurants, breweries, and distilleries in old apple sheds. Wander and graze.

Handline — 935 Gravenstein Hwy S. A modern coastal California spot for oysters, fish tacos, and ceviche in a sleek reworked drive in. Order the oysters.

Fern Bar — The Barlow. A plant filled craft cocktail bar and eatery focused on adaptogenic drinks and small plates. The date night cocktail.

Screamin' Mimi's — 6902 Sebastopol Ave. A local ice cream institution churning flavors like Mexican chocolate. Get a scoop of horchata.

Taylor Lane Coffee — The Barlow. A Sonoma roaster's cafe in the Barlow for a pour with industrial chic vibes. Caffeinate here.

Florence Avenue sculptures — Florence Ave. A residential street lined with Patrick Amiot's whimsical junk metal sculptures, free and delightful. Walk the whole block.

The Nectary — Sebastopol Ave. An organic juice and smoothie bar for a cold pressed refresher. The healthy stop.

Downtown Sebastopol — Main St. A few blocks of antique shops, galleries, and cafes in a funky small town. Browse the shops.

Eight in Sebastopol: the Barlow, Handline, Fern Bar, Screamin' Mimi's, Taylor Lane, the Florence Avenue sculptures, the Nectary, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: SF's Mission District
item.description: The Mission gave the world the Mission burrito, foil wrapped and stuffed with rice and beans, in a sunny neighborhood layered with the city's densest mural
item.content:encoded:
SF's Mission District

The Mission gave the world the Mission burrito, foil wrapped and stuffed with rice and beans, in a sunny neighborhood layered with the city's densest murals. Eight Mission District stops.

La Taqueria — 2889 Mission St. The James Beard honored taqueria serving its burritos with no rice, just beans, meat, and cheese, a purist's icon. Order the carnitas, dorado.

El Farolito — 2779 Mission St. The late night institution since 1983, the super quesabirria and a line at midnight. The after hours move.

La Palma Mexicatessen — 2884 24th St. A 24th Street mainstay pressing fresh masa for tortillas and huaraches since the 1950s. Watch the tortillas being made.

Bi-Rite Creamery — 3692 18th St. The cult ice cream shop by Dolores Park, salted caramel and honey lavender with a line out the door. Grab a cone for the park.

Foreign Cinema — 2534 Mission St. A courtyard restaurant that projects films on the wall, one of the city's best brunches. Book the patio.

Clarion Alley — Clarion Alley. A block long open air gallery of ever changing political murals between Mission and Valencia. Walk the whole alley.

Balmy Alley — Balmy Alley. The oldest concentration of murals in the city off 24th Street, decades of Latino art. See where it started.

Dolores Park — Dolores St. The sunniest lawn in the city with a downtown view, a weekend scene of picnics and vendors. Post up on the grass.

Eight in the Mission: La Taqueria, El Farolito, La Palma, Bi-Rite, Foreign Cinema, Clarion Alley, Balmy Alley, and Dolores Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Menlo Park (Peninsula)
item.description: Kepler's Books has been the literary heart of Menlo Park since 1955, a Beat era haunt now sitting a mile from the Sand Hill Road offices that fund Silicon
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Menlo Park (Peninsula)

Kepler's Books has been the literary heart of Menlo Park since 1955, a Beat era haunt now sitting a mile from the Sand Hill Road offices that fund Silicon Valley. Eight downtown Menlo Park stops.

Kepler's Books — 1010 El Camino Real. The independent bookstore since 1955, a deep selection and a packed author event calendar. Browse and catch a talk.

Cafe Borrone — 1010 El Camino Real. The European style cafe beside Kepler's, coffee and a croque monsieur on the patio, the town's living room. Sit outside with a book.

Bistro Vida — 641 Santa Cruz Ave. A neighborhood French bistro since 1998 for steak frites and mussels, sidewalk tables and a full bar. The reliable dinner.

Camper — 898 Santa Cruz Ave. A bright California Mediterranean spot for wood fired vegetables and pastas. The date night table.

Ann's Coffee Shop — 796 Santa Cruz Ave. A tiny old school diner counter for eggs and a milkshake, unchanged for decades. The retro breakfast.

Santa Cruz Avenue — Santa Cruz Ave. The walkable main street of boutiques, cafes, and a toy store under leafy trees. Stroll the strip.

Fremont Park — Santa Cruz Ave. A small downtown park with a gazebo and lawns, good for a picnic off the avenue. The green break.

Dutch Goose — 3567 Alameda de las Pulgas. A beloved dive bar since 1966 for deviled eggs, burgers, and graffiti carved booths. The old school hang.

Eight in Menlo Park: Kepler's, Cafe Borrone, Bistro Vida, Camper, Ann's, Santa Cruz Avenue, Fremont Park, and the Dutch Goose. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Santana Row (San Jose)
item.description: Santana Row was built to feel like a European boulevard dropped into San Jose, a walkable stretch of shops, restaurants, and fountains modeled on Barcelona
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Santana Row (San Jose)

Santana Row was built to feel like a European boulevard dropped into San Jose, a walkable stretch of shops, restaurants, and fountains modeled on Barcelona. Eight Santana Row stops.

Suspiro — 3060 Olsen Dr. A Spanish and Peruvian kitchen on the Row for ceviche, paella, and tapas, with a hidden speakeasy for cocktails. The special dinner.

Straits — 333 Santana Row. A stylish Singaporean and Asian fusion room, chili crab and roti prata. The date night plates.

Momosan — 378 Santana Row. Iron Chef Morimoto's izakaya for ramen, skewers, and sake, a lively bowl right on the Row. The people watching lunch.

Fitoor — Santana Row, San Jose. A modern Indian restaurant in the former Amber India space, tandoor plates, biryani, and cocktails. Order the butter chicken.

Cocola Bakery — 378 Santana Row. A French bakery and cafe for macarons, crepes, and a good espresso. The pastry stop.

The Row shops — Santana Row. Blocks of boutiques and flagship stores along a fountain lined promenade. Window shop the strip.

Westfield Valley Fair — 2855 Stevens Creek Blvd. The upscale mega mall right across the street, a Din Tai Fung and a Bloomingdale's. Cross over to shop.

Santana Row plaza — 377 Santana Row. The central park and fountains with live music and seasonal markets, the district's heart. Sit by the fountain.

Eight on the Row: Suspiro, Straits, Momosan, Fitoor, Cocola, the shops, Valley Fair, and the plaza. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Healdsburg (Sonoma County)
item.description: Healdsburg's tree shaded plaza sits where the Dry Creek, Alexander, and Russian River valleys meet, next to SingleThread, a globally acclaimed restaurant a
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Healdsburg (Sonoma County)

Healdsburg's tree shaded plaza sits where the Dry Creek, Alexander, and Russian River valleys meet, next to SingleThread, a globally acclaimed restaurant and farm that draws diners worldwide. Eight Healdsburg stops.

Healdsburg Plaza — Healdsburg Plaza. A tree shaded town square ringed by tasting rooms, shops, and restaurants, the heart of Wine Country. Start with a picnic on the grass.

SingleThread — 131 North St. A globally acclaimed restaurant, inn, and farm with an eleven course Japan meets Sonoma tasting menu. The trip of a lifetime dinner.

Bravas Bar de Tapas — 420 Center St. A lively Spanish tapas spot with a big backyard, jamon, gildas, and sangria. The group dinner.

Barndiva — 231 Center St. A garden restaurant of seasonal California cooking in a converted barn, cocktails under the trees. The special occasion.

Valette — 344 Center St. A refined farm to table room from a Healdsburg native, the scallops en croute the signature. The date night splurge.

Costeaux French Bakery — 44 Mill St. A Healdsburg bakery institution for sourdough, croissants, and a big breakfast. The morning stop.

Noble Folk Ice Cream — 116 Matheson St. A small batch ice cream and pie shop on the plaza, honey lavender and salted butterscotch. The sweet finish.

Oakville Grocery — Matheson St. A historic gourmet market on the plaza for picnic supplies and local wine. Build a picnic for the road.

Eight in Healdsburg: the Plaza, SingleThread, Bravas, Barndiva, Valette, Costeaux, Noble Folk, and Oakville Grocery. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Castro District
item.description: The Castro is where Harvey Milk ran a camera shop and won office as an early openly gay elected official, in the country's most famous gay neighborhood. Ei
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Castro District

The Castro is where Harvey Milk ran a camera shop and won office as an early openly gay elected official, in the country's most famous gay neighborhood. Eight Castro stops.

Castro Theatre — 429 Castro St. The 1922 movie palace with a mighty Wurlitzer organ, a neighborhood landmark freshly restored. Catch a screening or a singalong.

Harvey Milk's Castro Camera — 575 Castro St. The storefront where Milk ran his shop and campaigns, now marked with a mural and plaque. Stand where history was made.

Twin Peaks Tavern — 401 Castro St. The bar with the big plate glass windows, said to be the first gay bar in the country you could see into from the street. Toast at the corner.

Anchor Oyster Bar — 579 Castro St. A tiny marble counter serving oysters and cioppino since 1977, no reservations, worth the wait. Slurp a dozen.

Cliff's Variety — 479 Castro St. A beloved hardware and everything store for 80 years, glitter and lightbulbs side by side. Browse the wonderful clutter.

Hot Cookie — 407 Castro St. A cheeky little bakery famous for warm cookies late into the night. Grab a bag for the walk.

GLBT Historical Society Museum — 4127 18th St. A small museum of queer history with rotating exhibits, the first of its kind in the country. See the archives.

Rainbow Honor Walk — Castro St. Bronze sidewalk plaques honoring LGBTQ figures along the strip, plus the giant flag at Harvey Milk Plaza. Read the sidewalk.

Eight in the Castro: the Castro Theatre, Milk's camera store, Twin Peaks Tavern, Anchor Oyster Bar, Cliff's Variety, Hot Cookie, the GLBT museum, and the Rainbow Honor Walk. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Japantown
item.description: San Jose's Japantown is among the last historic Japantowns in the United States, a few blocks that survived the wartime incarceration and never left. Eight
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Japantown

San Jose's Japantown is among the last historic Japantowns in the United States, a few blocks that survived the wartime incarceration and never left. Eight San Jose Japantown stops.

Nichi Bei Bussan — 140 Jackson St. A Japanese goods store since 1902, kimono, fabric, and housewares over generations. Browse the fabric wall.

Shuei-Do Manju Shop — 217 Jackson St. A tiny shop making mochi and manju by hand for decades, a local treasure. Get a box of manju.

Roy's Station — 197 Jackson St. A coffee house in a restored 1930s gas station run by the founding family's descendants. Caffeinate in the old garage.

Minato — 617 N 6th St. A longtime family Japanese restaurant for tempura, teriyaki, and udon. The comfort dinner.

Kubota — Japantown. A classic Japanese American restaurant and sushi bar, a neighborhood mainstay. Sit at the counter.

Japanese American Museum of San Jose — 535 N 5th St. A museum telling the story of the community and the incarceration, moving and important. Take the time to read.

San Jose Buddhist Church Betsuin — 640 N 5th St. A grand temple at the heart of the community, host of the summer Obon festival. Time a visit for Obon.

Jackson Street — Jackson St. The walkable main strip of shops, restaurants, and a Sunday farmers market. Stroll the blocks.

Eight in Japantown: Nichi Bei Bussan, Shuei-Do Manju, Roy's Station, Minato, Kubota, the Japanese American Museum, the Buddhist temple, and Jackson Street. Where do you start?

item.description: Murphy Avenue is among Silicon Valley's oldest downtown streets, a pedestrian block of restaurants and a big Saturday market in the heart of Sunnyvale. Eig
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Sunnyvale (South Bay)

Murphy Avenue is among Silicon Valley's oldest downtown streets, a pedestrian block of restaurants and a big Saturday market in the heart of Sunnyvale. Eight downtown Sunnyvale stops.

DishDash — 190 S Murphy Ave. A wildly popular modern Middle Eastern restaurant, the mensaf and lamb shank the draws, a Valley favorite. Book ahead for dinner.

Il Postale — 127 S Murphy Ave. A warm Italian trattoria in an old post office, house pastas and a neighborhood feel. The reliable Italian.

Fibbar Magees — 156 S Murphy Ave. A proper Irish pub for a pint and live music on the pedestrian strip. Grab a booth.

Vaso Azzurro — 108 S Murphy Ave. A longtime Italian restaurant with a big menu and a loyal following. The old school dinner.

Bytes Cafe — 135 S Murphy Ave. A downtown coffee and sandwich stop for a work session or a quick bite. Caffeinate here.

Sunnyvale Farmers Market — S Murphy Ave. The big Saturday market filling the pedestrian street with produce and food stalls. Come Saturday morning.

Murphy Avenue — Murphy Ave. The historic car free block of restaurants, patios, and a summer concert series, the valley's oldest downtown street. Stroll and pick a patio.

Washington Park — Washington Ave. A green downtown park with a pool and playground just off Murphy. The family break.

Eight in Sunnyvale: DishDash, Il Postale, Fibbar Magees, Vaso Azzurro, Bytes Cafe, the Saturday market, Murphy Avenue, and Washington Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Larkspur (Marin)
item.description: Larkspur's Magnolia Avenue looks like a movie set, a redwood shaded main street anchored by a 1936 Art Deco theater, twenty minutes from the city by ferry.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Larkspur (Marin)

Larkspur's Magnolia Avenue looks like a movie set, a redwood shaded main street anchored by a 1936 Art Deco theater, twenty minutes from the city by ferry. Eight Larkspur stops.

Emporio Rulli — 464 Magnolia Ave. An Italian pasticceria and caffe for espresso, cakes, and a glass of wine, a Larkspur institution. Get a pastry and a cappuccino.

Lark Theater — 549 Magnolia Ave. A restored 1936 Art Deco cinema showing films and hosting events, the heart of downtown. Catch a movie.

Perry's on Magnolia — 234 Magnolia Ave. A lively all day American bar and grill on the main street, burgers, salads, and a busy patio. The reliable dinner.

Rustic Bakery — 1139 Magnolia Ave. The Marin bakery's original cafe for sourdough, flatbread crackers, and a good latte. The morning stop.

Marin Country Mart — 2257 Larkspur Landing Cir. An open air market by the ferry with shops, restaurants, a Sunday farmers market, and live music. Wander and graze.

Farmshop — Marin Country Mart. A farm to table restaurant and market at the Country Mart, seasonal California cooking. The special lunch.

Larkspur Ferry — Larkspur Landing. The ferry gliding to San Francisco in about thirty minutes with bay and skyline views. Ride it into the city.

Downtown Larkspur — Magnolia Ave. A few blocks of a redwood shaded historic main street, boutiques and cafes. Stroll the avenue.

Eight in Larkspur: Emporio Rulli, the Lark Theater, Perry's on Magnolia, Rustic Bakery, the Country Mart, Farmshop, the ferry, and downtown. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Fisherman's Wharf and Waterfront
item.description: The sea lions that pack the docks at Pier 39 showed up right after the 1989 earthquake and simply never left, now a permanent, barking fixture of San Franc
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Fisherman's Wharf and Waterfront

The sea lions that pack the docks at Pier 39 showed up right after the 1989 earthquake and simply never left, now a permanent, barking fixture of San Francisco's waterfront. Eight Fisherman's Wharf stops.

The Pier 39 sea lions — Pier 39. Dozens to hundreds of California sea lions hauled out on K-dock, free to watch, loudest and biggest in winter. Come for the barking crowd.

Boudin Bakery — 160 Jefferson St. The sourdough bakery baking since 1849, watch loaves shaped into crabs and turtles through the window. Get a bread bowl of clam chowder.

Musée Mécanique — Pier 45. A free to enter arcade of antique coin operated machines, fortune tellers and player pianos. Bring quarters.

Ghirardelli Square — 900 North Point St. The old chocolate factory turned shops and the original ice cream parlor. Split a hot fudge sundae.

Buena Vista Cafe — 2765 Hyde St. The bar that brought Irish coffee to America in 1952, still lining up glasses on the counter. Order an Irish coffee.

Fisherman's Wharf crab stands — Jefferson St. The sidewalk stands steaming fresh Dungeness crab and cracked crab cocktails in winter season. Get a crab cocktail.

Aquarium of the Bay — Pier 39. A walk through tunnel aquarium of local bay sea life, sharks and rays overhead. Walk under the sharks.

Powell-Hyde cable car turnaround — Hyde St at Beach. The end of the line where the cable car spins around by the bay. Ride it up over the hills.

Eight at the Wharf: the sea lions, Boudin, Musée Mécanique, Ghirardelli Square, the Buena Vista, the crab stands, Aquarium of the Bay, and the cable car turnaround. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Nob Hill
item.description: The Tonga Room on Nob Hill throws a tropical thunderstorm every half hour, rain and lightning over an indoor lagoon, inside a 1945 tiki bar in a grand hote
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Nob Hill

The Tonga Room on Nob Hill throws a tropical thunderstorm every half hour, rain and lightning over an indoor lagoon, inside a 1945 tiki bar in a grand hotel. Eight Nob Hill stops.

Tonga Room — 950 Mason St. A 1945 tiki bar in the Fairmont with a floating band and a fake rainstorm over a lagoon. Time a mai tai with the storm.

Grace Cathedral — 1100 California St. A Gothic cathedral with gilded Ghiberti doors and two labyrinths to walk, free to admire. Walk the outdoor labyrinth.

Top of the Mark — 999 California St. The sky lounge atop the Mark Hopkins with a wraparound city view. Sunset cocktail up top.

Huntington Park — 1 Nob Hill. A small elegant park with a fountain ringed by the grand hotels and Grace Cathedral. Sit by the fountain.

Nob Hill Cafe — 1152 Taylor St. A cozy neighborhood Italian trattoria beloved for its ravioli, tucked off the hill. The reliable dinner.

The Fairmont — 950 Mason St. A grand 1907 hotel with a lavish lobby rebuilt right after the earthquake, history to walk through. Wander the gilded lobby.

Cable Car Museum — 1201 Mason St. The free powerhouse where the cables that pull the cars still whir through giant wheels. See the machinery at work.

California Street cable car — California St. The first and quietest cable car line climbing over Nob Hill. Ride it up the hill.

Eight on Nob Hill: the Tonga Room, Grace Cathedral, Top of the Mark, Huntington Park, Nob Hill Cafe, the Fairmont, the Cable Car Museum, and the California Street cable car. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Dogpatch
item.description: Dogpatch is a rare San Francisco neighborhood whose Victorians survived the 1906 fire, an old shipyard district reborn with breweries, bakeries, and art ga
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Dogpatch

Dogpatch is a rare San Francisco neighborhood whose Victorians survived the 1906 fire, an old shipyard district reborn with breweries, bakeries, and art galleries. Eight Dogpatch stops.

Neighbor Bakehouse — 2343 Third St. A destination bakery for everything croissants, kimchi danishes, and morning buns out of an old industrial space. Get there early.

Museum of Craft and Design — 2569 Third St. A small, playful museum of craft, design, and making, with a great gift shop. See the current show.

Piccino — 1001 Minnesota St. A sunny corner spot for thin crust pizza and pasta with a cafe next door. The neighborhood dinner.

Harmonic Brewing — 1050 26th St. A warehouse brewery with long tables, house beers, and food trucks, dogs and kids welcome. Grab a pint at a picnic table.

Long Bridge Pizza — 2347 3rd St. A local pizzeria for blistered pies in a laid back room. The casual slice.

Third Rail — 628 20th St. A snug cocktail bar known for house made jerky and a great old fashioned. The nightcap.

Minnesota Street Project — 1275 Minnesota St. A cluster of contemporary art galleries in a converted warehouse, free to browse. Gallery hop under one roof.

Crane Cove Park — Illinois St. A bayfront park on the old shipyard with a little beach, lawns, and the historic gantry cranes. Walk the waterfront.

Eight in Dogpatch: Neighbor Bakehouse, the Museum of Craft and Design, Piccino, Harmonic Brewing, Long Bridge Pizza, Third Rail, Minnesota Street Project, and Crane Cove Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Inner Sunset (9th and Irving)
item.description: San Tung's dry fried chicken wings draw famously long lines to a modest Inner Sunset storefront, in a foggy neighborhood that quietly became a great eating
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Inner Sunset (9th and Irving)

San Tung's dry fried chicken wings draw famously long lines to a modest Inner Sunset storefront, in a foggy neighborhood that quietly became a great eating block. Eight Inner Sunset stops.

San Tung — 1031 Irving St. The Chinese spot famous citywide for its dry fried chicken wings in a garlic soy glaze. Order the wings, expect a wait.

Arizmendi Bakery — 1331 9th Ave. A worker owned co-op baking a different gourmet pizza every day plus killer scones and bread. Grab a slice of the daily pizza.

Marnee Thai — 1243 9th Ave. A beloved, plant filled Thai institution for the crispy angel wings and green curry. Get the angel wings.

Underdogs Tres — 1224 9th Ave. A surf themed taqueria and sports bar in the old Nopalito space, Baja fish tacos and games on. The casual taco night.

Hollow — 1435 Irving St. A tiny, charming cafe packed with curiosities for a pour over and a pastry. The cozy coffee stop.

The Little Shamrock — 807 Lincoln Way. A creaky Irish pub open since 1893, board games and a fireplace by Golden Gate Park. The old man bar hang.

Golden Gate Park museums — 9th Ave at Lincoln. The east end gateway to the de Young and the Academy of Sciences a short walk in. Pair a meal with a museum.

The 9th and Irving strip — 9th Ave at Irving. A dense few blocks of global food, bakeries, and shops by the N line and the park. Stroll and graze.

Eight in the Inner Sunset: San Tung, Arizmendi, Marnee Thai, Underdogs Tres, Hollow, the Little Shamrock, the park museums, and the 9th and Irving strip. Where do you start?

item.title: A Day in Berkeley
item.description: Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse on a Berkeley block in 1971 and more or less invented California cuisine, giving the Gourmet Ghetto its name. Eight Berkel
item.content:encoded:
A Day in Berkeley

Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse on a Berkeley block in 1971 and more or less invented California cuisine, giving the Gourmet Ghetto its name. Eight Berkeley stops.

Chez Panisse — 1517 Shattuck Ave. The restaurant that launched farm to table in 1971, a prix fixe downstairs and an à la carte cafe up. Book the cafe for the easier table.

Cheese Board Collective — 1512 Shattuck Ave. A worker owned bakery and cheese shop with a pizzeria next door serving one vegetarian pie a day, live jazz and a line. Get the pizza of the day.

The Gourmet Ghetto — North Shattuck Ave. The North Shattuck stretch that started the food revolution, cheese, chocolate, and cafes. Graze the whole block.

Fourth Street — 4th St. A leafy shopping district of boutiques, a great bookstore, and brunch spots. Stroll and shop.

Berkeley Bowl — 2020 Oregon St. A legendary grocery with a produce section like a farmers market, aisles of the obscure and fresh. Wander the produce jungle.

Telegraph Avenue — Telegraph Ave. The vibrant student strip by campus of bookstores, street vendors, and cheap eats. Browse the record shops.

UC Berkeley and the Campanile — University Dr. The historic campus with the Sather Tower bell tower you can ride up for a bay view. Take the elevator up the tower.

Berkeley Rose Garden — 1200 Euclid Ave. A terraced amphitheater of roses with a Golden Gate view, free and gorgeous in bloom. Time it for peak bloom.

Eight in Berkeley: Chez Panisse, the Cheese Board, the Gourmet Ghetto, Fourth Street, Berkeley Bowl, Telegraph Avenue, the Campanile, and the Rose Garden. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Fillmore, the Jazz District
item.description: The Fillmore was once called the Harlem of the West, a jazz mecca where the greats played nightclubs up and down the street, anchored by the legendary Fill
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Fillmore, the Jazz District

The Fillmore was once called the Harlem of the West, a jazz mecca where the greats played nightclubs up and down the street, anchored by the legendary Fillmore Auditorium. Eight Fillmore District stops.

The Fillmore — 1805 Geary Blvd. The legendary music hall where the psychedelic era exploded, still hosting big shows under chandeliers with apples at the door. Catch a concert.

Boom Boom Room — 1601 Fillmore St. A sultry blues and soul juke joint with live music most nights, a piece of the old Fillmore. Dance to the blues.

Sheba Piano Lounge — 1419 Fillmore St. An intimate lounge with live jazz seven nights and Ethiopian food by the fireplace. Order injera and a cocktail.

State Bird Provisions — 1529 Fillmore St. A Michelin starred spot serving small plates dim sum style off roving carts. Grab whatever comes by.

Black Bark BBQ — 1325 Fillmore St. A neighborhood smokehouse for brisket, ribs, and burnt ends on the historic strip. Get the brisket plate.

Fillmore Jazz Walk of Fame — Fillmore St. Bronze sidewalk plaques honoring the jazz legends who played the district. Read the sidewalk.

Japantown Peace Plaza — Post St at Buchanan. The pagoda and plaza at the edge of the Fillmore, host of festivals and cherry blossoms in spring. Stroll to the pagoda.

Fillmore Street shops — Fillmore St. An upscale stretch of boutiques and cafes running up the hill from the jazz blocks. Browse up the hill.

Eight in the Fillmore: the Fillmore, Boom Boom Room, Sheba, State Bird, Black Bark, the Jazz Walk of Fame, Japantown Peace Plaza, and Fillmore Street. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Divisadero and NoPa
item.description: The blocks north of the Panhandle were so overlooked that when a restaurant opened there it just called itself Nopa, and the name stuck to the whole neighb
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Divisadero and NoPa

The blocks north of the Panhandle were so overlooked that when a restaurant opened there it just called itself Nopa, and the name stuck to the whole neighborhood. Eight Divisadero and NoPa stops.

Nopa — 560 Divisadero St. The restaurant that named the neighborhood, wood fired California cooking served late in a buzzing room. Book late and order the pork chop.

Che Fico — 838 Divisadero St. A wildly popular Italian room upstairs with Roman Jewish dishes and a pink ceiling. Reserve well ahead.

The Mill — 736 Divisadero St. The bakery that made pricey toast a thing, thick cut bread and Four Barrel coffee. Get the cinnamon toast.

Bi-Rite Market — 550 Divisadero St. The beloved grocer's second shop, a deli, prepared foods, and soft serve to go. Build a Panhandle picnic.

4505 Burgers and BBQ — 705 Divisadero St. A smokehouse and burger joint with a backyard, brisket and a cheeseburger with frilly cheese edges. Get the best damn cheeseburger.

Beretta — 661 Divisadero St. A dark, lively Italian spot for thin crust pizza and cocktails on a big patio. The group dinner.

Horsefeather — 528 Divisadero St. A craft cocktail bar and restaurant with a retro vibe and inventive drinks. The nightcap.

Alamo Square — Steiner St at Hayes. The park with the Painted Ladies Victorians framing the downtown skyline, the classic postcard. Snap the Painted Ladies.

Eight in NoPa: Nopa, Che Fico, the Mill, Bi-Rite, 4505, Beretta, Horsefeather, and Alamo Square. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Bernal Heights
item.description: Bernal Heights climbs to a grassy summit with a full 360 view of San Francisco, over a village of a neighborhood where Cortland Avenue feels like a small t
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Bernal Heights

Bernal Heights climbs to a grassy summit with a full 360 view of San Francisco, over a village of a neighborhood where Cortland Avenue feels like a small town Main Street. Eight Bernal Heights stops.

Bernal Heights Summit — Bernal Heights Blvd. A grassy, rocky hilltop with a 360 view of the whole city and bay, a favorite for sunsets and dog walks. Hike up for the view.

Pinhole Coffee — 231 Cortland Ave. A warm, art filled corner cafe with local pastries, the neighborhood's living room. Start with a pour over.

Little Nepal — 925 Cortland Ave. A cozy Himalayan restaurant for momos and curries on the main strip. Order the momos.

Red Hill Books — 401 Cortland Ave. A tiny, well curated independent bookstore, a Cortland fixture. Browse a while.

Wild Side West — 424 Cortland Ave. A historic bar with a magical hidden garden out back, one of the oldest lesbian bars in the country. Have a drink in the garden.

Pig and Pie — 723 Cortland Ave. A little shop for house sausages and sweet or savory pies. Grab a sausage to go.

Emmy's Spaghetti Shack — Virginia Ave. A funky, beloved Italian American spot for big plates of spaghetti and meatballs. The comfort dinner.

Cortland Avenue — Cortland Ave. The walkable village strip of cafes, shops, and a small town feel any day. Stroll the whole street.

Eight in Bernal Heights: the summit, Pinhole Coffee, Little Nepal, Red Hill Books, Wild Side West, Pig and Pie, Emmy's, and Cortland Avenue. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Glen Park
item.description: Glen Park is a hidden village in the folds of San Francisco, a few blocks of shops wrapped around a wild rocky canyon where hawks nest in the middle of the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Glen Park

Glen Park is a hidden village in the folds of San Francisco, a few blocks of shops wrapped around a wild rocky canyon where hawks nest in the middle of the city. Eight Glen Park stops.

Glen Canyon Park — Elk St. A wild canyon of rock outcrops, a creek, and hawks, with trails and a rec center, surprisingly rugged for the city. Hike the canyon.

Gialina Pizzeria — 2842 Diamond St. A beloved thin crust pizzeria considered among the city's best, seasonal pies and a small room. Book or grab a pickup pizza.

La Corneta — 2834 Diamond St. A go to taqueria for big burritos and tacos on the village strip. The quick lunch.

Canyon Market — 2815 Diamond St. The village's full service grocer with a deli, prepared foods, and great bread. Build a picnic for the canyon.

Bird and Beckett Books — 653 Chenery St. A treasured independent bookstore and records shop with live jazz on Friday nights. Catch a set.

Le P'tit Laurent — 699 Chenery St. A warm French bistro for steak frites and a prix fixe, a neighborhood gem. The date night dinner.

Manor Coffee House — 321 Chenery St. A cozy corner cafe for coffee and a pastry off the main drag. The morning stop.

Glen Park village — Diamond St at Chenery. The walkable few blocks around the BART station, a small town feel in the city. Stroll the village.

Eight in Glen Park: Glen Canyon Park, Gialina, La Corneta, Canyon Market, Bird and Beckett, Le P'tit Laurent, Manor Coffee, and the village. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Alameda
item.description: Alameda is a whole island in the bay with Victorian streets, an aircraft carrier museum, and a Spirits Alley of distilleries on a decommissioned naval air
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Alameda

Alameda is a whole island in the bay with Victorian streets, an aircraft carrier museum, and a Spirits Alley of distilleries on a decommissioned naval air station. Eight Alameda stops.

Park Street — Park St. The walkable main drag of Victorian storefronts, restaurants, and an old movie palace. Stroll and window shop.

Tucker's Ice Cream — 1349 Park St. An old fashioned ice cream parlor on Park Street since 1941, super creamed scoops and fresh fudge. Get a waffle cone.

Alameda Theatre — 2317 Central Ave. A restored 1932 Art Deco movie palace still showing films downtown. Catch a movie under the marquee.

Crown Memorial State Beach — Shore Line Dr. A 2.5 mile bay beach with warm, calm, swimmable water and a skyline view. Swim on a warm afternoon.

USS Hornet Museum — 707 W Hornet Ave. A wartime aircraft carrier turned museum at the old naval base, planes and stories aboard. Tour the flight deck.

Spirits Alley — 2601 Monarch St. A cluster of distilleries and breweries in old airplane hangars at Alameda Point, tastings with a bay view. Taste around the hangars.

Webster Street — Webster St. The west end commercial strip of global eats and shops, quieter than Park Street. The local's block.

Alameda Point waterfront — Alameda Point. The old naval air station's edge with a straight on San Francisco skyline view across the bay. Watch the skyline at sunset.

Eight in Alameda: Park Street, Tucker's, the Alameda Theatre, Crown Beach, the USS Hornet, Spirits Alley, Webster Street, and Alameda Point. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's West Portal
item.description: West Portal is the small town Main Street hiding inside San Francisco, a walkable village where a streetcar tunnel empties onto the buzziest new dining str
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's West Portal

West Portal is the small town Main Street hiding inside San Francisco, a walkable village where a streetcar tunnel empties onto the buzziest new dining strip in the city. Eight West Portal stops.

Mozzarella di Bufala — 69 W Portal Ave, SF. The neighborhood pizzeria locals swear by, blistered crust and a line out the door on weekends. Get the margherita.

Elena's Mexican Restaurant — 255 W Portal Ave, SF. The Original Joe's family's 100 seat Mexican American room, huge and always buzzing. Come hungry.

Khao Tiew — 272 Claremont Blvd, SF. A modern Thai spot just off the strip drawing citywide crowds for its curries. Order the khao soi.

Binu Bonu — 230 W Portal Ave, SF. A wine bar from the La Ciccia team pouring Sardinian bottles you cannot find elsewhere. Let them pick.

George's Donuts — 163 W Portal Ave, SF. A marble and velvet donut and coffee stop that turned a plain morning run into a scene. Go early.

Hardware Coffee Co — 32 W Portal Ave, SF. An all day cafe in the old Papenhausen hardware store, coffee, wine, and a florist under one roof. Grab a window seat.

Little Original Joe's — 393 W Portal Ave, SF. The Italian American classic that kicked off the strip's revival, red sauce and martinis. Sit at the counter.

Bookshop West Portal — 80 W Portal Ave, SF. An independent bookstore that anchors the block, staff picks and author nights. Leave with something.

Eight in West Portal: Mozzarella di Bufala, Elena's, Khao Tiew, Binu Bonu, George's Donuts, Hardware Coffee, Little Original Joe's, and Bookshop West Portal. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Cole Valley
item.description: Cole Valley is the pocket village where the N Judah streetcar surfaces from its tunnel beside a 1930s soda fountain that still hand cranks egg creams. Eigh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Cole Valley

Cole Valley is the pocket village where the N Judah streetcar surfaces from its tunnel beside a 1930s soda fountain that still hand cranks egg creams. Eight Cole Valley stops.

Zazie — 941 Cole St, SF. The French bistro locals line up for at brunch, famous for gingerbread pancakes and a leafy back patio. Put your name down.

The Ice Cream Bar — 815 Cole St, SF. A restored 1930s soda fountain serving egg creams and phosphates from a real apothecary counter. Order a phosphate.

Kezar Bar and Restaurant — 900 Cole St, SF. A cozy corner pub named for the old stadium, dark wood and a solid burger. Grab a booth.

InoVino — 108 Carl St, SF. A snug wine bar pouring Italian by the glass to a neighborhood crowd. Ask for a taste first.

Say Cheese — 856 Cole St, SF. A cheese shop since the 1970s stacked with wedges and picnic fixings. Build a board.

Crepes on Cole — 100 Carl St, SF. A casual creperie by the streetcar stop, sweet and savory, good for a quick bite. Get a savory buckwheat.

Bambino's Ristorante — 945 Cole St, SF. A family Italian room with red sauce classics and a warm regular crowd. Split the pasta.

Cole Valley Tavern — 960 Cole St, SF. A newer corner tavern for cocktails and West Coast comfort food. Come for happy hour.

Eight in Cole Valley: Zazie, the Ice Cream Bar, Kezar, InoVino, Say Cheese, Crepes on Cole, Bambino's, and Cole Valley Tavern. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's SoMa and Yerba Buena
item.description: Yerba Buena Gardens is a rooftop lawn and waterfall built on top of an underground convention hall, so Moscone Center runs right beneath the grass. Eight S
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's SoMa and Yerba Buena

Yerba Buena Gardens is a rooftop lawn and waterfall built on top of an underground convention hall, so Moscone Center runs right beneath the grass. Eight SoMa and Yerba Buena stops.

SFMOMA — 151 3rd St, SF. Seven floors of modern art behind a rippling white facade, with a living wall and free entry under 18. Start up top.

Yerba Buena Gardens — 760 Howard St, SF. A rooftop lawn with a waterfall memorial to Martin Luther King Jr, the calm heart of SoMa. Bring lunch.

Museum of the African Diaspora — 685 Mission St, SF. A museum tracing the global African story across art and history. See the slave narratives floor.

Salesforce Park — 425 Mission St, SF. An elevated park floating above the transit center, a green mile of gardens in the sky. Ride the gondola up.

Metreon — 135 4th St, SF. A shopping and dining complex with a rooftop terrace overlooking the gardens. Eat on the terrace.

Children's Creativity Museum — 221 4th St, SF. A hands on museum for kids with a restored 1906 carousel out front. Ride the carousel.

Yerba Buena Center for the Arts — 701 Mission St, SF. A contemporary arts center with bold gallery shows and live performances. Check the current exhibit.

Moscone Center — 747 Howard St, SF. The giant convention hall under the gardens, the engine of the whole district. Walk the esplanade.

Eight in SoMa and Yerba Buena: SFMOMA, the gardens, MoAD, Salesforce Park, the Metreon, the Creativity Museum, YBCA, and Moscone. Where do you start?

item.title: The San Francisco Embarcadero
item.description: The Embarcadero was a double deck freeway until the 1989 quake knocked it down, and the waterfront boulevard that replaced it is now the best flat walk in
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco Embarcadero

The Embarcadero was a double deck freeway until the 1989 quake knocked it down, and the waterfront boulevard that replaced it is now the best flat walk in San Francisco. Eight Embarcadero stops.

Exploratorium — Pier 15, SF. A giant hands on science museum on the water with hundreds of exhibits you touch and play with. Do the Tactile Dome.

Ferry Building Marketplace — 1 The Embarcadero, SF. A grand 1898 hall of local food stalls under a clock tower, with a farmers market outside. Graze the stalls.

Vaillancourt Fountain — Embarcadero Plaza, SF. A blocky concrete fountain you can walk inside, loved and argued over in equal measure. Walk through it.

Cupid's Span — Rincon Park, SF. A giant bow and arrow sculpture planted in the lawn against the Bay Bridge. Frame the bridge behind it.

Red's Java House — Pier 30, SF. A no frills waterfront shack slinging cheap burgers and beer since the 1950s. Get a double and a beer.

Delancey Street Restaurant — 600 The Embarcadero, SF. A waterfront restaurant run by a renowned nonprofit, big menu and a bay view. Sit on the patio.

Oracle Park — 24 Willie Mays Plaza, SF. The Giants ballpark on the bay where home runs splash into McCovey Cove. Walk the waterfront arcade free.

Pier 14 — The Embarcadero, SF. A slim public pier that juts into the bay for a straight on Bay Bridge and skyline view. Walk to the end at dusk.

Eight on the Embarcadero: the Exploratorium, the Ferry Building, Vaillancourt Fountain, Cupid's Span, Red's Java House, Delancey Street, Oracle Park, and Pier 14. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Pleasanton
item.description: Pleasanton hides a picture book Main Street in the Tri-Valley, where a drive through dairy has scooped soft serve since before the freeways arrived. Eight
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Pleasanton

Pleasanton hides a picture book Main Street in the Tri-Valley, where a drive through dairy has scooped soft serve since before the freeways arrived. Eight Pleasanton stops.

Gay Nineties Pizza Co — 288 Main St, Pleasanton. A beloved old school parlor slinging award winning pies for decades. Get a pitcher and a pepperoni.

Meadowlark Dairy — 57 W Neal St, Pleasanton. A drive through dairy famous for soft serve, busy even on cold days. Roll up for a cone.

Baci Bistro and Bar — 500 Main St, Pleasanton. A downtown Italian room with a retro glow and a lively bar. Book a booth.

Towne Center Books — 555 Main St, Pleasanton. An independent bookstore that anchors the downtown, author events and staff picks. Ask for a rec.

Museum on Main — 603 Main St, Pleasanton. A local history museum in an old storefront telling the valley's story. Catch a walking tour.

Firehouse Arts Center — 4444 Railroad Ave, Pleasanton. A restored firehouse turned theater and gallery. Check the marquee.

The Rose Hotel — 807 Main St, Pleasanton. A boutique hotel on Main Street with old world rooms and a downtown perch. Stay the weekend.

Alameda County Fairgrounds — 4501 Pleasanton Ave, Pleasanton. The historic fairgrounds and horse track that hosts the summer county fair. Time a visit to the fair.

Eight in Pleasanton: Gay Nineties Pizza, Meadowlark Dairy, Baci Bistro, Towne Center Books, Museum on Main, the Firehouse, the Rose Hotel, and the Fairgrounds. Where do you start?

item.title: Bay Area Rooftop Bars
item.description: The Bay Area saves its best skyline views for its rooftops, from a Market Street penthouse bar to a Berkeley beer garden over Shattuck. Eight Bay Area roof
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Rooftop Bars

The Bay Area saves its best skyline views for its rooftops, from a Market Street penthouse bar to a Berkeley beer garden over Shattuck. Eight Bay Area rooftop bars.

Charmaine's — 1100 Market St, SF. A penthouse rooftop at the Proper Hotel with firepits and a sweeping city view. Get there for sunset.

620 Jones — 620 Jones St, SF. A big heated terrace bar off Union Square, planted and lively year round. Come for happy hour.

Kaiyo Rooftop — 701 3rd St, SF. A plant draped Nikkei rooftop near Oracle Park with Peruvian Japanese small plates. Order a pisco.

Cavaña — 100 Channel St, SF. A Mission Bay rooftop at the LUMA Hotel with firepits and DJ nights near the ballpark. Grab a firepit.

Rise Over Run — 950 Market St, SF. A greenhouse style rooftop atop The LINE hotel that shrugs off the fog. Sit in the atrium.

Dirty Habit — 12 4th St, SF. A fifth floor terrace lounge at Hotel Zelos with craft cocktails and small plates. Try the oysters.

The View Lounge — 780 Mission St, SF. A top floor sky lounge in the Marriott Marquis with floor to ceiling skyline windows. Go up at dusk.

Comal — 2020 Shattuck Ave, Berkeley. A downtown Berkeley rooftop beer garden over a modern Mexican kitchen. Start with a margarita.

Eight Bay Area rooftops: Charmaine's, 620 Jones, Kaiyo, Cavaña, Rise Over Run, Dirty Habit, the View Lounge, and Comal. Which view first?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Polk Street
item.description: Swan Oyster Depot has served raw oysters from the same marble counter on Polk Street since 1912, cash only, no reservations, a line out the door every day.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Polk Street

Swan Oyster Depot has served raw oysters from the same marble counter on Polk Street since 1912, cash only, no reservations, a line out the door every day. Eight Polk Street stops.

Swan Oyster Depot — 1517 Polk St, SF. The 1912 seafood counter locals line up for, oysters and cracked crab on ice. Get the combo and a beer.

Bob's Donuts — 1621 Polk St, SF. A 24 hour donut institution famous for a giant apple fritter. Try the fritter warm.

Cheese Plus — 2001 Polk St, SF. A corner cheese shop and deli building serious grilled cheese and picnic boards. Order the classic grilled cheese.

Amélie — 1754 Polk St, SF. A candlelit French wine bar with flights and a lively happy hour. Do a flight.

Nick's Crispy Tacos — 1500 Broadway at Polk, SF. A rowdy taco spot and bar, fish tacos done Nick's Way. Order them Nick's Way.

The Bell Tower — 1900 Polk St, SF. A classic corner pub with big windows and a solid brunch. Grab a window table.

Leopold's — 2400 Polk St, SF. An Austrian tavern with pretzels, schnitzel, and boots of beer. Split a boot.

House of Prime Rib — 1906 Van Ness Ave, SF. The 1949 prime rib palace a block off Polk, carved tableside from silver carts. Book ahead for the City cut.

Eight on Polk Street: Swan Oyster Depot, Bob's Donuts, Cheese Plus, Amélie, Nick's Crispy Tacos, the Bell Tower, Leopold's, and House of Prime Rib. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Potrero Hill
item.description: Potrero Hill catches more sun than almost any corner of foggy San Francisco, and its 18th Street spine is a village of sourdough pizza and hillside cafes m
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Potrero Hill

Potrero Hill catches more sun than almost any corner of foggy San Francisco, and its 18th Street spine is a village of sourdough pizza and hillside cafes most of the city drives past. Eight Potrero Hill stops.

Goat Hill Pizza — 300 Connecticut St, SF. A Potrero classic making sourdough crust pizza since 1975, Monday all you can eat. Come for the sourdough.

Plow — 1299 18th St, SF. The brunch spot with a line, famous for lemon ricotta pancakes and the potatoes. Get there early.

Farley's — 1315 18th St, SF. A beloved indie coffeehouse and community hub since 1989. Linger with a latte.

Chez Maman — 1401 18th St, SF. A tiny French bistro with mussels, crepes, and a cult burger. Squeeze in at the counter.

Aperto — 1434 18th St, SF. A neighborhood Italian room with handmade pasta and regulars at every table. Ask the daily pasta.

Christopher's Books — 1400 18th St, SF. A cozy corner indie bookstore anchoring the strip. Leave with a staff pick.

Klein's Deli — 501 Connecticut St, SF. A corner deli and market stacking big sandwiches for the hill. Grab one to go.

The Good Life Grocery — 1524 20th St, SF. A Potrero independent grocery since 1974, a neighborhood cornerstone. Pick up picnic supplies.

Eight on Potrero Hill: Goat Hill Pizza, Plow, Farley's, Chez Maman, Aperto, Christopher's Books, Klein's Deli, and the Good Life Grocery. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Outer Richmond
item.description: Out where San Francisco runs into the ocean fog, the Outer Richmond hides a sleeper strip of Balboa Street wine bars, a 1953 Russian bakery, and old school
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Outer Richmond

Out where San Francisco runs into the ocean fog, the Outer Richmond hides a sleeper strip of Balboa Street wine bars, a 1953 Russian bakery, and old school burger joints most of the city never reaches. Eight Outer Richmond stops.

Simple Pleasures Cafe — 3434 Balboa St, SF. A bohemian coffeehouse and SF Legacy Business since 1978, live music some nights. Sink into a couch.

Balboa Theatre — 3630 Balboa St, SF. A nearly century old twin cinema showing new releases and old indies. Catch a matinee.

Pizzetta 211 — 211 23rd Ave, SF. A tiny beloved wood fired pizzeria a block off Balboa, a weekly changing menu. Go early, it is small.

Ton Kiang — 5821 Geary Blvd, SF. A Cantonese and Hakka favorite with weekend cart dim sum. Come for the dumplings.

Cinderella Bakery — 436 Balboa St, SF. A Russian bakery and cafe since 1953, piroshki and black bread. Get a piroshki.

Kabuto — 5121 Geary Blvd, SF. A revered tiny omakase sushi bar in the Richmond. Sit at the bar.

Pearl 6101 — 6101 California St, SF. A sunny neighborhood restaurant with a great oyster happy hour near the Presidio edge. Do the oyster hour.

Bill's Place — 2315 Clement St, SF. A 1959 burger joint with a garden patio and named burgers. Order a namesake burger.

Eight in the Outer Richmond: Simple Pleasures, the Balboa Theatre, Pizzetta 211, Ton Kiang, Cinderella Bakery, Kabuto, Pearl 6101, and Bill's Place. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Jackson Square and the Classics
item.description: Tadich Grill has been open since 1849, the oldest restaurant in California, and it anchors a downtown pocket of Gold Rush saloons and white tablecloth room
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Jackson Square and the Classics

Tadich Grill has been open since 1849, the oldest restaurant in California, and it anchors a downtown pocket of Gold Rush saloons and white tablecloth rooms that outlasted everything around them. Eight downtown classics.

Tadich Grill — 240 California St, SF. California's oldest restaurant, since 1849, cioppino and sand dabs at a wood counter. Order the cioppino.

Sam's Grill — 374 Bush St, SF. An 1867 seafood house of curtained booths and old world service. Get a curtained booth.

The Old Ship Saloon — 298 Pacific Ave, SF. A saloon on the site of a beached Gold Rush ship, pouring since 1851. Toast the ship below the floor.

Kokkari Estiatorio — 200 Jackson St, SF. A fireside Greek institution in Jackson Square, lamb and meze. Get the lamb chops.

Cotogna — 490 Pacific Ave, SF. A rustic Italian favorite with wood fired pasta and pizza. Book ahead for the pasta.

Bix — 56 Gold St, SF. A supper club down a hidden alley with martinis and live jazz. Order a martini upstairs.

Comstock Saloon — 155 Columbus Ave, SF. A restored Barbary Coast saloon with classic cocktails and a ragtime piano. Sit at the antique bar.

William Stout Architectural Books — 804 Montgomery St, SF. A landmark design and art bookstore in Jackson Square since 1974. Browse the art shelves.

Eight downtown classics: Tadich Grill, Sam's Grill, the Old Ship Saloon, Kokkari, Cotogna, Bix, Comstock Saloon, and William Stout Books. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Presidio Heights
item.description: Sacramento Street through Presidio Heights is where San Francisco locals shop when they want quiet boutiques and a Michelin kitchen instead of a crowd, lea
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Presidio Heights

Sacramento Street through Presidio Heights is where San Francisco locals shop when they want quiet boutiques and a Michelin kitchen instead of a crowd, leafy blocks of storefronts near the Presidio gate. Eight Sacramento Street stops.

Spruce — 3640 Sacramento St, SF. A Michelin starred neighborhood restaurant with a famous burger at the bar. Get the Spruce burger.

Books Inc — 3515 California St, SF. The Laurel Village outpost of the Bay Area's oldest bookseller, since 1851. Catch an author night.

Cal-Mart — 3585 California St, SF. A beloved independent grocery with a great butcher and deli counter. Grab lunch at the deli.

Bryan's — 3445 California St, SF. A high end market and butcher, prime meat and prepared foods. Pick up a roast.

Osteria — 3277 Sacramento St, SF. A snug family trattoria with handmade pasta. Split the pasta.

Sue Fisher King — 3067 Sacramento St, SF. A refined home and gift boutique, linens and tableware. Find a hostess gift.

Ella's — 500 Presidio Ave, SF. A corner brunch institution famous for sticky buns and chicken hash. Come for the sticky buns.

b — Patisserie. 2821 California St, SF. A celebrated French patisserie near Presidio Heights, the kouign amann is the move. Get the kouign amann.

Eight in Presidio Heights: Spruce, Books Inc, Cal-Mart, Bryan's, Osteria, Sue Fisher King, Ella's, and b. Patisserie. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Union Square
item.description: Union Square is where San Francisco's cable cars turn around by hand on a giant wooden turntable, ringed by grand hotels, department stores, and a martini
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Union Square

Union Square is where San Francisco's cable cars turn around by hand on a giant wooden turntable, ringed by grand hotels, department stores, and a martini bar straight out of The Maltese Falcon. Eight Union Square stops.

Powell Street Cable Car Turnaround — Powell St at Market, SF. The downtown terminus where crews spin the cars by hand. Watch them turn a car.

John's Grill — 63 Ellis St, SF. A 1908 chophouse out of The Maltese Falcon, martinis and steaks. Order the Sam Spade lamb chops.

Westin St — Francis. 335 Powell St, SF. The 1904 grand hotel on the square with a famous magic clock in the lobby. Meet under the clock.

Britex Fabrics — 117 Post St, SF. A four floor fabric emporium and city institution since 1952. Get lost on the trim floor.

Maiden Lane — Maiden Lane, SF. A pedestrian shopping lane with the city's only Frank Lloyd Wright building. Walk the Wright spiral.

Union Square Park — 333 Post St, SF. The palm ringed heart of downtown under the Dewey victory column. Sit and people watch.

The Rotunda at Neiman Marcus — 150 Stockton St, SF. Lunch under a 1909 stained glass dome, popovers and tea. Come for a popover.

Chinatown Dragon Gate — Grant Ave at Bush St, SF. The dragon crowned gateway a block off the square into Chinatown. Walk through into Chinatown.

Eight at Union Square: the cable car turnaround, John's Grill, the Westin St Francis, Britex Fabrics, Maiden Lane, Union Square Park, the Neiman Marcus Rotunda, and the Chinatown Gate. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day On Burlingame Avenue
item.description: Burlingame Avenue is the Peninsula's small town main street, a walkable stretch of pizza ovens and candy counters just south of San Francisco, with the old
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day On Burlingame Avenue

Burlingame Avenue is the Peninsula's small town main street, a walkable stretch of pizza ovens and candy counters just south of San Francisco, with the old railway depot anchoring the far end. Eight Burlingame Avenue stops.

Il Fornaio — 327 Lorton Ave, Burlingame. A bustling Italian bakery and trattoria off the avenue, wood fired everything. Start with the bread basket.

Crepevine — 1310 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. A NorCal creperie for sweet and savory crepes and big breakfasts. Get a savory crepe.

Preston's Candy and Ice Cream — 1213 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. A 1946 candy and ice cream parlor making chocolates in house. Get a hand dipped cone.

Copenhagen Bakery — 1216 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. A Danish bakery and cafe with marzipan cakes and open faced sandwiches. Take home a kringle.

Steelhead Brewing — 333 California Dr, Burlingame. A longtime brewpub by the depot, house lagers and burgers. Grab a house lager.

Burlingame Railroad Station — 290 California Dr, Burlingame. The 1894 depot, among the oldest still in use in California. See the tile roof.

Books Inc — 1375 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. The avenue's independent bookstore branch, story times and staff picks. Grab a beach read.

Village Host Pizza and Grill — 1451 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. A casual local pizza and salad spot on the avenue. Split a pie.

Eight on Burlingame Avenue: Il Fornaio, Crepevine, Preston's, Copenhagen Bakery, Steelhead Brewing, the 1894 depot, Books Inc, and Village Host Pizza. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Cow Hollow and Union Street
item.description: Balboa Cafe has poured drinks on the same Cow Hollow corner since 1913, the anchor of a Union Street stretch of brunch spots and boutiques where cows once
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Cow Hollow and Union Street

Balboa Cafe has poured drinks on the same Cow Hollow corner since 1913, the anchor of a Union Street stretch of brunch spots and boutiques where cows once grazed the marsh. Eight Union Street stops.

Rose's Cafe — 2298 Union St, SF. The sunny corner brunch spot with mimosas and a sidewalk full of regulars. Get a window table.

Perry's — 1944 Union St, SF. A Union Street institution for burgers, martinis, and streetside people watching. Order the burger.

Balboa Cafe — 3199 Fillmore St, SF. A saloon since 1913, dark wood and a famous namesake burger. Belly up to the bar.

West Coast Wine and Cheese — 2165 Union St, SF. A cozy wine bar pouring California by the glass with boards to match. Ask for a flight.

Blue Barn — 2105 Union St, SF. A bright spot for big made to order salads and sandwiches. Build a chopped salad.

The Brixton — 2140 Union St, SF. A lively bar and grill packed on game nights. Come for happy hour.

Roam Artisan Burgers — 1785 Union St, SF. Grass fed burgers built your way with house sauces. Add the sweet potato fries.

Brazen Head — 3166 Buchanan St, SF. A hidden pub with no sign, candlelit and cash only, a Cow Hollow secret. Find the unmarked door.

Eight on Union Street: Rose's Cafe, Perry's, Balboa Cafe, West Coast Wine and Cheese, Blue Barn, the Brixton, Roam, and the Brazen Head. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Lower Haight
item.description: Toronado has poured a legendary beer list on Lower Haight since 1987, the loud anchor of a compact bar strip locals call the triangle of alcohol. Eight Low
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Lower Haight

Toronado has poured a legendary beer list on Lower Haight since 1987, the loud anchor of a compact bar strip locals call the triangle of alcohol. Eight Lower Haight stops.

Toronado — 547 Haight St, SF. A legendary beer bar since 1987 with a chalkboard of rare taps. Order something Belgian.

Mad Dog in the Fog — 530 Haight St, SF. A British pub for footy, fry ups, and pints. Catch a match.

Molotov's — 582 Haight St, SF. A punky dive with a pool table and no pretense. Stay late.

Noc Noc — 557 Haight St, SF. A cave like bar of steampunk booths and cheap beer and sake. Grab a booth.

Kate's Kitchen — 471 Haight St, SF. A beloved brunch counter with big biscuits and hush puppies. Come hungry, cash helps.

Uva Enoteca — 568 Haight St, SF. A warm Italian wine bar with small plates and by the glass pours. Split the burrata.

The Little Chihuahua — 581 Haight St, SF. A local favorite for sustainable tacos and plantain burritos. Get the plantain burrito.

Danny Coyle's — 668 Haight St, SF. An Irish pub with a patio, trivia, and live music. Post up on the patio.

Eight in Lower Haight: Toronado, Mad Dog in the Fog, Molotov's, Noc Noc, Kate's Kitchen, Uva Enoteca, the Little Chihuahua, and Danny Coyle's. Where do you start?

item.title: SF's Mission Bay
item.description: Mission Bay went from rail yards and warehouses to San Francisco's newest neighborhood in a decade, built around the Warriors arena, a food truck park, and
item.content:encoded:
SF's Mission Bay

Mission Bay went from rail yards and warehouses to San Francisco's newest neighborhood in a decade, built around the Warriors arena, a food truck park, and a creek where houseboats still bob. Eight Mission Bay stops.

Chase Center — 1 Warriors Way, SF. The Warriors arena and its plaza, concerts and games on the bay. Catch an event at Thrive City.

Gott's Roadside — 151 Warriors Way, SF. A modern roadside burger and shake stand at Thrive City. Get a burger and a shake.

Spark Social SF — 601 Mission Bay Blvd N, SF. A rotating food truck park with fire pits and a beer garden. Graze the trucks.

The Ramp — 855 Terry Francois Blvd, SF. A ramshackle bayfront restaurant with a patio and weekend live music. Sit on the water.

Mission Creek Park — Channel St at 4th, SF. A little waterway lined with houseboats and kayakers. Watch the houseboats.

Philz Coffee — 165 Berry St, SF. The Mint Mojito crowd's morning stop by the creek. Order a Mint Mojito iced.

UCSF Mission Bay — 1825 4th St, SF. The research campus green with public art and a quiet quad. Walk the Koret Quad.

Crane Cove Park — 18 Georgia St, SF. A waterfront park with a little beach and the old shipyard cranes. Bring a blanket.

Eight in Mission Bay: Chase Center, Gott's, Spark Social, the Ramp, Mission Creek Park, Philz, UCSF, and Crane Cove Park. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Hayes Valley
item.description: Hayes Valley traded a double deck freeway for a leafy boutique district after the 1989 quake brought it down, and now its blocks pack Michelin kitchens, ma
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Hayes Valley

Hayes Valley traded a double deck freeway for a leafy boutique district after the 1989 quake brought it down, and now its blocks pack Michelin kitchens, macarons, and nitrogen ice cream. Eight Hayes Valley stops.

Rich Table — 199 Gough St, SF. A Michelin star kitchen famous for sardine chips and porcini doughnuts. Start with the doughnuts.

Absinthe Brasserie — 398 Hayes St, SF. A French brasserie and cocktail bar, the neighborhood's grand old room. Order a classic cocktail.

Souvla — 517 Hayes St, SF. A fast fine Greek spot known for spit roasted lamb and frozen Greek yogurt. Get the lamb salad.

Hayes Street Grill — 320 Hayes St, SF. A seafood classic by the opera house since 1979. Order the fish of the day.

Birba — 458 Grove St, SF. A tiny wine bar with a heated patio and Italian pours. Grab a patio seat.

Smitten Ice Cream — 432 Octavia St, SF. Ice cream frozen to order with liquid nitrogen in a little kiosk. Watch it freeze.

Chantal Guillon — 437 Hayes St, SF. A macaron atelier with rows of pastel shells. Build a box of six.

Anina — 482 Hayes St, SF. A playful cocktail bar with frozen drinks and a patio. Do a frozen negroni.

Eight in Hayes Valley: Rich Table, Absinthe, Souvla, Hayes Street Grill, Birba, Smitten, Chantal Guillon, and Anina. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Los Gatos
item.description: Los Gatos tucks a Michelin Greek room, a cult bread bakery, and a 1927 movie palace into a walkable downtown at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Eight
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Los Gatos

Los Gatos tucks a Michelin Greek room, a cult bread bakery, and a 1927 movie palace into a walkable downtown at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Eight Los Gatos stops.

Dio Deka — 210 E Main St, Los Gatos. A Michelin Greek room with a fireplace at Hotel Los Gatos. Book the lamb chops.

Manresa Bread — 276 N Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. The cult bakery spun off from the famed restaurant, kouign amann and country loaves. Grab a pastry.

Los Gatos Coffee Roasting — 101 W Main St, Los Gatos. A downtown roaster and cafe on the corner for decades. Sit outside with a latte.

The Bywater — 532 N Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. Chef David Kinch's New Orleans kitchen, gumbo and po'boys with a raw bar. Order the gumbo.

Forbes Mill Steakhouse — 206 N Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. A downtown steakhouse named for the town's old flour mill. Get a martini and a ribeye.

Icing on the Cake — 50 N Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. A bakery famous for its towering layer cakes. Take home a slice.

Testarossa Winery — 300A College Ave, Los Gatos. A tasting room in an old stone winery, Pinot and Chardonnay. Taste a flight.

Los Gatos Theatre — 41 N Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. A 1927 movie palace with a neon marquee still lighting Main Street. Catch a show.

Eight in Los Gatos: Dio Deka, Manresa Bread, Los Gatos Coffee Roasting, the Bywater, Forbes Mill, Icing on the Cake, Testarossa, and the theatre. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Mountain View's Castro Street
item.description: Mountain View's Castro Street is Silicon Valley's real downtown, a walkable strip where engineers line up for tapas, wood fired pizza, and a Michelin tasti
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Mountain View's Castro Street

Mountain View's Castro Street is Silicon Valley's real downtown, a walkable strip where engineers line up for tapas, wood fired pizza, and a Michelin tasting menu hidden off the main drag. Eight Castro Street stops.

Cascal — 400 Castro St, Mountain View. A lively tapas bar of Spanish and Latin plates and sangria. Share a table of tapas.

Scratch — 401 Castro St, Mountain View. A from scratch American kitchen with a patio and brunch. Come for weekend brunch.

Doppio Zero — 160 Castro St, Mountain View. A Neapolitan pizzeria with a certified wood fired oven. Order a Margherita.

Red Rock Coffee — 201 Castro St, Mountain View. A two story community cafe with open mics and laptops. Grab an upstairs seat.

Books Inc — 317 Castro St, Mountain View. The downtown independent bookstore with author nights. Leave with a staff pick.

Casa Lupe — 253 Castro St, Mountain View. A family Mexican spot with margaritas and combo plates. Get the enchiladas.

Chez TJ — 938 Villa St, Mountain View. A Michelin tasting menu tucked in a Victorian off the strip. Book the tasting.

Steins Beer Garden — 895 Villa St, Mountain View. A big beer garden with house brews and long tables. Post up outside.

Eight on Castro Street: Cascal, Scratch, Doppio Zero, Red Rock Coffee, Books Inc, Casa Lupe, Chez TJ, and Steins. Where do you start?

item.description: Swensen's has scooped ice cream at the top of the Hyde Street cable car line since 1948, the sweet anchor of a Russian Hill worth the climb for crooked str
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Russian Hill

Swensen's has scooped ice cream at the top of the Hyde Street cable car line since 1948, the sweet anchor of a Russian Hill worth the climb for crooked streets and hidden stairways. Eight Russian Hill stops.

Swensen's Ice Cream — 1999 Hyde St, SF. The original parlor since 1948 at Hyde and Union, small batch scoops. Get a hot fudge sundae.

Frascati — 1901 Hyde St, SF. A cozy Italian bistro right on the cable car line. Book a window table.

Za Pizza — 1919 Hyde St, SF. A neighborhood slice shop with thin crust pies and a chill vibe. Grab two slices.

Pesce — 2227 Polk St, SF. A Venetian seafood spot built for grazing small plates. Order a spread of cicchetti.

Helmand Palace — 2424 Van Ness Ave, SF. A longtime Afghan restaurant famous for its pumpkin kaddo. Start with the kaddo.

Lombard Street — Lombard St at Hyde, SF. The famously crooked block of switchbacks and flower beds. Walk down the brick curves.

Ina Coolbrith Park — Vallejo St at Taylor, SF. A steep terraced hillside park with a knockout bay view. Climb up at golden hour.

Macondray Lane — Macondray Ln, SF. A hidden wooden staircase lane, the model for the Barbary Lane of Tales of the City. Find the secret stairs.

Eight in Russian Hill: Swensen's, Frascati, Za Pizza, Pesce, Helmand Palace, Lombard Street, Ina Coolbrith Park, and Macondray Lane. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Noe Valley
item.description: Noe Valley is San Francisco's sunny stroller valley, a 24th Street of bakeries and bistros tucked just below the fog line where the J Church rattles past.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Noe Valley

Noe Valley is San Francisco's sunny stroller valley, a 24th Street of bakeries and bistros tucked just below the fog line where the J Church rattles past. Eight Noe Valley stops.

Firefly — 4288 24th St, SF. A cozy contemporary American spot that has owned date night for decades. Book a table.

Noe Valley Bakery — 4073 24th St, SF. The neighborhood bakery for morning buns and celebration cakes. Grab a morning bun.

La Ciccia — 291 30th St, SF. A beloved Sardinian restaurant famous for spicy octopus and bottarga. Order the octopus.

La Boulangerie de San Francisco — 3898 24th St, SF. A French bakery cafe for kouign amann and quiche. Get a kouign amann.

Barney's Gourmet Hamburgers — 4162 24th St, SF. A local burger institution with a hidden back patio. Take a booth out back.

Chloe's Cafe — 1399 Church St, SF. A tiny brunch corner with a weekend line for the pancakes. Come early.

Hamlet — 1199 Church St, SF. A neighborhood wine bar with cheese and charcuterie. Split a board.

Toast Eatery — 1748 Church St, SF. An all day breakfast spot with big plates by the streetcar. Get the eggs benedict.

Eight in Noe Valley: Firefly, Noe Valley Bakery, La Ciccia, La Boulangerie, Barney's, Chloe's Cafe, Hamlet, and Toast. Where do you start?

San Francisco A Day in Petaluma

Petaluma kept the small town main street Hollywood keeps filming, a walkable riverfront of a wood fired bakery, a beer garden, and a 1911 music hall about an hour north of the city. Eight Petaluma stops.

Central Market — 42 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. A farm to table New American room with a wood oven and a nearby farm. Book ahead.

Della Fattoria Downtown Cafe — 143 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. The famous wood fired bakery and cafe for bread and breakfast. Get the egg on a bun.

Seared — 170 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. A live fire steakhouse with lobster mac and happy hour. Order a steak.

Petaluma Pie Company — 125 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. A little shop for sweet and savory hand pies. Grab a savory pie.

Brewsters Beer Garden — 229 Water St N, Petaluma. A riverside beer garden with fire pits and long tables. Grab a picnic table.

Lala's Creamery — 134 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. A downtown ice cream parlor with homemade scoops. Get a double.

Copperfield's Books — 140 Kentucky St, Petaluma. The North Bay indie bookstore's Petaluma shop. Browse the stacks.

Mystic Theatre — 21 Petaluma Blvd N, Petaluma. A historic 1911 music hall still booking live shows. Catch a set.

Eight in Petaluma: Central Market, Della Fattoria, Seared, Petaluma Pie, Brewsters, Lala's Creamery, Copperfield's Books, and the Mystic Theatre. Where do you start?

item.description: Downtown Napa turned its riverfront into a food hall, a Michelin bistro row, and a 1937 theater, proof the valley's best table might be in town instead of
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Downtown Napa

Downtown Napa turned its riverfront into a food hall, a Michelin bistro row, and a 1937 theater, proof the valley's best table might be in town instead of out on the vineyards. Eight downtown Napa stops.

Oxbow Public Market — 610 1st St, Napa. A riverside food hall of oyster bars, tacos, and coffee under one roof. Graze the stalls.

Oenotri — 1425 1st St, Napa. A downtown Italian spot with house salumi and a daily changing menu. Get the pasta.

Grace's Table — 1400 2nd St, Napa. A cheerful Bib Gourmand bistro for all day comfort food. Order the cast iron cornbread.

Angele Restaurant and Bar — 540 Main St, Napa. A French brasserie in an 1890s ship chandlery on the river. Sit on the riverfront patio.

Compline — 1300 1st St, Napa. A wine bar, shop, and restaurant from a master sommelier. Ask for a pour flight.

Cadet Wine and Beer Bar — 930 Franklin St, Napa. A lively downtown bar pouring off the beaten path bottles. Let them pick.

Napa Valley Wine Train — 1275 McKinstry St, Napa. A vintage rail dining trip up the valley from downtown. Book the lunch run.

Uptown Theatre — 1350 3rd St, Napa. A restored 1937 art deco theater booking live music. Catch a show.

Eight in downtown Napa: Oxbow Public Market, Oenotri, Grace's Table, Angele, Compline, Cadet, the Wine Train, and the Uptown Theatre. Where do you start?
