item.title: San Francisco SF's Speakeasies and Hidden Bars
item.description: San Francisco keeps its best cocktails behind unmarked doors and moving bookcases, a password speakeasy scene that started in a Tenderloin apothecary. Eigh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Speakeasies and Hidden Bars

San Francisco keeps its best cocktails behind unmarked doors and moving bookcases, a password speakeasy scene that started in a Tenderloin apothecary. Eight SF hidden bars.

Bourbon and Branch — 501 Jones St, SF. The original SF speakeasy behind an unmarked door, password required. Reserve the Library room.

Wilson and Wilson — 505 Jones St, SF. A detective themed speakeasy hidden inside Bourbon and Branch. Book the tiny room.

Local Edition — 691 Market St, SF. A subterranean newspaper themed bar with nightly live jazz. Go for the jazz set.

Pagan Idol — 375 Bush St, SF. A downtown tiki den with volcano cocktails and hut booths. Order a volcano to share.

The Devil's Acre — 256 Columbus Ave, SF. An apothecary themed bar mixing 1880s recipes in North Beach. Try an old remedy.

Smuggler's Cove — 650 Gough St, SF. A three story pirate tiki temple with hundreds of rums. Get the Dead Reckoning.

Trick Dog — 3010 20th St, SF. A Mission cocktail den with a menu that reinvents itself every few months. Order off the theme.

Rickhouse — 246 Kearny St, SF. A two story bourbon bar built from reclaimed barrel wood. Get a punch bowl for the table.

Eight SF hidden bars: Bourbon and Branch, Wilson and Wilson, Local Edition, Pagan Idol, the Devil's Acre, Smuggler's Cove, Trick Dog, and Rickhouse. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Live Music Venues
item.description: San Francisco's oldest bar has hosted live blues since 1861, the low end of a music scene that runs up to a chandeliered rock hall where the Dead cut their
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Live Music Venues

San Francisco's oldest bar has hosted live blues since 1861, the low end of a music scene that runs up to a chandeliered rock hall where the Dead cut their teeth. Eight SF music venues.

The Fillmore — 1805 Geary Blvd, SF. The legendary rock hall with chandeliers and free posters at the door. Grab an apple upstairs.

Great American Music Hall — 859 O'Farrell St, SF. An ornate 1907 hall with balconies and great sound. Get a spot on the balcony rail.

Bimbo's 365 Club — 1025 Columbus Ave, SF. A 1931 supper club with red curtains and old glamour. Dress up a little.

The Chapel — 777 Valencia St, SF. A former mortuary chapel with a 40 foot arched ceiling. Stand center floor.

The Warfield — 982 Market St, SF. A 1922 vaudeville theater turned mid size rock room. Book the balcony.

The Independent — 628 Divisadero St, SF. A beloved midsize club for breakout acts. Get there early, it is standing room.

Cafe du Nord — 2174 Market St, SF. A dark basement club below an old speakeasy. Catch a late set.

The Saloon — 1232 Grant Ave, SF. The oldest bar in the city, blues nightly in North Beach since 1861. Tip the band.

Eight SF music venues: the Fillmore, Great American Music Hall, Bimbo's, the Chapel, the Warfield, the Independent, Cafe du Nord, and the Saloon. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in San Rafael
item.description: San Rafael anchors Marin with a Fourth Street of Puerto Rican comfort food, craft cocktails, and a 1938 art deco movie house. Eight San Rafael stops.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in San Rafael

San Rafael anchors Marin with a Fourth Street of Puerto Rican comfort food, craft cocktails, and a 1938 art deco movie house. Eight San Rafael stops.

Sol Food — 903 Lincoln Ave, San Rafael. The Puerto Rican comfort food spot with a citywide following. Get the pernil.

Il Davide — 901 A St, San Rafael. An upscale Italian room with homemade pasta and arancini. Start with the arancini.

The Tavern on Fourth — 711 4th St, San Rafael. A craft cocktail bar on the main strip. Order a seasonal cocktail.

State Room — 1132 4th St, San Rafael. A downtown bar and gathering spot with a big beer list. Grab a booth.

Rustic Bakery — 1407 4th St, San Rafael. A Marin bakery cafe for flatbreads and pastries. Get a morning pastry.

Whipper Snapper — 1613 4th St, San Rafael. A Caribbean and Latin spot with rum drinks and a patio. Do the jerk chicken.

Ghiringhelli Pizzeria — 1535 4th St, San Rafael. A family pizzeria and sports bar downtown. Split a pie.

Rafael Film Center — 1118 4th St, San Rafael. A restored 1938 art deco theater screening indies. Catch a film.

Eight in San Rafael: Sol Food, Il Davide, the Tavern on Fourth, State Room, Rustic Bakery, Whipper Snapper, Ghiringhelli, and the Rafael. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco SF's Dive Bars
item.description: San Francisco's dive bars are living history, from a 1937 Chinatown lounge pouring Chinese mai tais to a Mission beer garden with 40 taps and a Simpsons pi
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco SF's Dive Bars

San Francisco's dive bars are living history, from a 1937 Chinatown lounge pouring Chinese mai tais to a Mission beer garden with 40 taps and a Simpsons pinball. Eight SF dive bars.

Zeitgeist — 199 Valencia St, SF. A beer garden dive with a huge backyard and famous bloody marys. Grab a picnic table.

Specs' Twelve Adler Museum Cafe — 12 William Saroyan Pl, SF. A cluttered North Beach classic since 1968. Squeeze in among the bric a brac.

Li Po Lounge — 916 Grant Ave, SF. A cavernous 1937 Chinatown lounge famous for Chinese mai tais. Order a mai tai.

The 500 Club — 500 Guerrero St, SF. A 1953 Mission den under a neon marquee. Post up at the bar.

The Homestead — 2301 Folsom St, SF. A Victorian corner bar with peanut shells on the floor. Shell some peanuts.

Kilowatt — 3160 16th St, SF. A Mission rock dive that birthed the Noise Pop festival. Catch a band.

Aub Zam Zam — 1633 Haight St, SF. A 1940s martini bar with a Persian mural and Sinatra on the box. Order a gin martini.

Bender's — 806 S Van Ness Ave, SF. A grungy Mission dive with tater tots and metal. Get tots and a shot.

Eight SF dive bars: Zeitgeist, Specs', Li Po Lounge, the 500 Club, the Homestead, Kilowatt, Aub Zam Zam, and Bender's. Where do you start?

item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Los Altos

Los Altos hides a small town downtown in the middle of Silicon Valley, where a 1970 family Chinese icon and a French bakery share the plazas with venture offices. Eight Los Altos stops.

State of Mind Public House and Pizzeria — 101 Plaza N, Los Altos. A sourdough pizza and craft beer hall on the plaza. Split a sourdough pie.

Voyageur du Temps — 288 1st St, Los Altos. A French bakery and cafe for croissants and quiche. Get a croissant.

Los Altos Grill — 233 3rd St, Los Altos. A polished American grill and bar downtown. Order the burger.

Sumika — 236 Central Plaza, Los Altos. A tiny Japanese grill for charcoal skewers. Get the yakitori set.

Chef Chu's — 1067 N San Antonio Rd, Los Altos. An iconic Chinese restaurant since 1970. Order the lettuce cups.

Linden Tree Books — 170 State St, Los Altos. A longtime children's bookstore on the strip. Pick out a picture book.

Cetrella — 400 Main St, Los Altos. An upscale Mediterranean room downtown. Book dinner.

Los Altos History Museum — 51 S San Antonio Rd, Los Altos. A free local museum beside an old adobe. Walk the orchard story.

Eight in Los Altos: State of Mind, Voyageur du Temps, Los Altos Grill, Sumika, Chef Chu's, Linden Tree Books, Cetrella, and the History Museum. Where do you start?

item.description: San Carlos calls itself the City of Good Living, and its Laurel Street packs a Belgian pastrami temple, a Greek taverna, and wood fired pizza into a few Pe
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in San Carlos

San Carlos calls itself the City of Good Living, and its Laurel Street packs a Belgian pastrami temple, a Greek taverna, and wood fired pizza into a few Peninsula blocks. Eight San Carlos stops.

PYLOS — 621 Laurel St, San Carlos. A Greek taverna with grilled octopus and saganaki. Order the octopus.

888 Ristorante Italiano — 888 Laurel St, San Carlos. A downtown Italian room with handmade pasta. Split the pasta.

Rouge Wine Bar — 890 Laurel St, San Carlos. A cozy wine bar with boards and by the glass pours. Ask for a flight.

Pazzo — 1179 Laurel St, San Carlos. A Neapolitan pizzeria with wood fired pies and housemade pasta. Get a Margherita.

The Refuge — 963 Laurel St, San Carlos. A cult spot for house cured pastrami and hundreds of Belgian beers. Order the pastrami.

Number5 Kitchen — 720 Laurel St, San Carlos. A modern American bistro on the main strip. Do the tasting plates.

Dumpling and Dough — 1131 Laurel St, San Carlos. A quick spot for soup dumplings and noodles. Get the xiao long bao.

Cafe La Tartine — 1219 Laurel St, San Carlos. A French cafe for crepes and croissants. Grab a crepe.

Eight in San Carlos: PYLOS, 888 Ristorante, Rouge, Pazzo, the Refuge, Number5 Kitchen, Dumpling and Dough, and Cafe La Tartine. Where do you start?

item.description: Menlo Park hides an old school downtown at the edge of Silicon Valley, where a legendary independent bookstore and its next door cafe have anchored the blo
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Menlo Park

Menlo Park hides an old school downtown at the edge of Silicon Valley, where a legendary independent bookstore and its next door cafe have anchored the block for generations. Eight Menlo Park stops.

Camper — 898 Santa Cruz Ave, Menlo Park. A market driven Californian room on the main strip. Do the tasting plates.

Porta Blu — 200 Independence Dr, Menlo Park. A polished New American dining room at Hotel Nia, seasonal plates and craft cocktails. Order the seasonal plates.

Bistro Vida — 641 Santa Cruz Ave, Menlo Park. A cozy French bistro with sidewalk seating. Get the steak frites.

Ann's Coffee Shop — 796 Santa Cruz Ave, Menlo Park. A classic old school diner for breakfast. Order the pancakes.

Kepler's Books — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. A legendary independent bookstore since 1955. Catch an author talk.

Cafe Borrone — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. The bustling cafe next to Kepler's for coffee and people watching. Grab a patio table.

Flea Street — 3607 Alameda de las Pulgas, Menlo Park. A farm to table pioneer running for decades. Book dinner.

Naomi Sushi — 1328 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. A longtime neighborhood sushi bar. Sit at the bar.

Eight in Menlo Park: Camper, Porta Blu, Bistro Vida, Ann's Coffee Shop, Kepler's Books, Cafe Borrone, Flea Street, and Naomi Sushi. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Mill Valley
item.description: Mill Valley is the Bay Area's woodsy hideaway at the foot of Mount Tam, where a 1929 train depot turned bookstore cafe anchors a downtown ringed by redwood
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Mill Valley

Mill Valley is the Bay Area's woodsy hideaway at the foot of Mount Tam, where a 1929 train depot turned bookstore cafe anchors a downtown ringed by redwoods. Eight Mill Valley stops.

Depot Cafe and Bookstore — 87 Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. A 1929 rail depot turned cafe and bookstore on the plaza. Read on the patio.

La Ginestra — 127 Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. A family Italian spot serving the town since 1964. Get the ravioli.

Piazza D'Angelo — 22 Miller Ave, Mill Valley. A bustling Italian trattoria and bar downtown. Sit on the patio.

Equator Coffees — 2 Miller Ave, Mill Valley. A corner cafe from a certified sustainable roaster. Order a cortado.

Watershed — 129 Miller Ave, Mill Valley. A California kitchen in the old Mill Valley lumberyard. Get a wood fired dish.

Sweetwater Music Hall — 19 Corte Madera Ave, Mill Valley. A legendary small music hall with big surprise guests. Catch a late show.

Mill Valley Market — 12 Corte Madera Ave, Mill Valley. A 1929 family grocery with a great deli counter. Build a picnic.

Old Mill Park — Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. A redwood park with a creek and the town's old sawmill. Walk under the redwoods.

Eight in Mill Valley: the Depot, La Ginestra, Piazza D'Angelo, Equator Coffees, Watershed, Sweetwater Music Hall, Mill Valley Market, and Old Mill Park. Where do you start?

item.title: SF Bay Area Farmers Markets
item.description: The SF Bay Area shops for groceries at the Ferry Building's showcase market and the oldest farmers market in the state, running under a freeway in San Fran
item.content:encoded:
SF Bay Area Farmers Markets

The SF Bay Area shops for groceries at the Ferry Building's showcase market and the oldest farmers market in the state, running under a freeway in San Francisco since 1943. Eight SF Bay Area farmers markets.

Ferry Plaza Farmers Market — 1 Ferry Building, SF. The famous Saturday market of top farms and chefs on the waterfront. Go early for the peaches.

Alemany Farmers Market — 100 Alemany Blvd, SF. The people's market, the oldest in the state since 1943. Bring cash and a cart.

Grand Lake Farmers Market — 746 Grand Ave, Oakland. A big Saturday market by Lake Merritt with prepared food galore. Get dim sum to walk with.

Old Oakland Farmers Market — 9th St, Oakland. A Friday market in the historic Victorian blocks. Shop then brunch nearby.

Berkeley Farmers Market — Center St, Berkeley. A pioneering organic market downtown on Saturdays. Fill a bag with greens.

Marin Civic Center Farmers Market — 3501 Civic Center Dr, San Rafael. One of the biggest weekly markets in the state, Sundays and Thursdays. Come hungry.

Mountain View Farmers Market — 600 W Evelyn Ave, Mountain View. A big Sunday market at the Caltrain lot with 70 growers. Graze the stalls.

Temescal Farmers Market — 5300 Claremont Ave, Oakland. A lively Sunday market in the DMV lot with hot food. Grab breakfast there.

Eight markets: Ferry Plaza, Alemany, Grand Lake, Old Oakland, Berkeley, Marin Civic Center, Mountain View, and Temescal. Where do you start?

item.title: Bay Area Day Trips You Sent Us
item.description: Every Bay Area day trip post fills with your own detours, so this whole list is the stops readers told us we missed, from the Sonoma coast to a Lodi zinfan
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Day Trips You Sent Us

Every Bay Area day trip post fills with your own detours, so this whole list is the stops readers told us we missed, from the Sonoma coast to a Lodi zinfandel. Eight Bay Area day trips.

River's End — 11048 Highway 1, Jenner. A bluff top restaurant over the mouth of the Russian River in Jenner. Book lunch for the view. A @artsyyvonne add.

Jettywave Distillery — 155 Broadway, Half Moon Bay. A newer Half Moon Bay distillery with outdoor seating and good vibes. Do a spirits tasting. A @waynemo66 add.

Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum — 1660 Park Ave, San Jose. The largest collection of Egyptian artifacts on the West Coast, near the Rose Garden. See the mummies. A @coopertown104 add.

Radke Martinez Regional Shoreline — 1 Ferry St, Martinez. A flat waterfront walk on the Carquinez Strait readers said not to miss. Walk the marsh boardwalk. A @lady_chapin add.

Macchia Wines — 7099 E Peltier Rd, Acampo. A family Lodi winery readers praise for its bold reds. Taste the Zinfandels. A @salcidoterry add.

The Restaurant at North Block — 6757 Washington St, Yountville. A Yountville hotel restaurant with a fantastic bar and wine list. Sit at the bar. A @brennaleeroth add.

Grassy Bar Oyster Company — 1215 Embarcadero Rd, Morro Bay. A no frills Morro Bay shop selling fresh oysters on the half shell. Slurp a dozen by the water. A @asianhalfpint add.

Tierra Luna Cellars — Acampo. A Lodi area winery from former astronaut Jose Hernandez. Pour the astronaut's red. A @salcidoterry add.

Eight Bay Area day trips: River's End, Jettywave, the Rosicrucian, the Martinez Shoreline, Macchia, North Block, Grassy Bar, and Tierra Luna. Which one first?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Benicia
item.description: Benicia is the Bay Area's overlooked waterfront town, a former state capital where First Street runs straight down to the Carquinez Strait. Eight Benicia s
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Benicia

Benicia is the Bay Area's overlooked waterfront town, a former state capital where First Street runs straight down to the Carquinez Strait. Eight Benicia stops.

Sailor Jack's — 123 First St, Benicia. A waterfront seafood spot at the bottom of First Street. Get a window table.

Drift Benicia — 366 First St, Benicia. A downtown pizza and coffee stop. Grab a slice and an espresso.

Lucca Bar and Grill — 439 First St, Benicia. A gastropub with a beer garden and live music. Sit in the garden.

Rellik Tavern — 726 First St, Benicia. A cozy tavern in a historic downtown building. Order a cocktail.

One House Bakery — 918 First St, Benicia. A wildly popular bakery on upper First Street. Get there before the pastries sell out.

Benicia Capitol State Historic Park — 115 West G St, Benicia. The only surviving pre Sacramento state capitol. Tour the 1852 chamber.

Benicia Historical Museum — 2060 Camel Rd, Benicia. A museum in 1850s sandstone buildings in the old Arsenal. Walk the Arsenal grounds.

Matthew Turner Shipyard Park — 1001 West 12th St, Benicia. A waterfront park honoring the busiest shipbuilder in North America. Watch the boats.

Eight in Benicia: Sailor Jack's, Drift, Lucca, Rellik Tavern, One House Bakery, the Capitol, the Historical Museum, and Shipyard Park. Where do you start?

item.description: Vallejo is the Bay Area's comeback waterfront, a former Navy town where Georgia Street meets the ferry and Mare Island's old munitions sheds pour beer. Eig
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Downtown Vallejo

Vallejo is the Bay Area's comeback waterfront, a former Navy town where Georgia Street meets the ferry and Mare Island's old munitions sheds pour beer. Eight Vallejo stops.

Provisions — 300 Virginia St, Vallejo. A downtown restaurant and community gathering spot. Come for a weekend dinner.

Alibi Bookshop — Georgia St, Vallejo. An indie bookshop anchoring the arts walk. Browse the local shelf.

Empress Theatre — 330 Virginia St, Vallejo. A restored historic theater for live music and film. Catch a show.

Coal Shed Brewery — Mare Island, Vallejo. A brewery in a former naval munitions shed with strait views. Drink a beer by the water.

Mare Island Brewing Ferry Taproom — Vallejo waterfront. The ferry terminal taproom pouring local craft beer. Grab a beer before the ferry.

Vallejo Naval and Historical Museum — Marin St, Vallejo. A museum of the city's Navy and Mare Island history. Dig into the shipyard past.

Vallejo Ferry — Mare Island Way, Vallejo. The fast ferry to San Francisco from the waterfront. Ride it across the bay.

Vallejo Farmers Market — Georgia St, Vallejo. A Saturday market on downtown Georgia Street. Shop the stalls.

Eight in Vallejo: Provisions, Alibi Bookshop, the Empress, the Coal Shed, the Ferry Taproom, the Naval Museum, the ferry, and the farmers market. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco A Day in Downtown Santa Cruz
item.description: Santa Cruz is the Bay Area's beach town over the hill, where Pacific Avenue runs from an indie bookshop and a punk club down to a 1907 boardwalk. Eight dow
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco A Day in Downtown Santa Cruz

Santa Cruz is the Bay Area's beach town over the hill, where Pacific Avenue runs from an indie bookshop and a punk club down to a 1907 boardwalk. Eight downtown Santa Cruz stops.

Bookshop Santa Cruz — 1520 Pacific Ave, Santa Cruz. The legendary indie bookstore on Pacific Avenue. Lose an hour in the stacks.

Abbott Square Market — 725 Front St, Santa Cruz. A food hall and plaza with live music behind the museum. Graze the stalls.

Verve Coffee Roasters — 1540 Pacific Ave, Santa Cruz. The surf town roaster's downtown cafe. Order a pour over.

Woodstock's Pizza — 710 Front St, Santa Cruz. The UCSC pizza and beer hub. Split a pie.

The Catalyst — 1011 Pacific Ave, Santa Cruz. A storied Pacific Avenue music club. Catch a show.

Del Mar Theatre — 1124 Pacific Ave, Santa Cruz. An art deco triplex for indie and midnight films. Catch a late movie.

Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk — 400 Beach St, Santa Cruz. A 1907 oceanfront amusement park with the Giant Dipper. Ride the wooden coaster.

Santa Cruz Wharf — Beach St, Santa Cruz. The half mile pier over the bay with sea lions below. Walk out for the view.

item.title: San Francisco Record Stores
item.description: Amoeba on Haight fills a former bowling alley, and the old bowling marquee still sits up on the roof. Everybody heads there. The real crate digging in San
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Record Stores

Amoeba on Haight fills a former bowling alley, and the old bowling marquee still sits up on the roof. Everybody heads there. The real crate digging in San Francisco hides in the smaller shops most people walk right past. Eight record stores worth the trip.

Amoeba Music — 1855 Haight St, San Francisco. The cavernous main room gets the tourists, but regulars make for the used bins and the bargain vinyl along the walls, and the free in store shows pull real crowds. Go on a weekday morning before the racks get picked over. @amoebasf

Rooky Ricardo's Records — 419 Haight St, San Francisco. Soul, funk, and doo wop 45s stacked deep, with a counter where they will spin one for you before you commit. Bring cash and give yourself a couple hours. @rooky_ricardos_records

Groove Merchant Records — 687 Haight St, San Francisco. A tiny Lower Haight room packed with rare soul, funk, and jazz that DJs fly in for, written up among the world's best record shops. Squeeze in and dig. @groovemerchantsf

Vinyl Dreams — 593 Haight St, San Francisco. The house, techno, and disco specialist, run by a former Amoeba electronic buyer, with listening stations so you can test imports before buying. If you chase 12 inch dance records, start here. @vinyldreamssf

Grooves — 1797 Market St, San Francisco. A vinyl only holdout near the Castro, heavy on oddball soundtracks, spoken word, and pop obscurities you did not know you needed. Great for the record you cannot find anywhere else. @groovesvinyl

Stranded Records — 1055 Valencia St, San Francisco. The record store arm of a reissue label, so the walls lean avant garde, punk, jazz, and experimental, tightly chosen, not sprawling. Come for the stuff the big shops skip. @strandedrecords

Originals Vinyl — 701 Fillmore St, San Francisco. A small family run used shop that also cleans and de warps records on an ultrasonic machine, with new arrivals daily. Bring that warped LP that has been sitting in your attic. @originalsvinyl

101 Music — 1414 Grant Ave, San Francisco. The last record shop in North Beach, actually two crammed storefronts, one for records and one for vintage instruments and stereo gear. Squeeze past the stacks and you will find something.

Eight for the record hunt: Amoeba, Rooky Ricardo's, Groove Merchant, Vinyl Dreams, Grooves, Stranded, Originals Vinyl, and 101 Music. Which bin do you lose track of time in?

item.title: San Francisco Vintage and Thrift Shops
item.description: Wasteland on Haight sells vintage out of a 1911 theater, an ornate Art Nouveau facade now painted fire engine red you can spot a block away. San Francisco
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Vintage and Thrift Shops

Wasteland on Haight sells vintage out of a 1911 theater, an ornate Art Nouveau facade now painted fire engine red you can spot a block away. San Francisco keeps its best secondhand on a handful of streets, not scattered across town. Eight vintage and thrift stops worth a Saturday.

Wasteland — 1660 Haight St, San Francisco. Behind that red facade is a huge floor of vintage denim, leather, and designer resale, and they buy off the street if you bring a bag to sell. Go early for the good size runs. @shopwasteland

Buffalo Exchange — 1555 Haight St, San Francisco. The dependable buy sell trade up the same block, well sorted and cheaper than the boutiques, paying cash or store credit on the spot. Bring a bag to sell and walk out with something new. @buffaloexchange

Relic Vintage — 1475 Haight St, San Francisco. This one leans older and dressier, real 1940s to 1960s pieces, hats, and costume jewelry, not 90s castoffs. The place to find something for a themed party that actually looks the part. @relicvintage

Crossroads Trading — 1901 Fillmore St, San Francisco. Over on Fillmore, this leans current and on trend resale, so it is the spot for near new brands at a fraction of retail. Check the clearance rack in the back first. @crossroadstrading

Relove — 1815 Polk St, San Francisco. A Black owned resale boutique on Polk with a tight, well priced mix of vintage and designer, more boutique than warehouse dig. Easy in and out when you want quality over quantity. @shoprelove

No Shop — 389 Valencia St, San Francisco. Kicks off the Valencia vintage stretch with cheap band tees, jewelry, and eclectic racks that reward a slow flip. Come for a $25 tee, stay for the odd jacket you did not plan on. @no_shop

Community Thrift Store — 623 Valencia St, San Francisco. A big nonprofit thrift where donations get credited to a local charity the giver names, so your bargain hunt quietly funds the neighborhood. Hit the books and housewares, not just the clothes. @communitythriftsf

Valencia Street Vintage — 714 Valencia St, San Francisco. A small, well edited shop with a killer $15 rack and rotating local art on the walls. A good last stop on a Valencia crawl when your arms are already full. @valenciastreetvintage

Eight for a vintage crawl: Wasteland, Buffalo Exchange, Relic Vintage, Crossroads Trading, Relove, No Shop, Community Thrift, and Valencia Street Vintage. Haight, Fillmore, or Valencia, which block do you start on?

item.title: San Francisco Whiskey Bars
item.description: Whiskey has been poured on the same Mission corner in San Francisco since 1858, and that saloon still is not the deepest back bar in the city. Eight SF whi
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Whiskey Bars

Whiskey has been poured on the same Mission corner in San Francisco since 1858, and that saloon still is not the deepest back bar in the city. Eight SF whiskey rooms where the bottle wall does the talking, from a Prohibition password door to a Scotch den hidden above Chinatown.

Elixir — 3200 16th St, San Francisco. A saloon has stood on this Mission corner since 1858, and the back bar now holds hundreds of whiskeys. Ask the bartender to point you toward something you have never tried. @elixirsf

Bourbon and Branch — 501 Jones St, San Francisco. Behind an unmarked Tenderloin door, and you will need the password, sits a Prohibition style speakeasy built for brown spirits. Book ahead and keep your voice down, house rules. @bourbonandbranchsf

Rickhouse — 246 Kearny St, San Francisco. This Financial District bar is built from salvaged pre 1906 barrel staves, with a wall of 400 plus bottles climbing toward the ceiling. Come for a bourbon flight before the after work crowd lands. @rickhousebar

Cold Drinks Bar — 644 Broadway, San Francisco. Up a stairwell above China Live hides a Scotch den with more than 350 bottles and bartenders in tuxedos. Follow the painted bats to the door and settle in. @colddrinksbar

83 Proof — 83 First St, San Francisco. A two story downtown den with a whiskey list that runs deep: dozens of ryes and bourbons, plus nearly every Scottish distillery you can name. Grab a stool upstairs and let them build something around your pour. @83proof

Swig — 561 Geary St, San Francisco. Just off Union Square, this multi level bar has quietly kept one of the city's deeper whiskey collections for years. Head upstairs for a calmer pour away from the front room noise. @swigbarsf

The Eighth Rule — 335 Powell St, San Francisco. Steph Curry's reservations only bourbon bar, tucked inside the Westin St. Francis, pours a six course cocktail tasting for those who plan ahead. Book a seat, this one is a special occasion night. @the8thrule

House of Shields — 39 New Montgomery St, San Francisco. This 1908 saloon across from the Palace Hotel keeps its old school feel and a serious back bar of brown spirits. Slide into a booth and order something neat. @houseofshieldssf

Eight for San Francisco whiskey: Elixir, Bourbon and Branch, Rickhouse, Cold Drinks Bar, 83 Proof, Swig, The Eighth Rule, and House of Shields. Which back bar are you starting at?

item.title: San Francisco Plant Shops and Nurseries
item.description: Eight plant shops are the reason a foggy San Francisco apartment can still feel like a greenhouse, and the oldest of them works out of a converted 1904 dai
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Plant Shops and Nurseries

Eight plant shops are the reason a foggy San Francisco apartment can still feel like a greenhouse, and the oldest of them works out of a converted 1904 dairy building on Clement Street. Most people grab a big box fiddle leaf that is brown by October and never meet the SF shops that keep one alive.

Flora Grubb Gardens — 1634 Jerrold Ave, San Francisco. A Bayview plant paradise with a coffee bar tucked among the succulents and a living wall that stops everyone at the door. Go on a Saturday and budget an hour longer than you planned. @floragrubbgardens

Clement Nursery — 1921 Clement St, San Francisco. San Francisco's oldest garden store still runs out of the old 1904 dairy buildings, and the staff will drill drainage holes and help you wrangle a six foot ficus into your Honda. Bring the awkward pot you have been avoiding. @clementnursery

Paxton Gate — 824 Valencia St, San Francisco. Part nursery, part cabinet of curiosities, this Mission shop sells carnivorous plants next to ethically sourced skulls and taxidermy. Come for a pitcher plant, leave wondering how a whole afternoon vanished. @paxtongate

Sloat Garden Center — 2700 Sloat Blvd, San Francisco. The Sunset flagship has anchored this corner near the zoo for more than fifty years, with rows of California natives that actually shrug off the coastal wind. Ask which ones survive an Outer Sunset balcony. @sloatgardens

The Plant Lady SF — 1637 Ocean Ave, San Francisco. An Ingleside jewel box packed wall to wall with tropicals and hard to find rarities you will not see at a chain. Go midweek when it is quiet and you can actually talk leaves with the owner. @theplantladysf

Flowercraft Garden Center — 550 Bayshore Blvd, San Francisco. Open since 1974, this sprawling yard on the Bernal edge is where you go for real dirt, edibles, and seedlings by the flat, not just a cute houseplant. Bring a car and a plan for spring tomatoes. @flowercraftgc

Savvy Nursery — 478 Union St, San Francisco. A tiny North Beach shop with a plant doctor on call for whatever you are slowly killing at home. Haul in the sad monstera and they will repot it and tell you the truth. @savvynursery

Houseplants and Plant Essentials — 283 9th St, San Francisco. A SoMa spot that stays open late enough to catch after work, stocked with statement plants and the soil, pots, and know how to match. Swing by after dinner and leave with a monstera and a pep talk. @houseplants_andplantessentials

Eight for a greener San Francisco: Flora Grubb, Clement Nursery, Paxton Gate, Sloat Garden Center, The Plant Lady SF, Flowercraft, Savvy Nursery, and Houseplants and Plant Essentials. Which windowsill are you starting with?

item.title: San Francisco Hardware Stores
item.description: Eight hardware stores have outlasted every big box that came for them in San Francisco, and the oldest has been open since 1880, decades before the 1906 qu
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Hardware Stores

Eight hardware stores have outlasted every big box that came for them in San Francisco, and the oldest has been open since 1880, decades before the 1906 quake. These are the SF corner institutions where a real person finds the one weird screw you need instead of pointing at an aisle.

Center Hardware — 3003 Third St, San Francisco. Open since 1880 and now a 20,000 square foot maker's paradise in Dogpatch with a 65,000 item inventory, this is where contractors and artists both get stuck for an hour. Go with a list or lose the afternoon. @centerhardware

Cole Hardware — 956 Cole St, San Francisco. The Cole Valley flagship of a beloved family run chain, where the staff will cut a key, match a paint chip, and talk you out of the wrong tool. Ask a question, any question, and watch them light up. @colehardware

Cliff's Variety — 479 Castro St, San Francisco. A Castro institution since 1936 that is equal parts hardware store and glitter emporium, so you can grab a plunger and a feather boa in one trip. Wander into the annex for fabric and notions before you leave. @hilario_sf

Brownies Ace Hardware — 1563 Polk St, San Francisco. A Polk Street mainstay where you can also grab Muni passes between picking up light bulbs and picture hooks. Handy the next time your Clipper card betrays you at the worst moment.

Fredericksen Hardware and Paint — 3029 Fillmore St, San Francisco. A Cow Hollow classic crammed floor to ceiling, the kind of place where staff walk you straight to the exact bin instead of leaving you to wander. Go in knowing it looks small and holds everything. @fredericksenhardware

Standard 5 and 10 Ace — 3545 California St, San Francisco. Serving Laurel Village since 1939, this one is half hardware and half old school five and dime, with toys and kitchen gadgets tucked behind the tools. Take a kid and let them get lost in the aisles. @standard510ace

Roberts Hardware — 1629 Haight St, San Francisco. A locally owned holdout right on Haight Street, where you can duck out of the crowds for a plumbing part and honest advice. Grab what you need and get back to people watching. @robertshardware

Discount Builders Supply — 1695 Mission St, San Francisco. The largest family owned hardware and building supply in the city, parked where the freeway meets South Van Ness, with free parking and lumber the little shops cannot stock. Go here when the project got real.

Eight for keeping San Francisco standing: Center Hardware, Cole Hardware, Cliff's Variety, Brownies, Fredericksen, Standard 5 and 10, Roberts, and Discount Builders. Which counter has saved your weekend?

item.title: San Francisco Comic and Game Shops
item.description: Eight San Francisco comic and game shops worth crossing town for, and the Hayes Valley lounge on this list keeps a wall of toilet seat lids hand painted an
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Comic and Game Shops

Eight San Francisco comic and game shops worth crossing town for, and the Hayes Valley lounge on this list keeps a wall of toilet seat lids hand painted and signed by comic royalty like Jim Lee and Brian K. Vaughan. The real SF comic crawl is not one store, it is a loop across eight neighborhoods. Here they are.

Isotope Comics — 326 Fell Street, San Francisco. The self styled Comic Book Lounge in Hayes Valley, red sofas, gallery lighting, and that famous wall of signed toilet seat lids. Owner James Sime has judged the Eisner Awards, so the staff picks actually land. Go for the graphic novels, stay for the wall. @isotopecomics

Comix Experience — 305 Divisadero Street, San Francisco. Open since April Fools Day 1989 and now an official SF Legacy Business, this NoPa corner runs two real graphic novel clubs with author signings. Ask about a pull list and they will actually remember your taste. @comixexperience

Mission Comics and Art — 2250 Mission Street, San Francisco. On Mission between 18th and 19th since 2008, part shop and part gallery with a back room art space. The city liked it enough to grant funding for a second location in the Excelsior. New Wednesday books, deep back issues. @missioncomics

Amazing Fantasy — 650 Irving Street, San Francisco. The Inner Sunset neighborhood comic shop since the late 1970s, named for the issue where Spider-Man first showed up. Long boxes to dig through, a tidy new release wall, and an owner who has kept the lights on through every downturn.

Sour Cherry Comics — 3187 16th Street, San Francisco. A queer, women owned shop near Valencia that leans indie, small press, and all ages, with a real community table feel. The kind of place that hand sells you a book you did not know you needed. @sourcherrycomics

Silver Sprocket — 1685 Haight Street, San Francisco. Indie publisher and punk hearted comic shop on Upper Haight, open seven days, heavy on zines, stickers, and socially conscious small press books you will not find at a chain. Part gallery, part clubhouse. @silversprocket

Invisible Jet Comics — 159 West Portal Avenue, San Francisco. A Wonder Woman themed, women owned shop in West Portal with the front of the store built for kids and YA readers. New singles every Wednesday, pull boxes with no minimum. A great first comic shop trip for a family. @invisiblejetcomicsinc

Gamescape — 333 Divisadero Street, San Francisco. Not a comic shop but the city's tabletop institution since 1985, up the block from Comix Experience. Board games, RPGs, Warhammer minis, and the widest puzzle wall in town, plus game nights that pull a real crowd. @gamescapesf

Eight for the San Francisco comic and game crawl: Isotope, Comix Experience, Mission Comics and Art, Amazing Fantasy, Sour Cherry, Silver Sprocket, Invisible Jet, and Gamescape. Which counter gets your Wednesday pull, and which SF shop should be on this list?

item.title: San Francisco Flower Shops and Florists
item.description: A family florist in San Francisco has been making bouquets here since 1928, and its SoMa shop still opens every single day of the year, holidays included.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Flower Shops and Florists

A family florist in San Francisco has been making bouquets here since 1928, and its SoMa shop still opens every single day of the year, holidays included. The good stuff in this city was never a delivery app default, it is the neighborhood shops. Eight San Francisco flower shops worth knowing.

Hoogasian Flowers — 615 7th Street, San Francisco. The same family has been selling flowers in this city since 1928, and the SoMa shop is famous for never closing, holidays and all. When you need a real arrangement at the last minute, this is the one. @hoogasianflowerssf

Bell and Trunk Flowers — 1411 18th Street, San Francisco. A Potrero Hill corner shop where owner Vanessa Marlin has been building loose, garden style bouquets for over two decades. Walk in without a plan and let her read the day for you. @bellandtrunkflowers

Urban Flowers — 4029 18th Street, San Francisco. Family run in the Castro for 22 years, open early and late seven days a week when everywhere else is shut. Grab a wrapped bunch on the way to dinner and nobody guesses it took five minutes. @_urban_flowers_

Love and Stem — 1585 Church Street, San Francisco. A women owned Noe Valley shop that doubles as a little gift store, so you leave with a bouquet plus the card and the candle. Their designer choice bunch is the move when you cannot decide. @loveandstem

Fiori Flowers — 2314 Chestnut Street, San Francisco. The Marina florist that pulls from an exclusive grower network, so the stems look garden picked, not grocery bucket. Loose, natural, a little wild. Tell them the room and they will match it. @fiorisanfrancisco

Sol Ambiance — 5522 Geary Boulevard, San Francisco. An Outer Richmond studio doing creative, color forward arrangements alongside local gifts, and one of the few real florists that far west. Weekend flowers without crossing town. @solambiance

Urban Botanica — 345 California Street, San Francisco. Tucked in the Financial District for about 20 years, this is the one downtown workers duck into for a proper bouquet instead of the corner deli bundle. Order ahead for a same day pickup. @urbanbotanica_sf

Nigella SF — 388 Market Street, San Francisco. A downtown boutique known for bespoke, slightly moody arrangements, the kind you send when a text will not cut it. Weekly subscriptions if you want fresh stems on the table every Monday. @nigella_sf

Eight for San Francisco flowers: Hoogasian, Bell and Trunk, Urban Flowers, Love and Stem, Fiori, Sol Ambiance, Urban Botanica, and Nigella SF. Which neighborhood shop gets your next bouquet?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Bookstores
item.description: Books Inc in Palo Alto traces its roots to 1851, which the chain bills as the oldest independent bookseller in the West. The Peninsula was a bookstore town
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Bookstores

Books Inc in Palo Alto traces its roots to 1851, which the chain bills as the oldest independent bookseller in the West. The Peninsula was a bookstore town long before it was Silicon Valley, and the good shops never left. Eight indie bookstores still standing, Menlo Park to the coast.

Kepler's Books — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. Open since 1955 and a hub for the Beat and folk crowd in its early days, it still works as the Peninsula's town square with a book section. The events calendar is stacked with author talks. Go browse, stay for a reading. @keplersbooks

Bell's Books — 536 Emerson St, Palo Alto. Family run since 1935, with something like 350,000 new, used, and rare books stacked floor to ceiling. This is where you hunt down the out of print title nobody else has. Downtown Palo Alto, and yes, that old book smell. @windowsofbells

Books Inc — 855 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. The Palo Alto branch of that 1851 bookseller, tucked into Town and Country Village across from the high school. Strong staff picks, a great kids section, and an easy afternoon of browsing. Come for one book, leave with a stack. @booksincstores

B Street Books — 1471 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. When the Books Inc here closed, this used bookshop kept Burlingame Ave in the book business. Deep secondhand shelves, fair prices, and a staff that actually knows the stock. Bring a tote, you will fill it. @bstreetbooks

Feldman's Books — 1075 Curtis St, Menlo Park. A quirky used and vintage shop that turned into a genuine scene, with author talks, poetry, live music, even a bike repair night. Open 12 to 5 daily. Come for the books, stay for whatever is happening. @feldmansbooks

Reach and Teach — 1179 San Carlos Ave, San Carlos. Part bookstore, part toy shop, built around peace, justice, and sustainability. The spot for gifts you will not find at a big box, plus STEM kits and puzzles for the kids. Closed Mondays. @reachandteach1

Florey's Book Co — 2120 Palmetto Ave, Pacifica. A Pacifica fixture since 1977, a short walk from the beach, mixing new and used with a strong local and teacher section. The kind of coastside shop you duck into when the fog rolls in. Open daily, later on Fridays.

Coastside Books — 432 Main St, Half Moon Bay. Serving the coast since 1972, right on Main Street for a post beach browse. Well curated fiction, a lovely kids corner, and cards and gifts from local artists. The owner knows her stock cold, so ask. @coastsidebooksinc

Eight for the Peninsula bookshelf: Kepler's, Bell's, Books Inc, B Street, Feldman's, Reach and Teach, Florey's, and Coastside. Which one gets your Saturday?

item.title: San Francisco Art Galleries
item.description: The best free art in San Francisco is not behind the SFMOMA ticket counter. It is in the commercial galleries, and in 2016 a Dogpatch warehouse called Minn
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Art Galleries

The best free art in San Francisco is not behind the SFMOMA ticket counter. It is in the commercial galleries, and in 2016 a Dogpatch warehouse called Minnesota Street Project pulled the priced out ones together under a single roof so dealers could stay in the city. Eight rooms you walk into for nothing.

Jenkins Johnson Gallery — 1275 Minnesota St, San Francisco. Inside that same Minnesota Street Project building, Karen Jenkins Johnson has shown major contemporary artists since 1996, with real depth in work by the Black diaspora. Free to enter, museum level on the walls. @jenkinsjohnsongallery

Fraenkel Gallery — 49 Geary St, San Francisco. Four floors up in the old Geary Street gallery block sits one of the most respected photography galleries in the country, the kind that hangs Diane Arbus. Ride the elevator to the top and work your way down through the other galleries. @fraenkelgallery

Haines Gallery — 2 Marina Blvd, Building C, San Francisco. After decades downtown on Geary Street, Haines moved out to Fort Mason, swapping a high rise for a waterfront pier shed full of contemporary art with the Bay right outside. Pair it with a walk along the marina. @hainesgallery

Catharine Clark Gallery — 248 Utah St, San Francisco. Open since 1991 and the first gallery in the city with a dedicated media room, this Potrero Hill space shows politically sharp work and the video and new media art most dealers avoid. Give the back media room real time. @cclarkgallery

Creativity Explored — 3245 16th St, San Francisco. A Mission nonprofit since 1984 where artists with developmental disabilities make and sell their work, and the studio doubles as a gallery. The art is bold, affordable, and often the most joyful room in town. @creativityexplored

Gallery Wendi Norris — 436 Jackson St, San Francisco. A Jackson Square gallery that helped rewrite the history of Surrealism, with decades of shows built around Leonora Carrington and other overlooked women of the movement. Weekday hours, so slip in on a lunch break. @gallerywendinorris

Jessica Silverman — 621 Grant Ave, San Francisco. One of the city's leading contemporary dealers, now in a big corner space on the Chinatown edge of Grant Avenue, representing artists like feminist pioneer Judy Chicago. Bright, ambitious, and free to walk through. @jessicasilvermangallery

Berggruen Gallery — 10 Hawthorne St, San Francisco. John Berggruen opened in 1970 and became the first San Francisco gallery of national stature, and since 2017 it has sat directly across from SFMOMA, dealing modern masters from Picasso and Miro to Bay Area painters. See that caliber for free. @berggruengallery

Eight for San Francisco galleries: Jenkins Johnson, Fraenkel, Haines, Catharine Clark, Creativity Explored, Wendi Norris, Jessica Silverman, and Berggruen. Every one free to walk into. Which neighborhood are you starting in?

item.title: San Francisco Antique and Vintage Home Shops
item.description: Gaslight and Shadows has anchored the same Clement Street corner since 1976, a half century argument that old San Francisco is not gone, just quieter. Eigh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Antique and Vintage Home Shops

Gaslight and Shadows has anchored the same Clement Street corner since 1976, a half century argument that old San Francisco is not gone, just quieter. Eight vintage and antique home shops still worth the hunt, from the Mission to the Richmond.

Stuff by Luxe — 1830 Harrison Street, San Francisco. When the beloved Stuff closed, a former tech guy reopened the idea in the Mission, forty some dealers packed into room after room of mid century furniture, lamps, and oddball decor. Go on a weekend and give yourself an hour. @stuffbyluxe

De Angelis — 573 Valencia Street, San Francisco. A tight 20th century design gallery where the chairs have names, Paul Evans, Finn Juhl, Hans Wegner, each piece restored instead of just dusted off. More museum than shop, but everything is for sale. Look, do not lean. @deangelissf

Woodchuck Antiques — 3597 Sacramento Street, San Francisco. Chuck opened in 1974 and still deals almost only in lighting, bronzes, table lamps, and chandeliers from the 1870s to the 1930s. The hours are tiny, think weekday early afternoons, so time it right and knock.

Mureta and Co — 2418 Fillmore Street, San Francisco. Look for the pineapple door. Inside, estate jewelry and antiques since 1983, Georgian mourning rings to Deco diamonds, the kind of old cut stones you cannot fake. Good for browsers, dangerous for gift shoppers. @muretaandco

The Perish Trust — 728 Divisadero Street, San Francisco. A modern general store since 2008, part apothecary, part cabinet of curiosities, stacked with well worn homegoods, local ceramics, incense, and odd little heirlooms. Come for a gift, leave with something for your own shelf. @theperishtrust

Gaslight and Shadows — 2335 Clement Street, San Francisco. Fifty years on the same Richmond block, run with the patience that implies. Bakelite jewelry, glass cases of collectibles, and reportedly the largest stash of hand painted Limoges boxes in town. The kind of shop that rewards a slow lap. @gaslight_shadows

Grand Central Station Antiques — 360 Bayshore Boulevard, San Francisco. Worth the drive to the edge of town, five thousand square feet of European furniture, most of it shipped in from Belgium, heavy on 19th century French, English, and Flemish. Closed Tuesdays, so plan around it. @gcsantiques

Belle Cose and Molte Cose — 2200 Polk Street, San Francisco. A sunlit corner of curated vintage, uranium glass and old barware and home odds mixed in with the racks. A neighborhood fixture that recently moved up Polk to better light. Easy to lose twenty minutes in the glassware. @bellecose_moltecose

Eight for the San Francisco vintage hunt: Stuff by Luxe, De Angelis, Woodchuck, Mureta and Co., The Perish Trust, Gaslight and Shadows, Grand Central Station, and Belle Cose and Molte Cose. Which window would pull you in first?

item.title: San Francisco Bike Shops
item.description: San Francisco's oldest bike shop has been truing wheels at 510 Frederick since 1941, when a track racer named Oscar Juner opened the doors. The city's cycl
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Bike Shops

San Francisco's oldest bike shop has been truing wheels at 510 Frederick since 1941, when a track racer named Oscar Juner opened the doors. The city's cycling scene is not all app rentals and big chain showrooms. Eight shops from the Presidio to the Mission still fix your flat, talk gearing, and know your neighborhood hills.

American Cyclery — 510 Frederick Street, San Francisco. The 1941 shop by Golden Gate Park is part working store, part museum, with track bikes and vintage steel hanging over the till. Closed Tuesdays, so plan around it. Bring the bike you swear is beyond saving. @americancyclery

Freewheel Bike Shop — 1920 Hayes Street, San Francisco. A neighborhood mainstay off the Panhandle, the kind of place that turns a flat or a quick tune up around while you wait and sends you back out before the fog burns off. Good with commuters and first bike nerves. Roll in on a weekday. @freewheelbikeshop

Roaring Mouse Cycles — 934 Old Mason Street, San Francisco. It moved into the Presidio, so now your flat repair comes with eucalyptus air and a view. Strong road and gravel bench, and mechanics who actually ride the trails out the door. Make a morning of it. @roaringmousecycles

Valencia Cyclery — 1077 Valencia Street, San Francisco. Same family, same block since 1985, and still the Mission's default for the part you need today. Two storefronts, a deep wall of tires, and no upsell energy. Walk in knowing your tube size and you will be out fast. @valenciacyclery

Box Dog Bikes — 494 14th Street, San Francisco. A worker owned cooperative that leans practical over flashy, big on city commuters, touring builds, and honest wrenching. Closed Sunday and Monday, so midweek is your window. Ask about their house frames if you love steel. @boxdogbikes

Mike's Bikes — 1233 Howard Street, San Francisco. The SoMa flagship is the big showroom play when you want to test ride a whole wall of bikes in a single stop. Real service desk, open daily, easy when your week is a mess. Come with a price range in your head. @mikesbikessf

Huckleberry Bicycles — 181 Greenwich Street, San Francisco. The old Market Street commuter savior reopened in Levi's Plaza near the waterfront, same quick flat fixes and honest wrenching, now with room to test ride out front. Closed Sundays. Great catch before an Embarcadero loop. @huckbikes

Warm Planet Bikes — 1098A Market Street, San Francisco. The folding bike specialists near Civic Center, born at the old Caltrain bike valet and still the spot for a Brompton fix or a tight tune up. Small shop, so call ahead. Ideal if your commute folds in half. @warmplanetbikessf

Eight for two wheels: American Cyclery, Freewheel, Roaring Mouse, Valencia Cyclery, Box Dog, Mike's Bikes, Huckleberry, and Warm Planet. Which is your neighborhood shop?

item.title: San Francisco Music and Instrument Shops
item.description: San Francisco has bought its reeds, rosin, and repairs from Union Music on Market Street since 1922, back when half of downtown had a music counter. Most o
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Music and Instrument Shops

San Francisco has bought its reeds, rosin, and repairs from Union Music on Market Street since 1922, back when half of downtown had a music counter. Most of those are long gone. The shops that hung on are the keepers. Eight instrument stops from Chinatown to the Sunset still let you hold the thing before you buy it.

Union Music Company — 1710 Market Street, San Francisco. The city's band and orchestra hub since 1922, wall to wall brass, woodwinds, and strings, plus a repair bench and rental racks for the kid who just joined band. Open Wednesday through Saturday. Bring the horn that has been buzzing wrong. @unionmusiccompany

Real Guitars — 15 Lafayette Street, San Francisco. The city's oldest vintage guitar shop, open since 1986 and stacked with old Fenders, oddball pawnshop gold, and amps that come with stories. Staff will let you plug in and lose track of time. Closed Sundays. Go on a slow weekday and noodle. @real_guitars

Guitar Solo — 230 Townsend Street, San Francisco. Nylon string heaven since 1974, classical and flamenco boxes, plus a sheet music wall that keeps teachers coming back. Quiet, serious, and happy to hand you a concert guitar to try. Ask them to steer you by budget. @guitarsolosf

SF Guitarworks — 323 Potrero Avenue, San Francisco. Not a sales floor, a repair shop, the place other stores quietly send their setups and fret work. Drop off is by appointment with walk in hours Saturday, so call ahead. Worth it when your action feels like cheese wire. @sfguitarworks

Mission Synths — 3026 24th Street, San Francisco. A tiny temple to knobs and patch cables, used modular gear, classic synths, local vinyl, and workshops for the curious. Even beginners walk out wanting a drum machine. Open Wednesday to Sunday. Go poke at something that bleeps. @missionsynths

Ellie and Eva Company — 709 Jackson Street, San Francisco. A Chinatown mainstay for over 50 years, where erhus and guzhengs share the room with vintage American and Japanese electric guitars. Friendly violins and ukuleles for first timers too. Push the door open and let them show you around.

101 Music — 1414 Grant Avenue, San Francisco. North Beach's cluttered wonder, two storefronts of vinyl, yes, but also a back stock of used horns, guitars, and old stereo gear. Dig a little and you turn up the deal. Cash is king and the hunt is the point. Give yourself an hour, minimum.

Sunset Music — 2311 Irving Street, San Francisco. The Outer Sunset's old school shop for sheet music, rentals, reeds, and a giant rubber band ball at the register that regulars swear by. The kind of counter that still knows the school band teachers by name. Closed Sunday and Monday.

Eight for the players: Union Music, Real Guitars, Guitar Solo, SF Guitarworks, Mission Synths, Ellie and Eva, 101 Music, and Sunset Music. What was the first instrument you ever owned?

item.title: San Francisco Tattoo Studios
item.description: Eight San Francisco tattoo shops worth planning a trip around, and the oldest has been inking the city since 1995. Say tattoo in SF and people picture the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Tattoo Studios

Eight San Francisco tattoo shops worth planning a trip around, and the oldest has been inking the city since 1995. Say tattoo in SF and people picture the Haight. Plenty of the best needles are down Valencia in the Mission too. Both strips made this list.

Black and Blue Tattoo — 3290 22nd St, San Francisco. Queer and woman owned since 1995, which in tattoo years makes it an institution. Walk in Tuesday through Sunday, noon to 6, and the crew covers everything from fine script to bold color. Ask for the artist whose flash matches your idea. @blackandbluetattoo

UNDRGRND SF — 3191 Mission St, San Francisco. Woman and queer owned, and the shop a local panel of pros names for fine line and the spiky cybersigilism style all over your feed. Mostly by appointment, though they answer fast about walk in openings. Bring screenshots, they speak that language. @undrgrnd.sf

Black Heart Tattoo — 177 Valencia St, San Francisco. On the Valencia strip since 2004, the one to beat for bold American traditional, blackwork, and black and grey. Open noon to 8 daily, walk ins always welcome. There is even a vintage photo booth inside, so document the before and after. @blackhearttattoo

Idle Hand Tattoo — 575 Haight St, San Francisco. A Lower Haight anchor since 2004, known for clean bold traditional that still reads sharp decades later. Open daily until 8, walk ins welcome, and the flash on the walls is worth a look even if you are only browsing. @idlehandsf

Cold Steel America — 1783 Haight St, San Francisco. An Upper Haight fixture since 1999, equal parts tattoo studio and serious piercing counter that regulars trust for both. Open noon to 8 every day. Go here when you want the piercing done right the first time, not redone later. @coldsteelpiercing

Mom's Body Shop — 1408 Haight St, San Francisco. Open since Mother's Day 1998 and still one of the busiest counters on Haight, tattoos and piercings both, with a deep case of titanium and gold jewelry. The kicker is the hours, 12 to midnight daily, so it catches the late night ideas. Walk ins all day. @moms_body_shop

Seventh Son Tattoo — 765 Clementina St, San Francisco. Tucked on a SoMa side street, this is the name other SF tattooers give you for Japanese work and big back pieces. Custom and appointment based, though walk ins get squeezed in. Come with a clear idea and let the artist run. @seventhsontattoo

Let It Bleed Tattoo — 1124 Polk St, San Francisco. A Polk Street mainstay since 2009 with a tight crew that handles traditional, Japanese, black and grey, and lettering without blinking. Open daily, 1 to 8, walk ins and appointments both. Easy energy for a first tattoo. @letitbleedsf

Eight for getting inked in San Francisco: Black and Blue, UNDRGRND, Black Heart, Idle Hand, Cold Steel America, Mom's Body Shop, Seventh Son, and Let It Bleed. Which chair are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Plant Nurseries and Garden Centers
item.description: Eight Peninsula nurseries worth the weekend, led by the oldest native plant nursery in California, growing natives since 1960 and now parked out on the Hal
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Plant Nurseries and Garden Centers

Eight Peninsula nurseries worth the weekend, led by the oldest native plant nursery in California, growing natives since 1960 and now parked out on the Half Moon Bay coast. Everyone defaults to a big box rack or a drive over the bridge. The good stuff hides on your side of the Bay Area, Palo Alto to Highway 92.

SummerWinds Nursery — 725 San Antonio Rd, Palo Alto. The dependable all rounder, open 9 to 6 every day when the smaller shops are dark, with a deep bench of annuals, veggie starts, and houseplants. The staff actually know their zones, so bring a photo of your sad corner and ask. Good first stop for a new garden. @summerwindsca

Wegman's Nursery — 492 Woodside Rd, Redwood City. Family run on the same corner for more than 50 years, now led by the founder's son Mark Wegman. It is the classic full service nursery, strong on indoor and outdoor plants and honest advice. Open daily 8 to 5. Go when you want a real person, not a QR code. @wegmansnursery

Golden Nursery — 1122 2nd Ave, San Mateo. Family owned since 1976 and beloved by plant geeks for roses, Japanese maples, rare shrubs, and an annual citrus tasting where you sample before you plant. Weekends run 10 to 5. Bring a list and leave room in the trunk. @goldennursery

Ladera Garden and Gifts — 3130 Alpine Rd, Portola Valley. Run by the Navarro family since 1981, part nursery, part gift shop, part florist tucked in the Ladera neighborhood. Come for the plants and leave with a pot, a candle, and a bouquet you did not plan on. Closed Mondays, otherwise 9 to 5. @laderagardenandgifts

Little Green A Plant Bar — 1101 Main St, Redwood City. The fun one downtown, a coffee bar wrapped in houseplants with a build your own succulent bar in the back. Grab a latte, pot up a little guy, and catch a maker's market or an evening class. Open weekdays, shorter hours on weekends. @littlegreenaplantbar

Half Moon Bay Nursery — 11691 San Mateo Rd, Half Moon Bay. Three acres of coastside growing since 1957, where the fog does half the watering and the stock runs from citrus to bamboo to color you will not find inland. Open daily, gate closes at 4:50. Make it the reward at the end of a Highway 92 drive. @hmbnurseryca

Yerba Buena Nursery — 12511 San Mateo Rd, Half Moon Bay. The oldest native plant nursery in California, started in 1960, now off Highway 92 with natives from every corner of the state plus seeds and garden art. Plant something the local bees and birds actually want. Open Tuesday to Saturday, 9 to 4. @yerbabuenanursery

Shelldance Orchid Gardens — 2000 Hwy 1, Pacifica. Historic greenhouses from 1949, now a rare orchid and bromeliad haven perched above the coast and partnered with the national park next door. Open weekends only, 11 to 4, so plan around it. Worth the trip just to wander the warm rooms and gawk. @shelldance_gardens

Eight for planting up your Peninsula yard: SummerWinds, Wegman's, Golden, Ladera, Little Green, Half Moon Bay Nursery, Yerba Buena, and Shelldance. Which one is getting your spring budget?

item.title: San Francisco Camera Shops and Film Labs
item.description: Eight San Francisco camera shops and film labs that outlived the phone camera, including the oldest community darkroom in the country, running since 1940.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Camera Shops and Film Labs

Eight San Francisco camera shops and film labs that outlived the phone camera, including the oldest community darkroom in the country, running since 1940. Film never died in this city, it just went quiet and got sharper. Where SF still buys, shoots, and develops a roll.

Glass Key Photo — 1230 Sutter Street, San Francisco. The film wall runs 35mm to 8x10, color and black and white, and they will hand you a Leica or a plastic Holga with the same straight face. This is where the city's shooters restock. Go on a weekday, the doors close on weekends. @glasskeyphoto

Photoworks SF — 2279 Market Street, San Francisco. Hand over your rolls and they develop, scan, and print in house, then frame the keepers before you leave. A Market Street fixture for film shooters and the walls they end up hanging. Open seven days. @photoworkssf

Camera Zone and Art Gallery — 662 Grant Avenue, San Francisco. Forty years deep on the busiest block in Chinatown, stocking vintage film bodies next to new digital glass. The kind of counter where you walk in for a battery and leave holding a rangefinder. @camerazonesf

Fireside Camera — 2117 Chestnut Street, San Francisco. The city's oldest independent camera store, holding down the Marina right next to the Apple Store. That's a quiet flex. Real humans who will talk you out of the wrong lens and into the right used one. Worth the walk up Chestnut. @firesidecamera

Oscar's Photo Lab — 790 Brannan Street, San Francisco. A family run lab in SoMa since 1982, still processing, scanning, and printing while the chains folded. Bring the shoebox of undeveloped rolls you have been too scared to open. @oscarsphotolab

Camera West — 120 Maiden Lane, San Francisco. The new arrival, three floors that opened on Maiden Lane in 2026, with Hasselblad and Fujifilm rooms downstairs and used bodies and darkroom supplies up top. Grab a coffee in Union Square and make an afternoon of it. @cameraweststore

Leica Store San Francisco — 463 Bush Street, San Francisco. Two blocks uphill from the Maiden Lane store sits the Leica gallery, red dots under glass, a serious photobook shelf, and a show that rotates through the year, free to walk. You do not have to buy an M to look. @leicastoresf

Harvey Milk Photo Center — 50 Scott Street, San Francisco. The oldest and largest community darkroom in the country, run by Rec and Parks out of Duboce Park since 1954. A membership buys you enlargers, chemistry, and a room full of people who still love the smell of fixer. Take the beginner class.

Eight for the film faithful in San Francisco: Glass Key, Photoworks, Camera Zone, Fireside, Oscar's, Camera West, Leica Store, and the Harvey Milk darkroom. Which counter develops your next roll?

item.title: San Francisco Toy Stores
item.description: Eight independent San Francisco toy stores worth crossing town for, including a Castro variety store that has sold toys and costumes since 1936. The famous
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Toy Stores

Eight independent San Francisco toy stores worth crossing town for, including a Castro variety store that has sold toys and costumes since 1936. The famous downtown shops closed, and the best ones turned out to be neighborhood corners all along. Kites, Gundam, blind boxes, Playmobil.

Tantrum — 248 Clement Street, San Francisco. A mom and pop toy shop since 2012, now on Clement with a vintage carnival look and shelves of European brands you will not find at a big box. Free gift wrap, which quietly saves you every birthday. @tantrumsf

Cliff's Variety — 479 Castro Street, San Francisco. Ninety years in the Castro and still the place for a last minute costume, a science kit, and a rubber chicken in the same trip. Part hardware store, part toy box, all institution. Go for the Halloween windows alone. @cliffsvariety

Woot Bear — 1512 Haight Street, San Francisco. Blind box heaven on Haight, stacked with Sonny Angel, Smiski, and designer vinyl, plus a gallery wall that turns over monthly. Genuinely dangerous if you have a Sonny Angel habit. Open daily. @wootbearbelly

Japantown Collectibles — 1581 Webster Street, San Francisco. Tucked in the Japan Center mall, packed floor to ceiling with Gundam kits, Godzilla, Nendoroids, and Pokemon. The model builders' clubhouse. Come knowing what you want or lose a happy hour to it. @japantownfun

Ying Hobbies and Toys — 63 Wentworth Place, San Francisco. Down a narrow Chinatown alley near Portsmouth Square, a tiny model and hobby shop that rewards anyone willing to find the door. Plastic kits, paints, and old school hobby gear. Come in with a project in mind.

Chinatown Kite Shop — 717 Grant Avenue, San Francisco. A whole store devoted to flight on the main drag of Chinatown, from paper dragons to stunt kites built to actually fly on Marina Green. The rare tourist stop locals still root for. Buy the dragon.

Just For Fun — 3982 24th Street, San Francisco. A Noe Valley classic crammed with toys, cards, puzzles, and gifts, plus weekly Magic and Pokemon tables in the back. Bring the kid who needs a booster pack and the adult who needs a birthday card.

Small Frys — 3985 24th Street, San Francisco. Right across 24th from Just For Fun, a Noe Valley shop stocking Playmobil, LEGO, Green Toys, and Haba for the little ones. Two toy stores facing off across one street is peak Noe Valley. Open seven days. @smallfrys24

Eight for San Francisco toy lovers: Tantrum, Cliff's Variety, Woot Bear, Japantown Collectibles, Ying Hobbies, Chinatown Kite Shop, Just For Fun, and Small Frys. Which neighborhood shop raised your inner kid?

item.title: San Francisco Spice Shops and Global Markets
item.description: The Oakland spice shop Food and Wine called among the world's best finally crossed the bridge, and Oaktown now grinds 300 spices fresh on Fillmore Street.
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Spice Shops and Global Markets

The Oakland spice shop Food and Wine called among the world's best finally crossed the bridge, and Oaktown now grinds 300 spices fresh on Fillmore Street. Eight San Francisco spice shops and global markets worth the trip.

Oaktown Spice Shop — 2132 Fillmore St, San Francisco. The Oakland favorite's first SF outpost, a cayenne red storefront where 300 spices, house blends, and chiles are ground in small batches and scooped to order. Grab a blend and go heavy. @oaktownspice

San Francisco Herb Co — 250 14th St, San Francisco. A wholesale spice house since 1973 that quietly opens its warehouse to the public, bulk bins from allspice to za'atar at prices that embarrass the supermarket. Bring a long list and stock up.

La Palma Mexicatessen — 2884 24th St, San Francisco. The Mission masa mothership since 1953, dried chiles by the bin and corn nixtamalized in back for fresh masa by the kilo. Grab guajillos, ancho, and a bag of masa. @lapalmamex.sf

Casa Lucas Market — 2934 24th St, San Francisco. A family Latin grocery a block down 24th, stacked with dried chiles, fresh epazote, achiote, and Latin American produce the chains never carry. Ask for a chile you have never cooked.

Samiramis Imports — 2990 Mission St, San Francisco. A Middle Eastern grocery on Mission for 50 years, bulk bins of za'atar, sumac, and Aleppo pepper, with house made muhammara at the counter. Smell everything before you scoop.

Lehr's German Specialties — 1581 Church St, San Francisco. A Noe Valley German shop since 1974 for quark, mustard seed, juniper berries, and the spice blends for a proper sauerbraten. Closed Mondays, so plan the schnitzel around it. @lehrssf

Rainbow Grocery — 1745 Folsom St, San Francisco. The worker owned cooperative since 1975 with a bulk spice wall the size of a studio apartment, jars by the hundred and refills by the ounce. Bring your own jars and go slow. @rainbow_grocery

New India Bazar — 1107 Polk St, San Francisco. The city's oldest Indian grocery, a designated Legacy Business over 30 years on Polk, whole cumin, curry leaves, asafoetida, and every dal you need. Ask which garam masala they cook with. @newindiabazarsf

Eight for San Francisco spice: Oaktown, SF Herb Co, La Palma, Casa Lucas, Samiramis, Lehr's, Rainbow, and New India Bazar. Which bin do you raid first?

item.title: San Francisco Stationery and Paper Shops
item.description: Tucked on the Buchanan Mall in Japantown, Paper Tree is an entire San Francisco store devoted to origami, with shelves of folding paper from Japan, Thailan
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Stationery and Paper Shops

Tucked on the Buchanan Mall in Japantown, Paper Tree is an entire San Francisco store devoted to origami, with shelves of folding paper from Japan, Thailand, and Italy. Eight SF stationery and paper shops for people who still love a pen.

Paper Tree — 1743 Buchanan St, San Francisco. The family run origami store on the Buchanan Mall in Japantown, walls of folding paper plus washi, kits, books, and thousand crane displays. Pick a paper you cannot pronounce and a book to match. @papertreesf

ARCH Art Supplies — 1490 17th St, San Francisco. The woman owned art and drafting shop that has anchored Potrero Hill for 40 years, deep racks of fine paper, sketchbooks, fountain pens, and Kakimori inks. Come for paper, leave with a pen. @archsupplies

Case for Making — 4037 Judah St, San Francisco. A tiny Outer Sunset studio that hand mixes over 100 watercolors and prints letterpress paper goods a block from the beach. Build a custom paint palette and watch them fill it. @caseformaking

General Store — 4035 Judah St, San Francisco. Right next door, a sunlit boutique of California made goods where the cards, art prints, and paper gifts are the reason to linger. Two paper stops, one block, ocean air included. @generalstore

Rare Device — 600 Divisadero St, San Francisco. A woman owned shop and gallery on Divisadero with a real stationery wall, cards, stickers, notebooks, and pens curated like the art on the walls. Grab a card worth keeping. @raredevice

Park Life — 220 Clement St, San Francisco. The Inner Richmond design store and gallery since 2006, art books, risograph prints, notebooks, and cards from artists you will start to collect. Shop the front, then the back gallery. @parklifesf

San Francisco Center for the Book — 375 Rhode Island St, San Francisco. A nonprofit devoted to letterpress and bookbinding, free gallery shows plus the Biblioshop selling handmade cards, paper, and type printed goods. See the presses, then browse. @sanfranciscocenterforthebook

SCRAP — 141 Industrial St, San Francisco. The Bayview creative reuse depot, part of Ruth Asawa's legacy, where donated paper, card stock, and art supplies fill bins for pennies. Fill a bag, fund arts education, skip the landfill. @scrapsf

Eight for San Francisco paper: Paper Tree, ARCH, Case for Making, General Store, Rare Device, Park Life, the Center for the Book, and SCRAP. Which is your kind of paper?

item.title: San Francisco Mezcal and Agave Bars
item.description: San Francisco keeps its best tequila list in a low key Yucatecan spot on Geary. Tommy's has poured only 100% agave since 1965, over 300 bottles deep, and g
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Mezcal and Agave Bars

San Francisco keeps its best tequila list in a low key Yucatecan spot on Geary. Tommy's has poured only 100% agave since 1965, over 300 bottles deep, and gave the world the Tommy's Margarita everyone copies. Eight SF bars where mezcal and tequila are the whole point, not a dusty top shelf.

Tommy's Mexican Restaurant — 5929 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A family Yucatecan room in the Richmond hiding over 300 tequilas, all 100% agave, since 1965. This is where the Tommy's Margarita was born and where Julio Bermejo turned SF into a tequila town. Sip an anejo neat and skip the sugary stuff. @tommysmexican

Mezcalito — 2323 Polk St, San Francisco. Russian Hill's neighborhood mezcaleria since 2016, dim and easy, with a long agave list and regional Mexican plates to slow you down. Get a smoky mezcal flight before dinner and grab a sidewalk table when the fog lifts. @mezcalitobarsf

Mosto — 741 Valencia St, San Francisco. The little agave bar next to Tacolicious, all tequila, mezcal and tacos al pastor off the trompo, now with a disco ball overhead. It quietly keeps one of the deeper mezcal lists on Valencia. Ask the bartender to take you off menu. @mosto_sf

Loló — 974 Valencia St, San Francisco. Jaliscan Californian cooking with an actual agave program, so a server can walk you through what separates a good tequila from a good mezcal. The room is a color explosion and the shrimp tacos earn the hype. Order a flight and take notes. @lolorestaurantsf

El Techo de Lolinda — 2518 Mission St, San Francisco. The Mission rooftop with 360 degree city views, heaters and a retractable roof, so it works nearly every day of the year. Agave cocktails carry the menu, from smoky palomas to pitchers for a crowd. Go at golden hour and stay for the lights. @eltechosf

Cavaña — 100 Channel St, San Francisco. A 17th floor Mission Bay rooftop leaning hard into agave, with mezcal and tequila cocktails and seasonal pours like watermelon and hibiscus. Views run over the ballpark and the bay. Walk ins welcome or book on Resy, and come for sunset. @cavana.sf

Santeria — 2251 Market St, San Francisco. A Castro cantina that calls itself a margarita bar but keeps mezcal on the rocks and bold agave cocktails like the Santera with jalapeno cordial and lava salt. Easy, loud and fun. Start here before a night out on the block. @santeria_sf

Flores — 2030 Union St, San Francisco. The Cow Hollow spot with a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a serious tequila and mezcal list behind fresh masa tortillas and molcajete guac. Margaritas come balanced, not sweet, and the sipping pours reward a slow night. Post up at the bar. @flores_sf

Eight for San Francisco agave: Tommy's, Mezcalito, Mosto, Loló, El Techo, Cavaña, Santeria, and Flores. Which one gets your first flight?

item.title: San Francisco Pottery and Ceramics Studios
item.description: San Francisco hides a public pottery studio inside Golden Gate Park. Sharon Art Studio has fired kilns in a historic park building for generations and runs
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Pottery and Ceramics Studios

San Francisco hides a public pottery studio inside Golden Gate Park. Sharon Art Studio has fired kilns in a historic park building for generations and runs some of the most affordable wheel classes in the city. You do not have to cross to Oakland to make a mug. Eight SF studios where a first timer can throw a bowl this weekend.

Sharon Art Studio — 300 Bowling Green Dr, San Francisco. The city's largest public art center, tucked into Golden Gate Park near the carousel, with ceramics classes for every age and level through Rec and Parks. Low prices mean sessions fill fast, so sign up the day enrollment opens. Bring a friend and split a bag of clay.

Ruby's Clay Studio and Gallery — 552A Noe St, San Francisco. A nonprofit community studio in the Castro run by and for potters, with classes, member shelves and a small gallery up front. The vibe is welcoming and unpretentious, exactly what a first wheel class should feel like. Try a beginner handbuilding night. @rubysclaystudio

Clayroom — 1431 17th St, San Francisco. A big, friendly Potrero Hill studio with wheel classes, memberships and a woodshop, plus paint your own pottery if you just want a low key afternoon. Good for total beginners and returning potters alike. Book a single wheel session and see if it grabs you. @clayroomsf

Wheelhouse Clay Studio — 2201 Sutter St, San Francisco. A Filipina and woman of color owned studio that treats clay as community, with six week wheel courses and one time Clay Play classes for the merely curious. Small groups, real instruction, zero snobbery. Grab a two hour Clay Play wheel spot and make a mess. @wheelhouseclaysf

SMAart Studio — 3135 24th St, San Francisco. Over 10,000 square feet in the Mission with wheel, hand building, sculpture and even Raku firing, plus one day workshops if you want to try before committing. Members get 24 hour access. Start with a one day wheel class, then chase the Raku night. @smaartstudio

Clay By The Bay — 1618 Pacific Ave, San Francisco. A roomy studio built around beginners, open seven days a week, known for Friday and Saturday try pottery nights where you make two pieces in one sitting. No experience, no problem. Bring a date and see who centers the clay first.

Mel Rice Studio Ceramica — 6138 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A sustainable Richmond studio that mixes its own glazes and recycles every scrap of clay, opened in 2016 by a San Franciscan artist. Classes stay small and the ethos is low waste. Take a handbuilding workshop and leave with something you made. @melriceceramica

Terra Mia Decorative Art Studio — 1314 Castro St, San Francisco. The original NorCal paint your own pottery spot, no experience or appointment needed, just pick a piece and glaze away. Great for kids, birthdays and a foggy Noe Valley afternoon. Walk in, paint a mug, pick it up a few days later.

Eight for San Francisco clay: Sharon, Ruby's, Clayroom, Wheelhouse, SMAart, Clay By The Bay, Mel Rice, and Terra Mia. Which studio gets your first bowl?
