item.title: Bay Area Climbing Gyms
item.description: Seven Bay Area climbing gyms worth the chalk, and the best story might belong to a former power plant. Say climbing and people picture Yosemite, but the Ba
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Climbing Gyms

Seven Bay Area climbing gyms worth the chalk, and the best story might belong to a former power plant. Say climbing and people picture Yosemite, but the Bay quietly built a world class indoor scene, three of them right here in San Francisco. Ropes, boulders, saunas, real community. Where to tie in first?

Mission Cliffs — 2295 Harrison Street, San Francisco. The one that started it all, the city's first climbing gym and still a Mission anchor three decades on. Fifty foot lead walls, a bouldering section, yoga, a weight room and a hot sauna for after. First timers and veterans share the same walls. Regulars swear by a weekday morning session. @missioncliffs

Dogpatch Boulders — 2573 Third Street, San Francisco. No ropes, all problems. Touchstone's largest bouldering gym stacks more than 300 problems on seventeen foot walls in a walkable corner of the Dogpatch. They reset often, so the wall you flailed on last month feels new. Upstairs weights and a roomy sauna seal it. @dogpatchboulders

Movement San Francisco — 924 Old Mason Street, San Francisco. Climbing with a Golden Gate Bridge view, tucked into the Presidio above Crissy Field. Twenty five thousand square feet, rope walls to forty five feet, two floors of bouldering, a Kilter board and two yoga studios. Send hard, then walk it off along the water. @movementgymsbayarea

The Oaks — 1875 Solano Avenue, Berkeley. They built a bouldering gym inside the historic Oaks Theater on Solano, so North Berkeley climbs under ninety year old movie house bones. Slabs, steep overhangs, dihedrals and aretes, 160 plus problems, and monthly movie nights that nod to the address. Character no new build can copy. @oaksclimbing

Berkeley Ironworks — 800 Potter Street, Berkeley. An East Bay staple with a forty five foot lead wall and, members say, the best natural light of any gym around. Fourteen thousand square feet of routes and boulders, plus a members only training center across the street with boards and world cup style terrain. @berkeleyironworks

Great Western Power Co — 520 20th Street, Oakland. Set inside a former steam power plant in Uptown, all historic brick and forty eight foot lead lines. Eleven thousand square feet, calm and quiet by day, social by night, and an easy walk from BART. An established favorite regulars quietly rank as their top Touchstone. @greatwesternpowerco

Hyperion — 801 Willow Street, Redwood City. The newest room here, and the Peninsula finally has a serious one. More than ten thousand square feet of bouldering, 250 plus problems, a real comp wall, with rope walls on the way. If you live south of the city, this is the move. @hyperionclimbing

Seven for the Bay Area climber: Mission Cliffs and Dogpatch in the city, Movement in the Presidio, the Oaks and Ironworks in Berkeley, Great Western in Oakland, Hyperion down the Peninsula. Three never make you cross a bridge. Which wall are you tying in on first?

item.title: San Francisco French Bistros
item.description: Seven San Francisco French bistros that never chase a trend, they just keep serving cassoulet. One has kept the same pot going more than eighteen thousand
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco French Bistros

Seven San Francisco French bistros that never chase a trend, they just keep serving cassoulet. One has kept the same pot going more than eighteen thousand days. Skip the hyped new openings for a night. These are the neighborhood rooms where escargot, steak frites and a glass of Burgundy still feel like a small trip to Paris, no passport required.

Zazie — 941 Cole Street, San Francisco. A Cole Valley bistro built for slow mornings, American style brunch and Provencal dinners, with a back garden patio that feels miles from the fog. Brunch runs first come first served, so put your name down and wander Cole Street while you wait. Dogs are welcome in the garden.

Chez Maman — 1401 18th Street, San Francisco. A neighborhood French bistro locals have leaned on long enough that it now comes in two, the original on Potrero Hill and a second in Hayes Valley at 401 Gough. Unfussy and warm, the kind of established corner room you return to without thinking. If 18th Street is full, point yourself toward Gough.

Chapeau — 126 Clement Street, San Francisco. A husband and wife team have run this Inner Richmond bistro since 1996, and it shows in the escargots, the coq au vin and the cassoulet. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays, so make it a Wednesday through Sunday plan and save room for the creme brulee. @chapeau.sf

Absinthe — 398 Hayes Street, San Francisco. A Hayes Valley mainstay since 1998, this brasserie pairs turn of the century Paris decor with French classics and a serious list of cocktails. It sits in the middle of the arts district, so it is an easy pre show table or a late convivial one. The bar is a fine solo perch. @absinthesf

Chouquet's — 2500 Washington Street, San Francisco. A corner French bistro in Pacific Heights built for people watching, sidewalk tables for brunch, a banquette for a long dinner, a bar for a quick lunch. Weekends bring live jazz from 12 to 4, and most of the menu stays thirty dollars and under. Unpretentious and easy.

Le Central — 453 Bush Street, San Francisco. Opened in 1974, this is the oldest French bistro in the city, a one story brick holdout with a pink neon sign near Union Square. The cassoulet has been going for more than eighteen thousand days. Order the steak frites or the moules and settle in where regulars have sat for fifty years.

Cafe de la Presse — 352 Grant Avenue, San Francisco. Right across from the Chinatown gate, this bistro and old newsstand has anchored its corner of the old French Quarter for decades. A 1920s dining room, a full bar of French spirits, and a terrace made for a coffee and a quiche. Open all seven days, breakfast through dinner. @cafedelapressesf

Seven for a French night in San Francisco: Zazie in Cole Valley, Chez Maman on Potrero Hill, Chapeau in the Richmond, Absinthe in Hayes Valley, Chouquet's in Pac Heights, Le Central by Union Square, Cafe de la Presse at the Chinatown gate. Which one gets your Friday?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Tattoo Studios
item.description: Five Peninsula tattoo studios worth parking for before you ever think about crossing a bridge. Everyone assumes the good work only happens in the city, but
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Tattoo Studios

Five Peninsula tattoo studios worth parking for before you ever think about crossing a bridge. Everyone assumes the good work only happens in the city, but San Mateo County has quietly built its own scene, traditional to single needle. Burlingame down to Redwood City.

Royalty Tattoo Collective — 1009 California Dr, Burlingame. Downtown Burlingame's walkable anchor shop, five stations plus a private room, licensed through San Mateo County Health. Seasoned collector or first tattoo, the vibe is friendly, not gatekept. Book by phone or stop in, closed Mondays. @royaltytattoocollective

Godspeed Tattoo — 620 S Norfolk St, San Mateo. A San Mateo landmark since 1998 and still owner run, the kind of established shop where walk ins are welcome and the artists actually draw custom. Tattoos only, no piercings, bring a valid ID. Open Tuesday to Sunday. @godspeed.tattoo

Hello Tattoo — 13 Lodato Ave, San Mateo. A tucked away, appointment only studio built for fine line and single needle work, botanicals, script, tiny matching pieces. Pink walled and calm, one client at a time. Message first, no walk ins, and ask to see healed work. @hello.tattoo

Paw Tattoo — 502 2nd Ave, San Mateo. Jia Kim tattoos roughly 600 micro pet portraits a year here, ten minutes from SFO, so it is the move for memorializing a dog or cat in single needle detail. Small, calm studio that books out far ahead, so plan early. @paw.tattoo

Ink Dripped Tattoo Studio — 1741 Broadway, Redwood City. Eight artists under one roof on downtown Redwood City's main drag, so whatever the style, someone here is built for it. Every piece gets customized to the client, easy to pair with a Broadway coffee before your slot.

Five for the Peninsula: Royalty in Burlingame, Godspeed, Hello and Paw clustered in San Mateo, Ink Dripped down in Redwood City. Traditional to fine line to pet portraits, no bridge toll required. Which one fits the piece you keep putting off?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Bookstores
item.description: Five Marin bookstores worth closing the laptop for, because the county quietly runs some of the best indie shelves in the Bay Area. Everyone ships books to
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Bookstores

Five Marin bookstores worth closing the laptop for, because the county quietly runs some of the best indie shelves in the Bay Area. Everyone ships books to the door and forgets you can still browse picks made by people who actually read them, from a Corte Madera events powerhouse to a coastal shop the Chronicle calls the platonic ideal of an indie. Go get lost in the stacks.

Book Passage — 51 Tamal Vista Blvd, Corte Madera. The Bay Area's author event powerhouse, a Corte Madera institution that hosts writers almost nightly and runs real classes for people who want to write their own book. Come for a signing, stay to graze a famously deep selection. Few bookstores anywhere pack this much community under one roof. @bookpassage

Copperfield's Books — 1200 4th Street, San Rafael. A North Bay indie chain born in Sonoma County, and this expansive branch anchors the heart of Fourth Street in downtown San Rafael. Big local author nights, a serious kids section, and staff picks worth trusting. The kind of established, walkable downtown bookstore every Main Street wishes it still had. @copperfieldsbooks

Depot Bookstore and Cafe — 87 Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. Books and a coffee counter together in the old train depot right on the Mill Valley plaza, open daily from 7am. Browse the magazine racks and kids section, then take your latte to a table looking out on the square. It has been the town's living room for decades.

Sausalito Books by the Bay — 100 Bay Street, Sausalito. A tiny community bookshop right on the waterfront boardwalk at the yacht harbor, dogs always welcome. It leans hard into local authors and the kind of hand sold picks a chain cannot fake. Grab a novel, walk out to the water, and read with the bay in front of you. @sausalitobooks

Point Reyes Books — 11315 CA-1, Point Reyes Station. Worth the drive out to West Marin, this is the shop the SF Chronicle called the platonic ideal of a modern indie bookstore. Owners Sparks and Parent stock a world class selection heavy on nature and place, in the town that is the gateway to the National Seashore. Make it the reward at the end of a coast day. @pointreyesbooks

Five for your Marin book run: Book Passage, Copperfield's Books, Depot Bookstore and Cafe, Sausalito Books by the Bay, and Point Reyes Books. From a Corte Madera events hub to a bookshop on the Point Reyes coast, this county still shows up for print. Which one are you browsing first?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Mediterranean and Greek
item.description: Eight Peninsula spots for Mediterranean and Greek, from white tablecloth Athens energy to a foil wrapped shawarma eaten over the steering wheel. Palo Alto
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Mediterranean and Greek

Eight Peninsula spots for Mediterranean and Greek, from white tablecloth Athens energy to a foil wrapped shawarma eaten over the steering wheel. Palo Alto hoards most of them, but Burlingame, San Mateo and San Carlos hold their own. This is the answer next time someone claims there is nowhere good to eat between showings.

Evvia Estiatorio — 420 Emerson St, Palo Alto. The grande dame of Peninsula Greek, sister to San Francisco's Kokkari, with an open kitchen, a cozy room and the lamb the founders grew up on. Reservations book out, so plan ahead, not wander in. Bring the client you want to close, order a whole grilled fish, and let the room do the talking.

Meyhouse — 640 Emerson St, Palo Alto. Two blocks from Evvia, a Turkish meyhane where meze, the grill and live jazz run late. It pulled a 2026 Diners' Choice nod, so it is not a secret anymore. Go with a table of friends, order a spread of small plates, and plan to linger past your reservation. @meyhouserestaurant

Oren's Hummus — 261 University Ave, Palo Alto. Hummus so silky it converted a generation of skeptics, scooped up with warm pita at a counter that is somehow always buzzing. Their own motto is rip, scoop, eat. That's about all the instruction you need. Grab a stool, then walk it off down University. @orenshummus

Mediterranean Wraps — 433 California Ave, Palo Alto. The California Ave lunch line regulars quietly guard, turning out falafel, shawarma and a loaded Greek salad for not much money. Parking is easy for once, and they will nudge you to order off their own site to dodge the app fees. Get the falafel deluxe wrap and eat it in the sun. @medwraps

Mykonos — 226 Lorton Ave, Burlingame. A meze house cooking over charcoal since 2020, where small plates and ouzo are meant to leave the table a happy mess. It anchors Burlingame's Lorton Ave, a walkable block worth the trip north. Bring a crew, order too much, and let someone else drive home.

Mediterranean Kitchen — 270 Lorton Ave, Burlingame. Same block as Mykonos, a warm room mixing Turkish, Greek and Middle Eastern plates with lamb and chicken turning on the rotisserie. Screens loop Mediterranean scenery. That's either soothing or a dare to book a flight. Come hungry, split the appetizer combo, save room for a gyro. @mkburlingame

SAJJ Mediterranean — 251 E 3rd Ave, San Mateo. Downtown San Mateo's build your own move, bowls and wraps loaded with shawarma, falafel and every sauce you can point at. They still run a food truck, so the flavors travel fine to a desk lunch or a park bench. Keep it simple with a chicken bowl, or go fully maximalist. Your call. @sajjstreeteats

Elia — 727 Laurel St, San Carlos. Aegean cooking with a floor show, think cheese set aflame tableside, live violin on weeknights and a DJ once the weekend hits. San Carlos keeps it a touch more low key than the city. That's the whole point. Go for a birthday, order the flaming cheese, and let them make a scene.

Eight for the Peninsula's Mediterranean and Greek: Evvia and Meyhouse for a real night out, Oren's and Med Wraps for a fast Palo Alto lunch, Mykonos and Mediterranean Kitchen for Burlingame's Lorton Ave, SAJJ for San Mateo, Elia for a San Carlos celebration. Which is your regular, and who got left off?

item.title: San Francisco Steakhouses
item.description: Eight San Francisco steakhouses worth the splurge, and the tourist lists always circle the same handful. The city's beef runs deeper than a Bay Bridge view
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Steakhouses

Eight San Francisco steakhouses worth the splurge, and the tourist lists always circle the same handful. The city's beef runs deeper than a Bay Bridge view, tableside carving carts, Jackson Square jazz, Japanese Wagyu, Brazilian rodizio, Prime and Dungeness crab. This is the list for the next anniversary, closing dinner, or when the in laws roll into town. Here is where locals book.

House of Prime Rib — 1906 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco. An institution since 1949, and still the toughest reservation in town for good reason. There is one decision here, how big a cut of 21 day aged prime rib, wheeled over on a silver cart and carved to your call, with the spun tableside salad and a puff of Yorkshire pudding. Come hungry, go easy on the bread basket, and book weeks ahead. @thehouseofprimerib

Harris' Restaurant — 2100 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco. The grand dame of the genre, dark wood and white tablecloths since 1984, with live jazz drifting over from the bar most nights. Order the dry aged Porterhouse or the bone in New York, chase it with a cold martini, and let the room do the talking. Two blocks from House of Prime Rib, so Van Ness is basically the city's steak row. @harrisrestaurantsf

Bix — 56 Gold Street, San Francisco. Tucked down a lamplit alley in Jackson Square, this two story supper club has poured some of the city's best martinis since 1988. It reads as modern American, but the USDA Prime flat iron and the steak tartare hold their own, and there is live jazz every single night. No hard dress code, but this is a room that rewards a jacket. @bixsf

Epic Steak — 369 The Embarcadero, San Francisco. Yes, it is the one with the Bay Bridge lights practically in your lap, and yes, it earns the view. Prime dry aged cuts and craft cocktails right on the water, plus a move most people miss, weekday happy hour from 4 to 6, Wagyu cheeseburger and beef tartare gougeres at the bar. Snag a patio seat before the fog turns on. @epicsteak

5A5 — 139 Steuart Street, San Francisco. When a plain slab of Prime feels too predictable, this is the move, real Japanese A5 Wagyu seared in front of you, izakaya skewers, and a whisky list that reads like a collector's brag. The small plates mean you graze your way through instead of committing to one giant steak. Bring the friend who swears they have tried everything. @5a5stk

Boboquivari's — 1450 Lombard Street, San Francisco. Locals call it Bobo's, a candlelit Marina hideaway where surf and turf is the entire personality. The 12oz bone in filet gets seared in rosemary garlic butter, and the whole roasted Dungeness crab arrives in a secret garlic sauce worth the bib. It is closed Sunday and Monday, so plan your week around it. @boboquivarissf

Niku Steakhouse — 61 Division Street, San Francisco. The special occasion splurge, a tiny Michelin listed room in SoMa from the Omakase Restaurant Group, built entirely around Wagyu. Expect Japanese Wagyu treated with the same fuss as a tasting menu, so it is precision over portion size. Reservations run through Tock and vanish fast, so set a reminder before date night. @nikusteakhouse

Espetus Brazilian Steakhouse — 1686 Market Street, San Francisco. The all you can eat antidote to fussy, right where Market meets Gough. Gaucho chefs work the room nonstop, carving 14 cuts of fire grilled meat straight onto your plate, rodizio style, with a loaded salad bar for backup. The parade keeps coming until you wave the white flag. This is the move when everyone shows up starving. @espetus

Eight for the city's best beef: House of Prime Rib for the carving cart, Harris' for old guard glamour, Bix for jazz, Epic for the Bay Bridge, 5A5 and Niku for Wagyu, Bobo's for surf and turf, Espetus for the rodizio parade. Which is your special occasion anchor, and who is missing from the list?

I'm an East Bay agent who eats all over the Bay Area. When you want the East Bay version of any of this, Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Joaquin counties are my home turf.

item.title: San Francisco Hotel Bars and Lounges
item.description: Six San Francisco hotel bars you can walk into without booking a room. Some float on the roof, some hide off the lobby, and all of them out pour the bar do
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Hotel Bars and Lounges

Six San Francisco hotel bars you can walk into without booking a room. Some float on the roof, some hide off the lobby, and all of them out pour the bar down the block.

Top of the Mark — 999 California Street, San Francisco. The penthouse lounge atop the Mark Hopkins has been pouring on Nob Hill since 1939, and the wraparound windows still outclass any rooftop the tour buses chase. Come Saturday for the live band (there's a small cover) or chip away at the 100 martini list. It's the Golden Gate view Nob Hill charges rent for, no lease required. @topofthemarksf

Charmaine's — 1100 Market Street, San Francisco. The Proper Hotel's rooftop floats 120 feet over Market Street, all fire pits and greenery, and it's indoor and outdoor both so the fog won't chase you off. Find the elevator at the 45 McAllister entrance, not the grand doors. Fair warning, groups of three plus hit a $50 per person minimum after dark, so treat it as a view and a cocktail night. @charmainesrooftop

Starlite — 450 Powell Street, San Francisco. Take the elevator to the 21st floor of the Beacon Grand and you get 360 degrees of city, green velvet, and an all vinyl DJ most nights. Cocktails come from Scott Baird of Trick Dog fame; order the Cable Car, his spin on a Sidecar. Thursday through Sunday, 21 and up, and the rare Union Square room worth changing out of the hoodie for. @starlitesf

The Post Room — 450 Powell Street, San Francisco. Ride the same Beacon Grand elevator back to the lobby and you land at its brasserie bar, all vaulted ceilings and cold, exact martinis. The move is weekday happy hour: ten dollar cocktails, seven dollar wine, two dollar oysters, prices that feel smuggled in from another decade. Sit at the bar and order a dozen. @beacongrand

Pied Piper — 2 New Montgomery Street, San Francisco. The Palace bar is named for the Maxfield Parrish mural behind it, painted after the 1906 quake and hanging here since 1909. That makes it the most valuable wallpaper in any bar you'll drink in. Mosaic floors, dark wood, a serious whiskey list, and a Wagyu burger locals quietly rank among the city's best. Open nightly from five. @piedpipersf

Garden Court Lounge — 2 New Montgomery Street, San Francisco. Cross the Palace lobby from the Pied Piper and you reach the GC Lounge, where you sip beneath the landmark glass dome without booking the full sit down feast. Cocktails, wine, and dessert under Austrian crystal. That's a lot of grandeur for a Tuesday. Open afternoons to evening, Monday through Saturday. Bring someone you're trying to impress. @palacehotelsf

Six for a San Francisco hotel bar night, no room required: Top of the Mark and Charmaine's for the view, Starlite for the party, the Post Room for cheap oysters, Pied Piper for the mural, the Garden Court Lounge for the dome. Which gets your first round?

item.title: San Francisco Karaoke Bars
item.description: Five San Francisco karaoke spots, and the loudest one isn't where the tourists pile in first. The Mint has run karaoke on Market Street since 1993, but the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Karaoke Bars

Five San Francisco karaoke spots, and the loudest one isn't where the tourists pile in first. The Mint has run karaoke on Market Street since 1993, but the private rooms hide a few blocks over by Japantown, where one keeps the mic on until 4am. Here's where to book your booth.

The Mint Karaoke Lounge — 1942 Market St, San Francisco. Thirty years in and still the name people mean when they say SF karaoke. No private rooms, one bright stage, 25,000 songs, and a crowd that claps for strangers. Singing is free if you tip the brave. Reserve a table on weekends or plan to stand. @themintkaraokelounge

Pandora Karaoke and Bar — 50 Mason St, San Francisco. Steps off Union Square, this is the private room play: grab a booth, shut the door, and butcher Whitney where only your friends can hear. Rooms run half off Mondays and Tuesdays. That's when the smart money books. Doors at 6, karaoke by 8, closed Sundays. @pandorakaraoke

Festa Wine and Cocktail Lounge — 1825A Post St, San Francisco. Upstairs in the Kinokuniya building, this Japantown room skips private booths for one retro Tokyo stage where everybody sings to everybody. Sake, cocktails, and regulars who will carry you through the key change you can't hit. Ask for Masae. Second floor, easy to walk past, worth the stairs.

K-Box Karaoke — 1660 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. The Japantown pick for when the night refuses to end: private rooms that stay open to 4am Fridays and Saturdays, long after Geary goes quiet. Cozy setup, a real sound system, and online booking so you're not the group circling for parking at midnight. Open daily.

Taisho — 1161 Post St, San Francisco. The rare karaoke room that's all ages, so it covers the office night and the family birthday alike. Private rooms that start around thirty dollars an hour, spam musubi and katsu curry to the door, sake by the carafe. Happy hour knocks the rates down early in the week. Rooms fill Fridays, so reserve. @taishosf

Five for the mic, from Market Street to Japantown: the Mint, Pandora, Festa, K-Box, and Taisho. Two put you on a stage, three give you a door you can close. What is the one song you would make the whole room sit through?

item.title: San Francisco Mediterranean and Greek
item.description: Five San Francisco tables that do Greek and Mediterranean right, from a Financial District fireplace to a Presidio hillside. Souvlaki, meze, wood-smoke and
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Mediterranean and Greek

Five San Francisco tables that do Greek and Mediterranean right, from a Financial District fireplace to a Presidio hillside. Souvlaki, meze, wood-smoke and Aegean wine, all inside city limits. Skip the flight to Athens for now.

Kokkari Estiatorio — 200 Jackson Street, San Francisco. The wood-burning hearth in Jackson Square has been turning out modern Hellenic plates since before you moved here, and the lamb still comes off that open fire like a Sunday on Samos. Grab a spot near the fireplace, order the moussaka, let the FiDi crowd fade. Book ahead, this room fills.

Souvla — 517 Hayes St, San Francisco. The original Hayes Valley counter that taught the city fast-fine Greek back in 2014, with a lively parklet out front made for people-watching. Get the lamb souvlaki, an all-Greek glass of white, and the frozen Greek yogurt you will think about for days. Walkable from the opera, low-key on a weeknight. @souvla

Dalida — 101 Montgomery Street, Presidio, San Francisco. Tucked inside the national park on the Main Post, this Michelin-listed Eastern Mediterranean room reads a little Turkish, a little Greek, Armenian and Arabic all at once. Come for the meze, the foraged Presidio aromatics in the cocktails, the hillside walk after. Reserve, then linger on the patio. @dalidasf

Troya — 2125 Fillmore St, San Francisco. The Fillmore anchor for Turkish-Mediterranean when you want mezze without ceremony, hummus and kebabs and a wood-grilled spread meant for sharing. Weekend brunch runs from ten, so it doubles as a slow Saturday. Wander the Fillmore shops after, one of the more walkable stretches in Pacific Heights. @troyasanfrancisco

Beit Rima — 138 Church Street, San Francisco. Counter-service Arabic comfort food where the Castro meets Duboce, no reservations, no fuss, a line that moves and plates that overdeliver. The rotisserie chicken and the hummus are the move, the garlic sauce is the reason you come back. Grab a table, or carry it up to Dolores a few blocks away. @beitrima

Five for the SF Mediterranean crawl: Kokkari, Souvla, Dalida, Troya and Beit Rima. Fireplace Greek, fast-fine souvlaki, Presidio meze, Fillmore Turkish and Castro Levantine, all inside the city. Which one is your Friday night?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Mediterranean and Greek
item.description: Eight South Bay spots for Greek and Mediterranean that locals drive across town for, from Sunnyvale gyros to Santana Row small plates. Bring an appetite an
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Mediterranean and Greek

Eight South Bay spots for Greek and Mediterranean that locals drive across town for, from Sunnyvale gyros to Santana Row small plates. Bring an appetite and maybe a spare napkin.

Dishdash — 190 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. The Murphy Avenue anchor everyone name-drops when a newcomer asks where to eat, and the wait at the door tells you the neighborhood agrees. Order the muhammara and the lamb shank, then decide if the hype is earned. Weekend reservations save you a sidewalk stakeout. @dishdashrestaurants

Agape Grill — 845 Stewart Dr, Sunnyvale. Tucked in a business park where you would not expect a family Greek kitchen. That's half the fun of finding it. Homemade since 2010, and the lunch crowd of engineers knows the lamb gyro plate by heart. Closed Sundays, so plan your craving around it. @agape_grill

Meso — 3060 Olsen Dr, San Jose. The polished one on Santana Row, small plates built for sharing and a wine list that wanders from Greece to Lebanon. Good for a date or a closing-day dinner when you want cloth napkins. Happy hour weekdays 3 to 6 softens the tab.

Athena Grill — 1505 Space Park Dr, Santa Clara. Bright, warm, and run like a Greek grandmother is watching the kitchen, because the hospitality shows. The moussaka and the roasted lamb are the move, and the patio is a quiet weekday reset. Closed Sundays here too. @theathenagrill

Mikonos Grill — 756 E Calaveras Blvd, Milpitas. Family run since 2008, generous plates, TVs with the game on, and parking that hides around back on Hillview Drive. The gyro plate feeds two if you pace yourself. A reliable pick when a Milpitas house hunt runs long. @mikonosgrill

Royal Kebabs and Gyros — 1712 W Campbell Ave, Campbell. A no-fuss counter spot where the kebabs come off the grill fast and the portions punch above the price. Grab a wrap between Campbell open houses and eat it in the car with zero regret. Order ahead at lunch to skip the line.

Hummus Mediterranean Kitchen — 185 Castro St, Mountain View. Right on the Castro Street stroll, rotisserie meats and hummus smooth enough to start an argument over the last scoop. Sidewalk tables make it a solid downtown Mountain View lunch. Busy at noon, so aim early or late. @eatathummus

SAJJ Mediterranean — 21666 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Build-your-own bowls and wraps done fast and halal-friendly. That makes it the weeknight workhorse of the bunch. Handy near the Cupertino tech corridor when you want fresh without a sit-down. The shawarma bowl travels well. @sajjstreeteats

Eight for the South Bay Mediterranean crawl: Sunnyvale for the classics, San Jose for the polish, Santa Clara and Milpitas for the family kitchens, Campbell for the quick kebab, Mountain View and Cupertino for the lunch rush. Which one is your regular order?

item.title: San Francisco Tiki and Rum Bars
item.description: Six San Francisco tiki and rum bars where volcano bowls still erupt and the rain still falls indoors. Locals learned the good rooms hide behind windowless
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Tiki and Rum Bars

Six San Francisco tiki and rum bars where volcano bowls still erupt and the rain still falls indoors. Locals learned the good rooms hide behind windowless doors on purpose. Bring a designated driver and a sweet tooth.

Smuggler's Cove — 650 Gough Street, San Francisco. Three floors of shipwreck packed into a windowless Hayes Valley storefront, with the largest rum selection in North America behind the bar. Order the Rum Barrel, then chase the punch card if you have the stamina. A 2026 James Beard nominee, so the wait at the opaque door is the local tax. @smugglerscovesf

Pagan Idol — 375 Bush Street, San Francisco. A Financial District office tower hides a wooden ship in its belly, with a back room that stages a starry sky and an erupting volcano on cue. It sits where Tiki Bob's stood decades ago, so this address has poured mai tais longer than your favorite startup has existed. Live surf bands roll through most weekends. @paganidolsf

Zombie Village — 441 Jones Street, San Francisco. The Pagan Idol crew built this Tenderloin grotto as a love letter to Skipper Kent's 1942 original, all carved tikis and low amber light. Book a thatched hut for your group and let the Villagers steer the round. Closed Sunday through Tuesday, so aim for a weekend if you want the full room. @thezombievillage

Tonga Room and Hurricane Bar — 950 Mason Street, San Francisco. The Fairmont's Nob Hill basement wraps a band on a floating boat around a lagoon that was the hotel pool back in the 1920s. A thunderstorm rolls through on schedule while you nurse what many call the city's best mai tai. Reserve ahead, dress for a night out, and let the rain surprise the newcomers.

Bamboo Hut — 479 Broadway, San Francisco. A bamboo-lined North Beach room that has poured Flaming Volcano Bowls since 1997, with no attitude beyond a little house sarcasm. Grab a booth, split a bowl between friends, and stay for the local DJs on weekends. It doubles as a dive, so your wallet gets a rare break in this town. @bamboohutsfca

Last Rites — 718 14th Street, San Francisco. A tucked away Duboce Triangle bar built like a crashed jungle plane, fuselage and foliage and all. The drinks lean tropical and the room leans immersive, an easy detour off the Market Street streetcar line. Small space, so slide in early before the after-work crowd claims the good seats. @lastritesbar

Six for a tropical escape without leaving town: Smuggler's Cove, Pagan Idol, Zombie Village, Tonga Room, Bamboo Hut, and Last Rites. Which mai tai in San Francisco earns your vote?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula and South Bay Steakhouses
item.description: Seven Peninsula and South Bay steakhouses worth the drive, and not a single national chain among them. Everyone books the big mall names, then wonders why
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula and South Bay Steakhouses

Seven Peninsula and South Bay steakhouses worth the drive, and not a single national chain among them. Everyone books the big mall names, then wonders why dinner felt like an airport lounge. These are the local rooms that know their cuts and greet regulars by name. Where the good steak lives.

Alexander's Steakhouse — 19379 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Open since 2005 and still the South Bay's special-occasion heavyweight, the kind of tasting-menu night that ends in Wagyu and a hot-towel sigh. Bring the appetite and the person you are trying to impress. @alexanderssteakhousesv

Sundance The Steakhouse — 1921 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. Fifty years on El Camino and still packed with Silicon Valley lifers closing deals over prime rib. Old-school booths, a serious wine list, zero interest in trends. Book the early happy hour if you want a shot at parking. @sundancethesteakhouse

Arya Steakhouse — 140 University Ave, Palo Alto. A Persian steakhouse that butchers in house and dry-ages its ribeye 28 days, then sends out saffron rice and kebabs alongside it. The whole menu is halal, the tomahawk a two-hands affair. Go hungry, downtown parking is its own sport. @aryasteakhouse

LB Steak — 334 Santana Row, San Jose. The polished modern room on the Row, all marble and martinis, where the shopping crowd lands for a proper filet after a day of browsing. Sit on the patio, order the truffle fries, watch the promenade go by.

BE.STEAK.A — 1887 S Bascom Ave, Campbell. An Italian-leaning steakhouse in the Michelin guide, plating wagyu next to handmade pasta and a Sunday all-you-can-eat sparkling buffet locals guard like a secret. Odd name, serious kitchen. Save room, or don't, the buffet forgives. @be.steak.a

Willard Hicks — 280 E Campbell Ave, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's handsome corner spot for 100% Angus and a blackberry-glazed filet that regulars order without glancing at the menu. Deep cocktail list, weekend brunch, easy to love. Grab a patio table when the avenue lights up. @willardhicks

Wild Rose — 200 E Campbell Ave, Campbell. Two doors down the same avenue, a candlelit eatery and bar built around Tomahawk Tuesday, a 40 oz flame-broiled monster with sides and dessert for the table. Craft cocktails carry the rest of the week. Bring friends, split the beast. @wildrosecampbell

Seven for the South Bay steak run: Alexander's, Sundance, Arya, LB Steak, BE.STEAK.A, Willard Hicks, Wild Rose. Skip the chain at the mall, the independents plate a better night. Which one is booking your next celebration?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Sunnyvale, Murphy Avenue
item.description: Eight downtown Sunnyvale spots that make Murphy Avenue the South Bay's most walkable block. One historic street, the old Murphy Station, and a lineup you c
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Sunnyvale, Murphy Avenue

Eight downtown Sunnyvale spots that make Murphy Avenue the South Bay's most walkable block. One historic street, the old Murphy Station, and a lineup you can cover on foot from the Caltrain platform. Here's the walk, anchor to nightcap.

Dishdash — 190 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. The Levantine anchor of the block, packed at lunch since long before the tech crowd found it. Order the crab falafel and the toum, and pretend you'll share the toum. Weekend dinner books up, so reserve or wander over early. @dishdashrestaurants

Siam Taste — 172 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. Downtown's steady Thai kitchen, the kind of local spot regulars guard like a secret they keep telling everyone. The pompano and the lamb chops go past the usual pad thai run. Patio seats fill first on warm evenings. @siamtastethai

Gumba's Italian Foods — 176 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. A slice shop and red sauce institution that has fed Murphy Avenue for decades, no white tablecloth required. Grab a sausage slice at the counter or sit down for the chicken marsala. Open till 9:30pm, your call. @gumbas.sunnyvale

Roberto's Cantina — 168 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. Jalisco-style plates and a bar stocked with more than 150 tequilas. That explains the Friday crowd spilling toward the 1am last call. Get the birria and a Cadillac margarita. Cozy inside, so a reservation helps. @robertos_cantina

Fibbar MaGees — 156 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. An established Irish pub since 1994, holding the South Bay's largest whiskey list and sixteen screens for the match. Two patios, trivia Tuesdays, DJs on weekends. Thursday steak and potato runs ten bucks, no catch. @fibbarmagees

Burma Taste — 124 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. The block's Burmese corner, where the tea leaf salad wins over the friends who swear they never try anything new. Get that and the coconut chicken noodles, then thank whoever dragged you. Small room, so off-peak is the move. @burmataste

Moods Wine Bar and Bistro — 111 W Evelyn Ave, Sunnyvale. Tucked in the Murphy Square building across from the historic strip, pairing a curated wine list with Afghan small plates and live music. Try a flight with the bolani. Happy hour runs 4 to 6, Tuesday through Sunday. @moods_wine_bar

Philz Coffee — 125 S Frances St, Sunnyvale. Half a block off Murphy in Plaza del Sol, across from the Caltrain station. That makes it the downtown morning move before the platform fills. Order a Mint Mojito made one cup at a time. Opens at 5am on weekdays. @philzcoffee

Eight for one walkable block: Levantine anchor, Thai, Italian, Mexican, Irish whiskey, Burmese, a wine flight, and coffee for the train. Which Murphy Avenue stop gets your first weekend?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown Mill Valley
item.description: Seven stops in downtown Mill Valley, the walkable Marin core where Throckmorton, Miller and Corte Madera meet at Lytton Square. Park once and you can hit a
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown Mill Valley

Seven stops in downtown Mill Valley, the walkable Marin core where Throckmorton, Miller and Corte Madera meet at Lytton Square. Park once and you can hit a coffee roaster, a bakery, a market from 1929, and a historic theater without touching your car again. This is the redwood town with a stage. Here's the loop.

Equator Coffees — 2 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley. The downtown cafe from a Marin roaster that's been at it since 1995, and the patio catches the morning sun before the fog gives up. Order a pour-over, grab an outside seat, and watch the town wake up. The dog crowd claims the benches early. @equatorcoffees

Flour Craft Bakery — 129 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley. Fully gluten free and you would not guess it from the flaky morning buns and focaccia flying off the shelf. Tucked in the Lumber Yard plaza, it's Marin's answer for anyone who thought good pastry was off the table. Get there before the scones vanish. @flourcraft

Mill Valley Market — 12 Corte Madera Avenue, Mill Valley. Family run since 1929 and still the last true neighborhood grocer in town, with a deli counter locals will happily line up for. Build a picnic here, carry it two blocks to the square, and eat like you live here. The sandwich order form is a local secret. @millvalleymarket

Piazza D'Angelo — 22 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley. Southern Italian named for the piazza it sits on, family owned, with wood-fired pizzas and a house tiramisu people plan around. The bar is where the regulars land and the bartender knows them all. Book ahead on weekends or wait it out with a negroni. @piazzadangelo

Bungalow 44 — 44 East Blithedale Avenue, Mill Valley. Modern American cooking that's anchored downtown dinner since 2005, from the chili-honey fried chicken to a properly stirred martini at the bar. Fireside tables in winter, patio under the lights in summer. The Kobe burger has a quiet cult following. @bungalow44

Sweetwater Music Hall — 19 Corte Madera Avenue, Mill Valley. A local institution since 1972 where you might catch a national act one night and a hometown songwriter the next, all ages, with a full kitchen so dinner and the show share one room. Check the calendar, then walk over early for a table. @sweetwatermusichall

Throckmorton Theatre — 142 Throckmorton Avenue, Mill Valley. The town's performing arts anchor, running Tuesday night comedy, noon concerts, gallery shows, and the DjangoFest gypsy jazz weekend every fall. It's the kind of stage a small town has no business having, and somehow does. Grab seats before they go. @throckmortontheatre

Seven for a car-free day downtown: Equator, Flour Craft, Mill Valley Market, Piazza D'Angelo, Bungalow 44, Sweetwater, Throckmorton Theatre. Which one anchors your Mill Valley afternoon?

item.title: San Francisco Downtown San Rafael, Fourth Street
item.description: Eight reasons Downtown San Rafael runs on Fourth Street, the most walkable stretch in Marin. Locals treat this corridor as the heart of the county seat: co
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Downtown San Rafael, Fourth Street

Eight reasons Downtown San Rafael runs on Fourth Street, the most walkable stretch in Marin. Locals treat this corridor as the heart of the county seat: coffee roasted since 1935, a historic movie palace, and dinners worth the drive. Here's the honest walk, storefront by storefront, no tourist filler.

Sol Food — 903 Lincoln Ave, San Rafael. The Puerto Rican spot that put this downtown on the map, and yes, the line out the door moves faster than it looks. Order the garlicky pollo al horno, grab a jibarito, and plan to leave humming. A Marin classic that earned its crowd. @solfoodca

Il Davide — 901 A Street, San Rafael. An established Italian room feeding Marin since 1995, one block off Fourth and worth the half-block detour. The truffle ravioli has a quiet cult following, and the patio on a cool evening is the move. Book ahead on weekends, the locals do. @ildavidesanrafaelca

Lotus Cuisine of India — 812 Fourth Street, San Rafael. Organic-leaning Indian that leans harder into fresh than most, from clay-pit naan to a chicken tikka masala regulars order on repeat. Vegans and gluten-free folks get a real menu here, not an afterthought. A downtown anchor for a reason. @lotuscuisineofindia

Aroma Cafe — 1122 Fourth Street, San Rafael. Mediterranean fusion that's held down this block since 2002, pouring Graffeo espresso from up the street. Soups and dressings are made in house, the salads show up fresh daily, and there's beer and wine if lunch runs long. A dependable walkable stop mid-corridor. @aromacafesanrafael

Christopher B — Smith Rafael Film Center. 1118 Fourth Street, San Rafael. The historic movie palace that anchors downtown, restored and running as Marin's arthouse home for the Mill Valley Film Festival. Catch a foreign gem or a screening-and-conversation night under that lit-up neon tower. The blade sign alone is worth the walk. @cafilm

Graffeo Coffee Roastery — 1314 Fourth Street, San Rafael. One of North America's oldest artisan roasters, family-run since 1935, and yes, those are the beans served at big-name hotels. One dark, one light, one decaf, no gimmicks. Grab a pound whole-bean and you've got the local barista secret. @graffeocoffee

Johnny Doughnuts — 1617 Fourth Street, San Rafael. The Marin original, handcrafting doughnuts from a 1920s potato-dough recipe since the food-truck days. The apple fritter is a downtown institution, the crodough sells out, and the Johnny Joe coffee holds its own. Open daily at 7am, so beat the after-school rush. @johnnydoughnuts

Pond Farm Brewing Co — 1848 Fourth Street, San Rafael. A husband-and-wife brewpub at the walkable west end, with award-winning beer brewed on site, wine and cider for the non-beer crowd, and a real kitchen. Live music Saturdays, trivia Mondays, big airy taproom. The neighborhood living room that happens to make great beer. @pondfarmbrewing

Eight for a Fourth Street afternoon: Sol Food, Il Davide, Lotus Cuisine, Aroma Cafe, the Rafael Film Center, Graffeo, Johnny Doughnuts, and Pond Farm. Roaster, arthouse, brewpub, and three cuisines inside a few walkable blocks. Where do you start?

item.title: San Francisco Soul Food and Southern
item.description: Eight San Francisco soul food, Southern, and Creole kitchens still cooking the real thing, from a Richmond mainstay that opened in 1999 to a Bayview chef c
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Soul Food and Southern

Eight San Francisco soul food, Southern, and Creole kitchens still cooking the real thing, from a Richmond mainstay that opened in 1999 to a Bayview chef chasing a national gumbo. Everybody names the same couple of spots and misses the rest. Here they are, in the order you should eat your way through them.

Brenda's French Soul Food — 652 Polk Street, San Francisco. New Orleans by way of the Tenderloin, and the line out front is doing you a favor by buying you time to choose between the crawfish beignets and the shrimp grits. Get both. Open till 8, and it closes early on Tuesdays. @brendasfrenchsf

Brenda's Meat & Three — 919 Divisadero Street, San Francisco. The bigger sister on Divisadero runs on a Southern diner rule: one meat, three sides, and a long argument with yourself over which three. The heated back patio lets you linger from breakfast into supper. @brendasmeatandthree

Hard Knox Cafe — 2448 Clement Street, San Francisco. Chef Tony Hua opened the first Hard Knox in 1999, and the fried chicken and catfish still land piled past the edge of the plate. Bring an appetite you can be honest about and plan on a box to go. @hardknoxcafe

The Front Porch — 65 29th Street, San Francisco. On the Bernal and Mission line since 2006, this is the fried chicken and waffles you rearrange a night around, with beignets that show up under a snowdrift of powdered sugar and a tart raspberry dip. Dinner most nights, weekend brunch, and a room that fills the minute the doors swing open. @thefrontporchsf

Po'Boys Kitchen — 317 Connecticut Street, San Francisco. A Potrero Hill counter turning out Cajun-Creole plates, jambalaya, and dressed po'boys with a Bay Area lean. Small room, loud flavors, so call ahead if you want catering trays for the office. @poboyskitchen

Gumbo Social — 5176 3rd Street, San Francisco. Chef Dontaye Ball learned his roux from his grandmother, the one he calls The Big G, and now he wants gumbo named America's national dish from a corner of Bayview. Go Wednesday through Saturday and get the bowl with sausage. @gumbosocial

Old Skool Cafe — 1429 Mendell Street, San Francisco. A youth-run, jazz-themed supper club in Bayview where young people cook and serve international soul food while a live band plays nightly. Book a Wednesday through Saturday dinner and stay for the set. @oldskoolcafe

Peaches Patties — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. Chef Shani Jones bakes the flaky Jamaican patty the city did not know it was missing, packed with curried beef or callaloo, with jerk plates and rice and peas alongside. Grab one at the Ferry Building kiosk facing the water and eat it out on the pier. @peachespatties

Eight for soul food across San Francisco: Brenda's French Soul Food, Brenda's Meat & Three, Hard Knox, The Front Porch, Po'Boys Kitchen, Gumbo Social, Old Skool Cafe, and Peaches Patties. Which bowl, plate, or patty gets your Sunday first?

item.title: San Francisco Gastropubs
item.description: Eight San Francisco gastropubs where the beer list runs as deep as the dinner menu and nobody makes you pick one. From the Haight to North Beach to SoMa, t
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Gastropubs

Eight San Francisco gastropubs where the beer list runs as deep as the dinner menu and nobody makes you pick one. From the Haight to North Beach to SoMa, this is where locals land when the fog rolls in and a good burger and a proper pour both sound right.

The Alembic — 1725 Haight St, San Francisco. Upstairs from the Haight Street chaos, this narrow room pours a whiskey list longer than most lease agreements and plates small bites that punch well above dive-bar weight. The duck confit and a barrel-aged cocktail is the move. Grab a stool at the tin-topped bar before the after-work crowd claims them. @alembicsf

Magnolia Brewing — 1398 Haight St, San Francisco. The neighborhood brewpub came back from the dead in 2024, and the basement tanks are pouring Kalifornia Kolsch and Proving Ground IPA again like nothing happened. House beer, a burger built for two hands, cocktails now too. Corner of Haight and Masonic, kitchen open til 10. Post up. @magnoliahaight

Comstock Saloon — 155 Columbus Ave, San Francisco. The last standing bar of the Barbary Coast, all 1907 mahogany and pressed tin, where the bartenders take their classics as seriously as the kitchen takes its oysters Kirkpatrick. Come for a Martinez and stay for the pork chop. Aim for the back booths, the front fills fast at happy hour. @comstocksaloon

Bartlett Hall — 242 O'Farrell St, San Francisco. A block off Union Square, this cavernous brick brewhouse makes its own beer and pours barrel-aged cocktails, a small miracle in a neighborhood built for tourists and overpriced hotel bars. The wings and a house lager after a day downtown earn their keep. Big groups fit easy, so bring the crew. @bartletthallsf

The Sycamore — 2140 Mission St, San Francisco. Push through to the hidden back patio and you will forget you are on Mission Street at all. Rotating craft drafts, a kitchen slinging solid burgers and vegan plates, trivia Mondays and bingo Wednesdays for the regulars. It is the kind of low-key corner every neighborhood hopes it lands. Go on a sunny afternoon. @sycamorebeer

Southern Pacific Brewing — 620 Treat Ave, San Francisco. A cathedral-sized Mission warehouse with a mezzanine, a dog-friendly patio, house pilsners and IPAs, and a kitchen leaning Cajun. This is your spot when a party of ten needs beer, burgers, and room to breathe, which the Mission rarely offers. Claim the patio before the sun drops. @southernpacificbrewing

The Willows — 1582 Folsom St, San Francisco. A SoMa gastropub with a craft-beer room, a full bar, board games, and a pinball machine or two for when the conversation lags. The kitchen holds its own past midnight, a rare thing in this city. Rotating drafts, cozy back corners, open til 2 most nights. Land here when dinner runs late. @thewillowssf

The Pig and Whistle — 2801 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A proper British pub on Geary since 1991, pouring ales from around the world with fish and chips, bangers and mash, and shepherd's pie that tastes like it has nothing to prove. Trivia Wednesdays and Sundays, three-dollar happy-hour pints, dartboard in the back. Duck in out of the Richmond fog. @pigwhistlesf

Eight for when you want the pint and the plate to matter equally: Alembic, Magnolia, Comstock, Bartlett Hall, Sycamore, Southern Pacific, Willows, and Pig and Whistle. Which SF neighborhood still hides your favorite beer-and-a-real-meal spot?

item.title: San Francisco Poke Bowls
item.description: Eight San Francisco poke counters worth the walk-up line, ranked by how fast the fish disappears. Where locals go when the sushi bar wants forty bucks and
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Poke Bowls

Eight San Francisco poke counters worth the walk-up line, ranked by how fast the fish disappears. Where locals go when the sushi bar wants forty bucks and an hour.

Poke Origin — 716 Irving St, San Francisco. The Inner Sunset workhorse near Golden Gate Park, where the line moves fast and the mix-ins stay generous. You point, they build, you leave full for under fifteen bucks. Grab a bowl before you walk the park, not after, when everything good is gone. @thepokeorigin

Fish In The Box — 800 Masonic Ave, San Francisco. This tiny Panhandle spot treats poke like a sashimi counter, bluefin toro and Hokkaido scallop over rice instead of the usual scoop-and-sauce. They close midday to reset, so time it or stand outside reading the hours like the rest of us. Worth the trip up Masonic. @fishinthebox_sf

Happy Poke — 2760 Octavia St, San Francisco. A pocket-sized Cow Hollow counter where you fill out a little clipboard menu and they cut the fish silky, sashimi style. Snag one of the few outdoor tables near Union Street or eat it walking, nobody judges. Closed Mondays, so plan the craving around it. @happypokesf

I'a Poke — 314 Church St, San Francisco. The Mission Dolores standby for a fat sushi burrito or a build-your-own bowl, right where the J-Church spits you out. Counter service, quick turnover, the kind of lunch you eat on the Dolores Park grass ten minutes later. Go before the weekend crowd claims the whole hillside. @iapokesf

Poke Delish — 601 Mission Bay Blvd North, San Francisco. A poke stall parked inside Spark Social, the Mission Bay food yard with fire pits and picnic benches. Traditional Hawaiian bowls with a California hand on the sauce, best eaten out back while somebody's dog steals attention. Closes at five on Sundays, so it's a lunch play. @pokedelish

Poke Bowl — 1250 Ocean Ave, San Francisco. The Ingleside neighborhood pick, a mark-the-sheet build-your-own that stays open till nine thirty when everything else near City College has folded for the night. No frills, big portions, the reliable one when you're out past the tourist map. Parking is easy out here, a small SF miracle. @thepokebowls

Da Poke Man — 24 Willie Mays Plaza, San Francisco. Hawaiian poke slinging out of a truck by Oracle Park, and yes, they set up inside near section 112 on Giants home games. Catch it on a non-game day when the line isn't a hundred orange jerseys deep. Fresh, generous, and cheaper than a ballpark hot dog by a mile. @da_poke_man

Bimi Poke — 135 4th St, San Francisco. Tucked in the Metreon by the AMC, a Hawaiian-Japanese counter doing poke bowls and sushi burritos for the pre-movie crowd. Downtown lunch that won't wreck the afternoon, order the burrito if you want to eat one-handed in a dark theater. Open late enough for the last showtime. @maywen1985

Eight for the poke crawl: Poke Origin and Poke Bowl for fast neighborhood scoops, Fish In The Box and Happy Poke for sashimi-grade cuts, I'a Poke and Poke Delish for the bowl-plus-burrito crowd, Da Poke Man and Bimi Poke for eating on the move. Which SF neighborhood gets your line next?

item.title: San Francisco Indonesian and Malaysian
item.description: Eight San Francisco spots for Indonesian and Malaysian food, a category the city keeps quiet about. Rendang, laksa, sambal, kaya toast, all inside city lim
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Indonesian and Malaysian

Eight San Francisco spots for Indonesian and Malaysian food, a category the city keeps quiet about. Rendang, laksa, sambal, kaya toast, all inside city limits, no bridge toll required. If you figured SF topped out at pho and dim sum, these are the ones worth crossing town for.

Fikscue — 7 Warriors Way, San Francisco. Indonesian spice meets Texas smoke at Thrive City, the rare brisket that tastes of sambal and lemongrass. It made the New York Times best list, then kept the line moving on Warriors nights. Go early on a game day or the good cuts sell out before tip off. @fikscue

Nusa — 3450 Third Street, San Francisco. A Bayview kitchen turning out rendang and nasi campur the way a grandmother in Java would nod at. Chef Jennifer Huang grew up on these flavors and it shows in the depth of every sauce. Catch the Saturday stand at the Ferry Building if Third Street is a trek. @nusa.sf

Rasa Rasa Kitchen — 2200 Bryant Street, San Francisco. The Mission spot known as R2K plates gado gado in a crispy tortilla bowl, which sounds like a gimmick until the peanut sauce wins you over. Beef rendang and soto round out a short, confident menu. Weeknights are calmer if you want a table without the wait. @sf.rasarasakitchen

Warung Nasi Indonesia — 1200 Market Street, San Francisco. A Mid Market counter doing homestyle Indonesian, the kind of nasi and sambal that regulars order without glancing at the menu. Portions lean generous and the heat is honest, so ask where you land before they ladle. Lunch is the sweet spot. @warungnasi.indonesia

Lime Tree Southeast Asian Kitchen — 836 Clement Street, San Francisco. A Richmond mainstay blurring the line between Malaysian, Singaporean, and Indonesian, with a roti canai that has quieted many a debate about who does it best. There is a second kitchen on Irving if the avenues are your side of town. Closed Mondays, plan around it. @limetreekitchensf

Penang Garden — 728 Washington Street, San Francisco. Tucked into Chinatown, a Malaysian and Singaporean menu that surprises anyone expecting another Cantonese room. Order the Hainan chicken or the char kway teow and settle in. It has cooked quietly through decades of the block turning over around it.

M&Y Malaysian Food — 1661 Tennessee Street, San Francisco. A tiny Dogpatch operation built around laksa, wraps, and bowls that travel well if the shipyard fog chases you back to your desk. Bold, colorful plates, portions that earn the trip out here. Weekdays open at noon when the neighborhood is hunting lunch.

Kopiku Indonesian Coffee — 1443 Lombard Street, San Francisco. The city's first Indonesian coffee bar, pulling shots from small Sumatran and Javanese farms and pairing them with kaya toast. Pandan lattes and a pour over worth slowing down for, tucked on a Marina stretch built for drive by. Seating is tight, so time it off peak. @kopikusf

Eight for the Southeast Asian corner SF forgets it has: Fikscue for smoke, Nusa and Rasa Rasa for rendang done right, Warung Nasi for the homestyle plate, Lime Tree for roti, Penang Garden for the Chinatown surprise, M&Y for laksa, Kopiku for the kaya toast finish. Which one are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Vegan and Vegetarian
item.description: Eight San Francisco vegan and vegetarian spots that turn skeptics into regulars. The city has been cooking meatless since Greens opened at Fort Mason in 19
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Vegan and Vegetarian

Eight San Francisco vegan and vegetarian spots that turn skeptics into regulars. The city has been cooking meatless since Greens opened at Fort Mason in 1979, and the range now runs from Buddhist temple food to vegan barbecue. Bring the friend who insists they need meat on the plate and watch them go quiet halfway through.

Greens — 2 Marina Blvd, San Francisco. The one that started it all, tucked into a Fort Mason warehouse with the Golden Gate framed in the windows like a postcard nobody staged. Order the mesquite grilled brochettes and grab a window table before the sunset crowd claims them. Weekend brunch is the quiet secret. @greensrestaurant

Shizen — 370 14th Street, San Francisco. Vegan sushi that sounds like a dare and eats like a revelation, ten years deep in the Mission and still packed. The rolls lean on marinated tomato and eggplant where the fish would be, and you stop missing it by the second piece. Go early or brace for the wait. @shizensf

Wildseed — 2000 Union Street, San Francisco. Cow Hollow's airy plant based hangout where the patio does most of the talking on a sunny afternoon. The menu wanders the Mediterranean, the wine list is all vegan, and the crowd skews date night. Split the flatbreads and a carafe, thank yourself later. @wildseedsf

Golden Era — 395 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco. A Tenderloin fixture serving Asian comfort food that happens to be entirely vegan, no announcement necessary. The mock meats have converted more carnivores than any pamphlet ever could, and the portions forgive a big appetite. Get the Dragon Phoenix. @goldenerasf

Cha-Ya — 762 Valencia Street, San Francisco. Family run Japanese vegetarian cooking rooted in Buddhist shojin tradition, small room, big flavors, gentle prices. The tempura and the agedashi tofu arrive quiet and confident, the kind of meal that makes vegetables feel like the whole point. Come hungry, leave calm. @chayasanfrancisco

Vegan Mob — 90 Charter Oak Avenue, San Francisco. Toriano Gordon's plant based barbecue landed in the Bayview and the rib tips have a waitlist for a reason. Brisket burritos, garlic noodles, smoked everything, all vegan, none of it apologizing. Bring napkins and low expectations for leftovers. @officialveganmob

Aiso — 4068 18th Street, San Francisco. The Castro newcomer plating vegan tapas that look like they wandered off a fine dining tasting menu. Small sharing plates, a proper cocktail list, and a room that hums on weekends without shouting. Book ahead, order wide, let the table graze. @welcometoaiso

Om Sabor — 370 Grove Street, San Francisco. Cosmic vegan comfort food tucked inside Phonobar in Hayes Valley, hopping across Mexican, Korean, Indian and Venezuelan in one sitting. It started as a pop up and earned a home. That tells you plenty. Pregame the symphony here and skip the tourist traps. @omsabor

Eight for meatless done right: Greens for the view, Shizen for the sushi, Wildseed for the patio, Golden Era for the converts, Cha-Ya for the calm, Vegan Mob for the smoke, Aiso for the date, Om Sabor for the road trip on a plate. Which one wins your Friday?

I'm an East Bay agent who eats all over the Bay Area. When you want the East Bay version of any of this, Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Joaquin counties are my home turf.

item.title: San Francisco Persian and Middle Eastern
item.description: Eight San Francisco spots for Persian and Middle Eastern food, one for each night you swear you'll cook and then don't. From North Beach kababs to a Lower
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Persian and Middle Eastern

Eight San Francisco spots for Persian and Middle Eastern food, one for each night you swear you'll cook and then don't. From North Beach kababs to a Lower Haight falafel shaped like a donut, this is the SF crawl worth the parking karma. Save it before your next hummus craving hits.

Maykadeh — 470 Green St, San Francisco. A North Beach fixture since 1983, back when the neighborhood was all red sauce and this was the lone saffron in the room. Come for the lamb, the koobideh off the open flame, and a dining room that still feels like a special occasion. @maykadehrestaurantsf

Lavash — 511 Irving St, San Francisco. Family run in the Inner Sunset, closed Mondays and worth planning your week around. The tahdig comes out crackly and golden, the stews taste like someone's grandmother is checking your plate, and the wine list is built to love Persian food back. @lavashsf

Reem's California — 2901 Mission St, San Francisco. Named for the man'oushe, the Arab flatbread that comes out of the oven blistered and folded warm into your hands. Reem Assil built this Mission bakery as a love letter to Arab street food and California mornings. Order the za'atar, then a second one for the walk. @reemscalifornia

Beit Rima — 138 Church St, San Francisco. Arabic comfort food near Duboce Triangle, the kind of place that turned a whole city onto garlicky chicken and crispy cauliflower. The mujadara is quiet and perfect, the vibe is loud and happy, and the wait is a rite of passage. @beitrima

La Mediterranee — 2210 Fillmore St, San Francisco. Pacific Heights has changed a hundred times since 1979 and this little cafe has not, thank goodness. The chicken pomegranate and the meat cigars run on secret Armenian and Lebanese family recipes. Grab a sidewalk table and watch Fillmore go by. @lamedfillmore

Z Zoul Cafe — 295 Eddy St, San Francisco. The only Sudanese kitchen in the Bay, tucked into the Tenderloin and run like a family reunion. The Emperor Bowl and the shawarma are the move, the prices are a throwback, and the welcome is warmer than the block lets on. @zzoulcafesf

Aicha Moroccan Cuisine — 1303 Polk St, San Francisco. Lower Nob Hill Moroccan built on Fez region recipes, where the tagine arrives under a cone of steam and the couscous is a Friday tradition. Come hungry, stay for mint tea poured from a theatrical height, leave planning a trip to Marrakech.

Palmyra — 700 Haight St, San Francisco. A Lower Haight Syrian counter run by one family, named for an ancient desert city and famous for falafel shaped like a donut. The rotisserie chicken and the hummus with the good olive oil are why regulars keep the line moving. Big platters, small prices.

Eight San Francisco tables, from Persian saffron in North Beach to Syrian falafel in the Lower Haight. Maykadeh, Lavash, Reem's California, Beit Rima, La Mediterranee, Z Zoul, Aicha, Palmyra. Print it, pin it, and start crossing them off. Which SF neighborhood should the next food crawl hit?

item.content:encoded:
San Francisco's Excelsior, Mission Street

Eight stops down one stretch of Mission Street in San Francisco's Excelsior, where the cross streets are named Persia, Russia, Naples and Peru and the food follows suit. Most people ride BART past it to the fancier end of the Mission. Their loss. Silver to Geneva, no bridge required.

Excelsior Coffee — 4495 Mission St, San Francisco. Black and Brown owned, flying the flags of Barbados, the Philippines and Mexico over the espresso machine. Come for a cortado, leave with an ube brownie from Ube Area you did not plan on. The corner where the neighborhood wakes up. @excelsiorcoffeesf

Restaurante Familiar — 4499 Mission St, San Francisco. Salvadoran and Mexican under one roof, so the pupusas revueltas and the carne asada plate land on the same table. Cheese-crisped masa, a mound of curtido on top, horchata to wash it down. Family name, family portions.

Recovery Room — 4528 Mission St, San Francisco. A proper neighborhood bar with food, drinks and music all under one sign, open to 2am most nights. A kitchen collab with Hidden Spot EXL means you can eat well past when other kitchens quit. The Excelsior after dark, minus the pretense. @recoveryroomsf

Hong Kong Bakery — 4711 Mission St, San Francisco. A Cantonese buns counter where a dollar or two buys a warm cocktail bun or a BBQ pork bun still fogging its bag. Cash, quick, no frills, gone by mid afternoon on the good days. Regulars grab a pink box and keep walking.

Calabria Bros — 4763 Mission St, San Francisco. The Excelsior still has an old-school Italian deli, and this is it, subs from around 8 dollars on Mission between Russia and Persia. House vinegar and a garlic spread the regulars order extra of. One sandwich feeds you twice if you have any restraint. @calabriabros

El Farolito — 4817 Mission St, San Francisco. The Excelsior outpost of the taqueria that made the Mission-style burrito famous, and the line still moves fast. Super burrito about the length of a forearm, al pastor under ten bucks, salsa bar doing half the work. Cash only, ATM inside. @taquerias_elfarolito

Superstar Restaurant — 4919 Mission St, San Francisco. A Filipino silog counter where 5 to 8 dollars gets you longsilog or tosilog, garlic rice and a fried egg included. Cash only, closed Wednesdays and Sundays, so time it right. The kind of cheap, filling plate the Excelsior runs on.

Mission Comics and Art — 5196 Mission St, San Francisco. The longtime Mission comic shop opened a second store here in 2026, a block past Geneva in a former optometry office, likely the first comic shop the Excelsior has ever had. New releases, back issues and a reason to end the walk indoors. @missioncomics

Eight down Mission Street in the Excelsior: Excelsior Coffee, Restaurante Familiar, Recovery Room, Hong Kong Bakery, Calabria Bros, El Farolito, Superstar, and Mission Comics. Silver to Geneva, no bridge, no BART transfer. Which corner do you start on?

I'm an East Bay agent who eats all over the Bay Area. When you want the East Bay version of any of this, Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Joaquin counties are my home turf.
